full_text: Generating useful robot-training data requires more than visually plausible scenes: objects must support interaction, placements must remain physically valid, and tasks must admit repeatable execution. We present Awomo-SimDataEngine, an agentic system that connects asset and scene generation to robot demonstration synthesis. Shared asset services provide rigid and articulated objects, including structure-grounded part and joint generation with ISArt. Scene generation supports two complementary routes: Unravel reconstructs editable scenes from images, while SimForge builds single-room and multi-room environments from text. A graph-native harness coordinates construction, validation, and bounded repair, routing failures to the responsible module while retaining unaffected scene state. PolicyForge binds validated worlds to tasks and robot embodiments to produce replayable demonstrations. Evaluations cover asset geometry, scene quality, and downstream policy learning. On MuJoCo-based LIBERO-Plus, co-training with Isaac Sim demonstrations improves the overall success rate of a World-Action Model (WAM) from to . Goal and spatial success improve by and percentage points, respectively. These results support the utility of the generated data for cross-simulator policy training, with more limited gains on long-horizon tasks. Introduction sec:intro Robot learning depends on demonstrations that cover varied objects, environments, and manipulation goals. Collecting such coverage in the real world is costly, while manually preparing each simulated environment limits the scale and diversity of synthetic data. Generative models offer a way to expand this training distribution, but their outputs must support interaction: a plausible image or textured mesh can still hide invalid collision geometry, inaccessible interiors, incorrect joints, unstable placements, or an unreplayable initial state. These defects affect both whether demonstrations can be collected and what policies learn from them. Recent progress spans image-conditioned 3D assets, agentic scene construction, and automated demonstration synthesis hunyuan3d22025tencent,sam3dteam2025sam3d3dfyimages,scenesmith,sage,mimicgen,simfoundry . Connecting these capabilities requires agreement on object identities, coordinate frames, physical representations, task requirements, and validation results. An asset replacement changes the geometry available for registration; a revised scene changes the reset and interaction conditions seen by a controller. An integrated system must preserve these dependencies and return failures to the stage that can resolve them. We introduce Awomo-SimDataEngine, an agentic system for constructing simulation-ready worlds and converting them into robot demonstrations. The system connects asset generation, scene generation, and demonstration synthesis through a Graph-Native Harness for execution and repair. Scene generation supports both visual references and language descriptions: Unravel reconstructs editable scenes from single-view images, whereas SimForge builds single-room and multi-room environments from text. Both routes use shared asset services and produce worlds that can be checked, edited, and bound to robot tasks. Figure~ fig:simforge-overview illustrates the shared execution framework and the image-driven route. From assets to interactive scenes. Scene construction begins with assets that are usable beyond rendering. The asset module combines retrieval and generation with common geometry, collision, and physical checks (Section~ sec:asset ). Articulated objects add a structural requirement: their parts and joints must describe an executable mechanism. ISArt addresses this through geometric--kinematic planning, structure-conditioned part generation, and articulation binding. The two scene-generation routes use these assets differently (Section~ sec:scene ). Unravel progressively removes objects from a reference image to expose occluded regions, then uses accumulated point-map evidence to register and reassemble independently editable assets. SimForge instead plans room geometry, object requirements, and spatial arrangements from language, supporting both individual rooms and multi-room houses. For both routes, plausible appearance alone does not establish valid support, collision geometry, or articulation. From validated worlds to demonstrations. Construction failures need not be repaired where they are detected. A missing asset calls for acquisition; an intersecting object calls for a placement change; an incorrect joint may require revising the articulated asset. The Graph-Native Harness (Section~ sec:harness ) makes these handoffs explicit through shared state, validation evidence, bounded retries, and checkpoints. It retains unaffected work and revalidates the dependencies of each edit before construction proceeds. PolicyForge then binds an accepted world to a task, robot embodiment, and reset specification (Section~ sec:policyforge ). Scripted or motion-planned teachers execute in Isaac Sim, producing synchronized images, proprioception, and actions; successful validated episodes are retained for training. Scene variants, object substitutions, and initial-state and language augmentation diversify the resulting data. World validity, demonstration success, and downstream policy performance remain distinct outcomes. Experimental evidence. Module evaluations support the geometry and reconstruction methods: ISArt achieves part-geometry CD versus for the combined TRELLIS.2 + P3-SAM + X-Part baseline on 60 objects, while Unravel improves blind human asset-fidelity scores from to on 160 objects. These protocols are detailed in Sections~ sec:isart and~ sec:unravel-evidence . Text-driven scene quality is evaluated separately on 179 room prompts and 31 multi-room prompts using the SceneEval and SceneSmith protocols (Section~ sec:simforge-text ). These evaluations test complementary properties rather than a single pooled quality score. On the MuJoCo-based LIBERO-Plus benchmark, SimData-Ultra co-training increases World-Action Model success from to when comparing each configuration's best evaluated checkpoint up to and including 13K steps, selected by overall success, with gains of and percentage points in goal and spatial generalization (Section~ sec:experiments ). These results support the training utility of the combined data-generation system across simulator boundaries; they do not isolate each generator or augmentation's contribution. The smaller long-horizon gain motivates richer sequential task supervision. This report makes four contributions: Simulation-ready asset generation, including ISArt's structure-grounded articulated-object pipeline and shared candidate validation, canonicalization, collision construction, and physical augmentation. Complementary scene-generation routes: image-driven reconstruction with Unravel and text-driven single-room and multi-room construction with SimForge. Integrated execution and demonstration synthesis: a Graph-Native Harness coordinates attributed repair and acceptance, while PolicyForge generates replayable demonstrations across scenes, tasks, and robot embodiments. Cross-simulator policy-learning evidence, showing a -point overall gain on LIBERO-Plus at the best evaluated checkpoints within a 13K-step budget, with the largest improvement in goal generalization. Related Work sec:related Awomo-SimDataEngine connects interactive asset generation, text- and image-driven scene construction, agentic execution, and demonstration synthesis. We position these components against the corresponding literature and distinguish world-construction capabilities from downstream policy measurements. 3D assets and interactive environments sec:related-simulation Hunyuan3D, TRELLIS, and SAM 3D generate geometry and appearance from visual conditions hunyuan3d22025tencent,lai2025hunyuan3d25highfidelity3d,xiang2024structured,sam3dteam2025sam3d3dfyimages . Their outputs supply candidate assets for Awomo-SimDataEngine, which additionally checks canonical orientation, measured extents, collision compatibility, and physical attributes before simulator use. For articulated objects, Section~ sec:asset introduces ISArt: structural planning conditions part generation, and agentic binding and motion verification connect the parts to an executable kinematic representation. PartCrafter and OmniPart address part-level geometry generation, while Articulate AnyMesh, Articulate-Anything, and SPARK estimate or reconstruct articulated representations isart_partcrafter,isart_omnipart,isart_articulateanymesh,isart_articulatea,isart_spark . ISArt connects explicit structural planning to a learned multi-part generator and then refines articulation through simulation feedback. Its fixed-geometry binding comparison separates joint estimation from the quality of generated meshes; the part-generation comparison evaluates the latter independently. HSSD-200, RoboCasa, and BEHAVIOR-1K provide reusable assets, scenes, or household interaction settings hssd200,robocasa,behavior1k . They motivate the interaction requirements that generated assets must satisfy. Awomo-SimDataEngine exposes retrieval and generation through a common asset lifecycle, preserving source provenance separately from instance poses, articulation states, and simulator-specific packaging. Scene synthesis and single-view construction sec:related-layout ATISS and DiffuScene learn distributions over indoor object arrangements; InstructScene, LayoutGPT, and PhyScene incorporate instructions, structured relations, or physical constraints atiss,diffuscene,instructscene,layoutgpt,physcene . These approaches provide useful priors for scene composition. Awomo-SimDataEngine's image-driven path follows Unravel (Section~ sec:scene ), using object removal to expose occluded regions and fixed-camera point evidence to guide reconstruction and recomposition. Its execution graph records stage dependencies; removal order provides local occlusion evidence rather than a global support or depth order. sec:related-multimodal Text2Room, GraphDreamer, DreamScene, AnyHome, WonderWorld, and MIDI explore text-, graph-, or image-conditioned 3D scene construction text2room,graphdreamer,dreamscene,anyhome,wonderworld,huang2024midi . Awomo-SimDataEngine uses SimForge for text-driven single-room and multi-room construction, and Unravel for single-image reconstruction. The latter retains object identities, masks, point provenance, and registration evidence. Settling and visual audit check the recomposed scene before packaging. This image-driven route does not imply multi-view reconstruction or uniquely recoverable metric geometry from an unconstrained image. Agentic generation and execution harnesses sec:related-agents ReAct, Reflexion, Tree of Thoughts, and Graph of Thoughts make tool use, feedback, or structured reasoning explicit react,reflexion,treeofthoughts,graphofthoughts . Holodeck, SceneCraft, SceneWeaver, SceneSmith, SAGE, and SceneCode connect language-model reasoning to 3D scene tools or executable representations holodeck,scenecraft,sceneweaver,scenesmith,sage,scenecode . Awomo-SimDataEngine coordinates specialized modules through the execution contract in Section~ sec:harness . Each repair records typed state, evidence, the responsible module, affected workset, remaining budget, and checkpoint decision. The contract spans ISArt articulation refinement, Unravel editing and reconstruction, and world-owned PolicyForge feedback. Preserved state is reused only when its input dependencies remain valid. These mechanisms support recovery within a run; the policy experiments do not independently establish harness efficiency or learning in the orchestrator. title: World-Calibrated Proposal-to-Action Flow for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies generate action chunks by transporting samples from a task-agnostic isotropic Gaussian source. As this source is conditioned on neither recent execution nor predicted future evolution, (i) it discards the local continuity established by recently executed motion. (ii) Even when predictive world representations are introduced, they often only condition the transport dynamics rather than determine where generation starts, how far it may deviate, or along which action directions it may expand. Building on this observation, we introduce ProAct, a world-calibrated proposal-to-action framework that makes the generative source itself predictable. (i) To preserve motion continuity, a lightweight Proposal Expert converts recent actions into a scene-aware hypothesis via one motion-anchored endpoint flow-matching step, initializing generation near the demonstrated action manifold. (ii) To jointly capture intended scene evolution and proposal-future compatibility, a prospective World Expert treats the hypothesis as a soft motion prior while predicting the task-consistent latent future. (iii) From this compatibility, the model calibrates a proposal-centered anisotropic source, where a bounded per-step extent controls the allowed deviation and a trace-normalized low-rank geometry under a condition-number budget allocates refinement over coupled translation, rotation, and gripper directions. Compared with $π_{0.5}$, ProAct improves performance across simulation and real-world tasks while reducing denoising steps by 50%, inference latency by up to 25.8%, and increasing throughput by up to 34.8%.

As this source is conditioned on neither recent execution nor predicted future evolution, it discards the local continuity established by recently executed motion. Even when predictive world representations are introduced, they often only condition the transport dynamics rather than determine where generation starts, how far it may deviate, or along which action directions it may expand. Building on this observation, we introduce , a world-calibrated proposal-to-action framework that makes the generative source itself predictable. To jointly capture intended scene evolution and proposal--future compatibility, a prospective World Expert treats the hypothesis as a soft motion prior while predicting the task-consistent latent future. From this compatibility, the model calibrates a proposal-centered anisotropic source, where a bounded per-step extent controls the allowed deviation and a trace-normalized low-rank geometry under a condition-number budget allocates refinement over coupled translation, rotation, and gripper directions. Compared with , improves performance across simulation and real-world tasks while reducing denoising steps by 50 , inference latency by up to 25.8 , and increasing throughput by up to 34.8 . Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models~ pi0, bjorck2025gr00t, li2026causal, luo2026being, shao2025large increasingly use diffusion~ chi2025diffusion or flow matching~ lipman2022flow to generate continuous robot actions, building on broader progress in fine-grained multimodal understanding and visual grounding~ peng2026finegrained, shao2024detecting, shao2023detecting, shao2019multi . However, these generative decoders typically initialize each action chunk from a generic source distribution~ pi05, zheng2026x , forcing the policy to repeatedly transport uninformed samples toward executable trajectories, as illustrated in the upper panel of Fig.~ fig:intro . Such a generic source ignores readily available context that could inform where action generation should begin. By making the source distribution itself contextually predictable, action generation can begin from a more informed region of the action space, yielding a policy that is both more accurate and substantially cheaper to sample during closed-loop policy execution. A generic isotropic source leaves two useful sources of information unexploited. The first is . Although task-level behavior can be highly multimodal, physical motion often exhibits strong local regularity over short horizons, and recently executed, reliable actions are already available during closed-loop control~ black2026real, wang2026real . A naive strategy is to extrapolate this motion and reuse it for the next action chunk~ jia2026action, zhan2026seam . Yet such continuation becomes unreliable around contact, reorientation, gripper actuation, or task-phase transitions, where appropriate motion may deviate sharply from recent behavior~ yang2026chunkflow . Local continuity therefore indicates what is plausible from the recent past, but not necessarily what remains appropriate for the current scene and task. Recent motion should thus be treated as a proposal to be evaluated against the intended future, rather than as the action itself. The second is , which provides prospective evidence for calibrating such a proposal. Prospective world modeling~ zhao2025cot, zhang2025up, tian2025predictive, zhang2026dreamvla, li2026drivevla, zhu2026delta, li2026unimpa has increasingly been incorporated into VLA policies, but typically as auxiliary supervision or additional conditioning. In these formulations, prospective information helps predict what should happen next, but is not explicitly used to calibrate an existing action hypothesis according to whether it remains appropriate for the anticipated task evolution. The missing element is therefore an explicit interface between a candidate motion, prospective world reasoning, and generative refinement. We build this missing interface around a propose--calibrate--refine principle and instantiate it as , a World-Calibrated Proposal-to-Action Flow framework. first constructs a scene-aware motion hypothesis, then uses prospective world reasoning to estimate the correction required to realize the intended future, and finally converts this calibration into the source distribution for flow-based action generation, as illustrated in the lower panel of Fig.~ fig:intro . Specifically, a lightweight first converts recently executed actions into a scene-aware motion hypothesis. It extrapolates short-horizon motion and uses it to initialize the motion-anchored flow module, which grounds the proposal in the current VLM context through a single endpoint flow step. Rather than producing an executable action, this stage places generation near a plausible region of the demonstrated action manifold and provides a for subsequent reasoning. A prospective calibrates this proposal against the task-consistent future. The motion hypothesis is provided as contextual evidence for prospective reasoning, while the prediction target remains the demonstrated future encoded in the latent space of a frozen V-JEPA~2 encoder~ assran2025vjepa2 . Calibration readouts are further supervised by the residual between the demonstrated action and the proposal, forcing the shared world representation to encode both the task-consistent latent future and the proposal--future compatibility. The resulting calibration is finally expressed as a for action generation. A bounded per-step limits how far generation may deviate from the proposal, while trace-normalized low-rank determines along which coupled action directions that correction should occur. An Action Expert then transports samples from this calibrated source into executable action chunks using the base VLA's original flow parameterization. Thus, changes where and how action generation begins while preserving the flexibility to depart from the proposal when needed. Our primary contributions are summarized as follows: [leftmargin=1.2em] We formulate generative action prediction from a propose--calibrate--refine perspective, where recent motion provides a soft local hypothesis calibrated by task-consistent prospective reasoning, providing an interface between local motion continuity and future-aware action generation. We introduce an asymmetric proposal-aware World Expert that uses motion to assist future prediction while anchoring the desired future independently of proposal correctness, and jointly predicts proposal-specific refinement extent and geometry at every horizon step. We replace the isotropic Gaussian of flow-based VLAs with a world-calibrated, proposal-centered source while leaving their transport parameterization unchanged. We validate across extensive simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, where it consistently outperforms strong baselines while reducing denoising steps by up to 50 , demonstrating both superior effectiveness and inference efficiency. sec:method As shown in Fig.~ fig:framework , follows a propose--calibrate--refine pipeline. A grounds recent motion into a scene-aware hypothesis, a prospective models latent future and proposal--future compatibility, and an transports the calibrated source into executable actions. This calibration determines where refinement starts, how far it may travel, and along which coupled directions it should proceed at each horizon step. title: SCION: Scene Composition with Instanced Neural Primitives
summary: Real-world scenes are compositional: bricks, blades of grass, pebbles, and tree leaves recur across human-built and natural environments. Existing neural scene representations model these elements independently. Most 3D Gaussian Splatting and follow-up abstraction and compression methods treat each element as unique, fitting millions of independent Gaussians per scene. Prior methods like Splat and Replace fit template objects, but they require mostly manual selection of repeated elements. As a result, these representations store redundant parameters and provide weak manipulation handles for downstream tasks. We introduce SCION, a hier- archical compositional scene representation that replaces independent Gaussians with a compact vocabulary of reusable primitives and lightweight world-space instances that place transformed copies throughout the scene. We fit this represen- tation to multi-view captures via a joint optimization over discrete and continuous scene parameters, combining two-level densification over splats and instances with an adversarial loss that preserves detail across shared primitives. The recovered structure yields a compact, controllable representation while maintaining high quality even at 1.2 MB. SCION achieves rate-distortion favorable to existing Gaussian compression methods, and it enables instance-level scene editing and animation without retraining. Our results show that neural scene representations need not memorize scenes as independent primitives; they can discover reusable parts. Project webpage: https://light.princeton.edu/SCION
full_text: Real-world scenes are compositional: bricks, blades of grass, pebbles, and tree leaves recur across human-built and natural environments. Existing neural scene representations model these elements independently. Most 3D Gaussian Splatting and follow-up abstraction and compression methods treat each element as unique, fitting millions of independent Gaussians per scene. Prior methods like Splat and Replace fit template objects, but they require mostly manual selection of repeated elements. As a result, these representations store redundant parameters and provide weak manipulation handles for downstream tasks. We introduce , a hierarchical compositional scene representation that replaces independent Gaussians with a compact vocabulary of reusable and lightweight world-space that place transformed copies throughout the scene. We fit this representation to multi-view captures via a joint optimization over discrete and continuous scene parameters, combining two-level densification over and with an adversarial loss that preserves detail across shared . The recovered structure yields a compact, controllable representation while maintaining high quality even at 1.2 MB. achieves rate-distortion favorable to existing Gaussian compression methods, and it enables instance-level scene editing and animation without retraining. Our results show that neural scene representations need not memorize scenes as independent ; they can discover reusable parts. Project webpage: Introduction sec:introduction The natural and built world is full of repetition. A meadow is a few species of grass blade copied a million times; a brick wall is one brick under different poses; a forest canopy is a handful of leaf shapes scattered across branches. Traditionally, in computer graphics, we therefore do not manually handcraft every single leaf individually, but just a handful of templates which we then instantiate using a particle system or array~ Prusinkiewicz1990TheAB,stava2014inverse . This does more than save labor: the resulting scenes are much easier to animate, are faster to edit, and require significantly less memory. 3D reconstruction deals with the inverse problem: going from images to a 3D representation. Neural radiance fields and related neural graphics primitives shifted reconstruction toward photorealistic view synthesis~ mildenhallNeRFRepresentingScenes2020,mullerInstantNeuralGraphics2022 . However, because these scenes are represented as neural fields rather than physical structures, they are hard to integrate into graphics workflows. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl3DGaussianSplatting2023 in turn uses an explicit representation, which makes rendering and integration into other tools easier and more efficient. Yet 3DGS fits millions of independent Gaussians per scene, each carrying its own position, covariance, opacity, and color. The reconstructions are accurate but they are also large, and structureless: nothing in the representation tells us when the ten thousand covering a lawn are of the same few blades. Lack of structure limits the downstream usefulness of these scenes in two ways. First, it makes edits hard to express: an intuitive operation such as placing grass on a surface requires manually instantiating and tuning thousands of individual , instead of inserting a few reusable . Second, it makes animation hard: the user must deform an unstructured collection of Gaussians instead of transforming coherent objects. Semantic segmentation can isolate large objects, but it does not recover the fine-grained repeated structure of leaves, grass, or other repetitive elements. Recovering structure requires a representation that discovers repetition. Neural rendering has largely left this problem untouched. Prior codebook-style methods target compression~ takikawaVariableBitrateNeural2022,leeCompact3DGaussian2024,durvasulaContraGSCodebookCondensedTrainable2025 : they share parameters across distinct rather than building shared . They identify repetition in parameters, not in geometry. Explicit repetition has mostly appeared in analysis or exemplar pipelines. Regularity detection analyzes input point clouds or meshes to discover similarity-group repetitions, rather than reconstructing them from images~ paulyDiscoveringStructuralRegularity2008 . The closest 3DGS work in this area, Splat and Replace, starts from an already trained 3DGS scene and relies on human-guided instance selection~ violante2025splat . This makes it suitable for larger annotated objects, but difficult to scale to dense fine-grained repetitions. Identifying repetition creates two optimization challenges: choosing the unit of reuse, and tolerating variation across reused elements. A scene element can be represented as one of a large containing many , or as many of a smaller with fewer ; the latter uses parameters more efficiently and yields a more structured representation, but is harder to optimize. This is a minimum description length problem. At the same time, real of the same element are not identical, so direct pixel-wise sharing drives templates toward blurry averages and erases high-frequency detail. It also means that there is no optimal solution to our minimum description length problem. We introduce , which recovers a scene's decomposition end-to-end from multi-view captures ( ). represents a scene as a small library of reusable , each being a bundle of 3D Gaussians in a local frame, and a set of : lightweight world-space placements with pose , scale , opacity , and assignment . The representation scales primarily with the number of sparse lightweight instances rather than the number of or . This leads to better rate--distortion tradeoffs. The factorization into furthermore gives the scene direct editing and animation handles. Recovering this factorization is challenging: each aggregates gradients from all referencing , and averaged reconstruction losses (e.g., L1) drive templates toward blurry means, erasing high-frequency detail. We address this with -local birth and relocation, world-space pruning, cloning, and subdivision, together with an adversarial patch loss that preserves per-instance sharpness while still enabling shared structure. We make the following contributions in this work We introduce , a hierarchical representation learning method for compositional scene reconstruction that replaces independent Gaussians with a reusable vocabulary of and lightweight transformed . The resulting 3D scenes are compact, structured, and directly manipulable. We learn repetitions with new densification strategies for -local and world-space , and integrate them in a joint optimization procedure that preserves sharpness across aggregation. We demonstrate that the recovered structure has favorable rate--distortion tradeoffs over Gaussian compression methods at matched storage, while additionally enabling -level editing and animation without retraining. Related work sec:related lies at the intersection of neural rendering, repeated-structure discovery, and controllable scene representations. We review each of these areas: Prior compression methods largely preserve independent while encoding them more efficiently; pattern-recognition methods often recover repeated objects under stronger priors; and editing methods usually add controls on top of unstructured . In contrast, makes repetition part of the representation itself by learning shared geometric and lightweight assignments directly from multi-view images. Neural rendering compression. 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl3DGaussianSplatting2023 represents scenes with millions of independently parameterized anisotropic elements. Many variants improve this representation by modifying underlying geometry, optimization, or organization, e.g., surface-aligned disks or surfels~ huang20242d,Dai2024GaussianSurfels , mesh-attached Gaussians~ guedon2023sugar , hierarchical levels of detail~ hierarchicalgaussians24 , or sampling-based densification and pruning~ kheradmand3DGaussianSplatting2024,kimMetropolisHastingsSampling3D2025,durvasulaContraGSCodebookCondensedTrainable2025 . However, these methods largely preserve the per- parameterization. A large body of work compresses 3DGS by improving parameter encoding, entropy modeling, quantization, or predictive coding while keeping the underlying representation fixed~ luScaffoldgsStructured3d2024,chenHACHashgridAssisted2024,zhanCAT3DGSContextadaptiveTriplane2025,wangContextGSCompact3D2024,chenHAC100XCompression2025,liu3DGaussianSplatting2025,liuCompGSEfficient3D2024,xuLearningHierarchicalSparse2026,pcgs2025,liuFeedForward3DGaussian2025 . Other approaches modify the representation more directly through codebooks, residual quantization, distilled appearance, 2D projections, or alternative primitive elements such as textured surfels and billboards~ Niedermayr_2024_CVPR,leeCompact3DGaussian2024,leeOptimizedMinimal3D2025,fan2024lightgaussian,morgenstern2024compact,rongNexelsNeurallyTexturedSurfels2025,svitovBillBoardSplattingBBSplat2025 . Related compression ideas also appear in NeRFs, neural fields, point clouds, and 3D-aware generative models, where shared networks, grids, latent codebooks, or local decoders reduce storage~ mildenhallNeRFRepresentingScenes2020,mullerInstantNeuralGraphics2022,tangNeuralgsBridgingNeural2026,watanabeNeuralGaborSplatting2026,maPixelCodecAvatars2021,vandenoordNeuralDiscreteRepresentation2017,takikawaVariableBitrateNeural2022,youPatchBasedDeepAutoencoder2021,liCompressingVolumetricRadiance2023,schwarz2020graf,Niemeyer2020GIRAFFE . Across these methods, the atomic unit is still typically an independently stored , feature, or latent code. In contrast, reduces the number of independent parameters by sharing concrete geometric across many through a discrete vocabulary , improving compression while preserving perceived quality across scenes. Instance and pattern recognition. Recovering repeated structure has a long history, but most previous methods assume existing geometry, manual inputs, or strong structural priors. Classical regularity detection fits similarity-group lattices and representative elements to point clouds or meshes~ paulyDiscoveringStructuralRegularity2008 , while inverse procedural modeling fits authored grammars to curated exemplars such as polygonal tree scans~ stava2014inverse or pre-segmented part hierarchies~ liGRASSGenerativeRecursive2017 . Splat and Replace is closer to ours in using 3DGS, but starts from a trained scene and human-guided instance selection, then registers and fuses object-scale repeats post hoc~ violante2025splat . title: SocialVLA: A Social Perception Gateway for Human-Reaction-Based Failure Detection and Recovery in VLA Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies enable diverse robotic manipulation but can fail during execution without recognizing their own errors. Human observers provide complementary signals, as unexpected robot behavior can trigger rapid vocal, facial, or verbal reactions before failure is completed. We introduce SocialVLA, a local, policy-agnostic social perception gateway that converts spontaneous human reactions into runtime intervention signals for VLA manipulation. SocialVLA combines causal paralinguistic audio detection, visual reaction recognition, explicit stop phrases, and robot-relevance estimation. An asynchronous first-event fusion mechanism triggers a VLA hold from the earliest sufficiently confident signal, while a separate speech channel captures verbal corrections for participant-directed continuation, restart, or instruction revision. We evaluate SocialVLA on physical Unitree G1 manipulation using 15 participants, with 238 annotated intervention-worthy episodes and 1.038 h of non-intervention behavior. Frozen offline replay achieves 54.6% recall and 69.5% precision, while unfiltered audio-video fusion reaches 64.3% recall. Relevance estimation reduces false-stop episodes from 100 to 57 and increases precision from 60.5% to 69.8%. In prospective deployment on an unseen 16th participant, the frozen system achieves 59.5% recall and 91.7% precision. Median detector-to-fusion latency is 47.9 ms, VLA-gate-to-physical-hold latency is 336 ms, and reaction-onset-to-hold latency is 1.021 s. These results demonstrate a complete local pathway from spontaneous social reaction to physical VLA interruption and participant-directed recovery.
full_text: We introduce SocialVLA, a local social-perception gateway that uses spontaneous human reactions---including speech, vocal affect, and facial behavior---to detect emerging VLA manipulation errors in real time, request a VLA hold, and record the participant's verbal correction. fig:gasp_overview Vision-language-action (VLA) policies enable diverse robotic manipulation but remain susceptible to execution failures that may not be recognized by the policy itself. An observing human provides complementary information: unexpected robot behavior can elicit rapid vocal, facial, or explicit verbal reactions before an undesirable manipulation outcome is completed. We introduce SocialVLA, a local and policy-agnostic social perception gateway that converts spontaneous human reactions into runtime intervention signals for VLA manipulation. SocialVLA combines causal paralinguistic audio detection, visual reaction recognition, explicit stop phrases, and robot-relevance estimation. An asynchronous first-event fusion mechanism allows the earliest sufficiently confident signal to request a VLA hold without waiting for complete multimodal agreement. After intervention, a separate speech channel records the participant's verbal correction and associates it with the interrupted VLA action, enabling participant-directed continuation, restart, or instruction revision. We evaluate SocialVLA during physical Unitree G1 manipulation using recordings from 15 participants, comprising 238 annotated intervention-worthy reaction episodes and 1.038~h of annotated non-intervention behavior. Frozen offline replay of the multimodal cascade achieves 54.6 event recall and 69.5 precision, while unfiltered first-event audio--video fusion reaches 64.3 recall. The relevance module reduces false-stop episodes from 100 to 57 and increases precision from 60.5 to 69.8 . In a prospective deployment on a 16th unseen participant, the frozen system achieves 59.5 recall and 91.7 precision. Median detector-to-fusion delivery is 47.9~ms, median VLA-gate-to-physical-hold latency is 336~ms, and matched reaction-onset-to-physical-hold latency is 1.021~s. These results demonstrate a complete local pathway from spontaneous social reaction to physical VLA interruption and a participant-directed recovery interface. Terms---Failure Detection and Recovery, Multi-Modal Perception for HRI, Human Factors and Human-in-the-Loop. INTRODUCTION introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, enabling policies to generalize across objects, tasks, and semantic commands ref1,ref2 . Their generality, however, does not eliminate execution failures. During pick-and-place manipulation, a policy can select the wrong object, generate an unsuitable approach, fail to establish a grasp, drop an object, or place it at an incorrect location. These failures may occur even when individual actions appear locally plausible. Recent methods detect failures from robot observations, trajectories, uncertainty estimates, or internal VLA representations. SAFE learns a failure score from VLA features and successful and failed rollouts ref3 . FAIL-Detect frames runtime monitoring as sequential out-of-distribution detection ref4 . AHA uses a vision-language model to identify and explain manipulation failures ref5 . These approaches provide direct task evidence, but they may require access to policy internals, compatible observations, representative training data, or an explicit model of task progress. An observing person provides a different source of information. Humans can discriminate complex visual scenes within a fraction of a second ref6 , while nonverbal vocalizations can communicate recognizable affect within several hundred milliseconds ref7 . When a robot acts unexpectedly, a person may use an explicit stop phrase, alter vocal prosody, display a negative facial reaction, shake their head, or redirect attention. These responses reflect the person's appraisal of the interaction ref8 and may reveal discrepancies that were not enumerated during policy training. Moreover, an observer need not wait until a failure is physically complete. From the evolving scene, motion direction, and task context, a person may recognize that a grasp or placement is developing incorrectly and react before the object is dropped, displaced, or released at the wrong location. Recent HRI benchmarks explicitly distinguish such anticipatory responses from reactions observed after failure completion ref18 . Prior human-robot interaction (HRI) studies have established that human reactions correlate with robot errors ref9,ref10,ref11,ref12,ref13,ref14 . However, retrospective reaction classification is not equivalent to an operational gate for a continuously executing VLA. In manipulation, detection time is part of the task: a correct decision made after an object has already been dropped or incorrectly placed cannot prevent the consequence. A runtime system must therefore process the earliest reliable signal with low delay, handle missing or uncertain modalities, and avoid waiting for unnecessary multimodal agreement. It should run locally without dependence on an Internet service, remain independent of the internal VLA architecture, and connect as an external layer to any policy that exposes a pause, hold, or stop interface. Repeated evidence must reinforce an intervention rather than reverse an already issued stop. The key challenge is therefore to convert spontaneous social behavior into a sufficiently fast and reliable runtime intervention signal for a continuously executing VLA, while avoiding unnecessary stops caused by unrelated human behavior. We address this challenge with SocialVLA, a modular social perception gateway between a human observer and an executing VLA. Rather than attempting to infer physical failure solely from the robot state, SocialVLA detects human-perceived discrepancies from continuous audio-visual behavior and converts them into structured runtime intervention events. The framework is local and does not require access to VLA activations, action probabilities, or internal uncertainty estimates. In this work, failure detection refers to detecting human-perceived intervention need during robot execution rather than exhaustively identifying all physical robot failures. The main contributions are: ) SocialVLA, a local and policy-agnostic social perception gateway that converts spontaneous human audio-visual reactions and explicit stop commands into runtime interventions during VLA-controlled humanoid manipulation; a causal multimodal intervention architecture that combines fast and extended-context paralinguistic detection, visual reaction recognition, explicit stop phrases, separately estimated robot relevance, and asynchronous first-event fusion, allowing the earliest sufficiently confident signal to request a hold without waiting for complete multimodal agreement; and a real-robot evaluation on the Unitree G1 using a 15-participant annotated corpus and a prospective frozen-system deployment on a 16th, previously unseen participant, measuring reaction detection, false interventions, timely recall, and end-to-end physical stopping latency. Together, these contributions establish spontaneous social behavior as an operational input to VLA execution rather than only an offline observation signal. SocialVLA complements robot-internal failure monitors by contributing the observer's task-level assessment while remaining independent of the internal architecture of the underlying VLA. RELATED WORK related-work Failure Detection for Robot Policies failure-detection-for-robot-policies VLA policies extend vision-language representations to robotic action generation ref1,ref2 . SAFE estimates task failure using internal VLA features and studies the trade-off between detection accuracy and timeliness ref3 . FAIL-Detect extracts uncertainty-related signals from policy inputs and outputs and applies conformal sequential detection ref4 . AHA instead observes robot trajectories and produces semantic failure judgments and explanations ref5 . SocialVLA is complementary to these methods. It does not require VLA activations, action probabilities, uncertainty estimates, or a task-specific success predicate. The same external reaction channel can therefore be attached to different policies. The cost of this independence is that SocialVLA cannot verify whether the observer's interpretation is physically correct. A practical robot should combine human-centered and robot-internal evidence rather than treating either source as universally reliable. Human Reactions to Robot Errors human-reactions-to-robot-errors Stiber et al.~showed that multimodal human responses can support timely robot-error detection ref9 . The BAD dataset subsequently captured bystander reactions to recorded robot failures ref10 , while REFLEX studied multimodal reactions to robot failures and subsequent explanations ref12 . ERR@HRI introduced standardized multimodal benchmarks and time-sensitive evaluation of error-related human behavior ref13,ref18 . Recent observations further show that human reactions remain informative in less controlled environments, although unrelated stimuli, groups, and repeated failures introduce substantial noise ref14 . Most closely related to SocialVLA, Stiber et al.~implemented a proactive system that combines facial behavior, speech, explicit feedback, and robot-error context during live interaction ref11 . SocialVLA differs in its intended role as an external gateway around a continuously executing VLA: it does not require access to VLA internals, explicitly separates reaction recognition from robot-relevance estimation, and prioritizes causal first-event intervention so that a sufficiently strong unimodal signal need not wait for multimodal agreement. The objective is therefore not only to recognize a human response retrospectively, but to convert that response into a actionable hold request during physical VLA execution. Human Reactions as Temporal Supervision human-reactions-as-temporal-supervision Beyond triggering intervention, a detected human response indicates that the recent execution has become inconsistent with the observer's expected task outcome. SocialVLA records this evidence without requiring the observer to operate a dedicated control device. The synchronized stop record identifies the active VLA action or chunk and associates it with the subsequent verbal correction. Such synchronized reaction and correction records may provide temporal supervision for future failure-aware or preference-based policy learning. title: Rethinking World-Action Model for Compositional and In-Context Robotic Manipulation
summary: Long-horizon compositional manipulation has become increasingly important for real-world robot deployment, where a single task involves multiple coordinated subtasks. Existing world-action models (WAMs) jointly predict short-horizon visual futures and actions, but typically lack explicit subtask-level reasoning. We propose Visual Goal-conditioned Action Reasoning (ViGAR), a hierarchical framework that factorizes manipulation into a visual subgoal planner and a subgoal executor. Given the current observation and global instruction, the subgoal planner predicts a visual subgoal for the next subtask. The subgoal executor then jointly generates future visual trajectories and actions conditioned on the predicted subgoal. Both components share a pretrained world-model representation, enabling task-level planning and action generation to benefit from common physical knowledge. Moreover, our framework naturally supports in-context learning: using a global goal image as context can induce different subtask decompositions and behaviors without parameter updates. On the RoboTwin Clean2Random benchmark, ViGAR achieves 82.00% and 67.02% success rates under the Clean and Random settings, respectively, surpassing the strongest baseline by 12.86 percentage points in average success rate. Real-world robot experiments on five compositional and two in-context learning tasks further confirm the effectiveness of ViGAR.
full_text: Sec: intro Robots in production and service settings increasingly face compositional manipulation tasks that involve multiple coordinated subtasks. Such tasks require policies to maintain progress across subtask transitions while generalizing to unseen scenes, objects, and spatial layouts, rather than replaying a fixed sequence from training. Policies for real-world deployment therefore need both embodied generalization and mechanisms for organizing behavior over extended task horizons. World-Action Models (WAMs) offer an appealing paradigm for this goal. By jointly predicting future visual states and actions, WAMs learn physically grounded action dynamics from dense video supervision and have demonstrated strong generalization across tasks, environments, embodiments, and visual distribution shifts~ chen2025large, li2026causal, ye2026world, agarwal2026cosmos . Despite these strengths, existing WAMs are not explicitly designed for long-horizon compositional manipulation. WAM formulations typically provide a useful local control signal by modeling what is likely to happen next, but do not explicitly organize behavior across a sequence of subtasks or expose a task-level interface through which the desired progression can be specified. Recent studies~ black2024zero,zhu2026dswam,intelligence2025pi_ reveal that long-horizon task progression requires more than supervision on short-term evolution of the physical world, and further demonstrate the value of predicting semantic subtasks for open-world long-horizon manipulation and generalization. The core challenge is therefore to endow WAMs with explicit task-level decision making while preserving their strong world-centric prediction and physical generalization. One line of work externalizes this decision making to a language planner that exploits VLMs to decompose a task into linguistic subtasks for a policy to execute. However, language subtask descriptions often underspecify precise spatial outcome without ambiguity, whereas visual subgoals impose stronger constraints on the desired scene configuration~ intelligence2026pi . Our key insight is that compositional manipulation can be factorized into long-term future selection and short-term future realization. World-action modeling for long-horizon tasks should first make explicit the target state robot intends to realize, and then generate the actions that will bring it about. To this end, we propose Visual Goal-conditioned Action Reasoning (ViGAR), which treats subgoal images as explicit decision variable linking task-level reasoning to physical action generation. Given the current observation and the global task instruction, ViGAR first performs visual goal reasoning to predict the desired subtask goal image. Then, conditioned on the current observation, global task instruction and predicted subgoal image, it jointly predicts future visual trajectories and corresponding robot actions leading to the subgoal. Both task-level decision and physical realization are learned in one shared generative world-model representation, so that the model can leverage the same physical knowledge for both stages. Moreover, our framework naturally supports in-context learning: with the scene and instruction held fixed, changing only the global goal induces a different composition of behaviors, forcing the policy to reorganize its action sequence rather than default to the most likely training trajectory. We term this in-context robotic manipulation: the global goal image serves as context for inferring a subtask decomposition, so an out-of-distribution global goal elicits a task composition unseen in training, with no parameter update. Experiments on both simulation benchmark and real-robot compositional tasks validate the effectiveness of ViGAR. On the RoboTwin Clean2Random benchmark~ chen2025robotwin , ViGAR achieves success rates of 82.00 and 67.02 under the Clean and Random settings, respectively, surpassing the strongest baseline~ yang20264d by 12.86 percentage points in average success rate. In real-robot experiments, ViGAR outperforms strong VLA and Cosmos3-Nano-Policy baselines on five compositional tasks, and exhibits in-context learning ability on unseen global goals, confirming the validity of our method. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We factorize compositional manipulation into long-term future selection and short-term future realization, and propose ViGAR, a hierarchical framework that predicts the next subgoal as an explicit decision variable and conditions joint video-action generation on it. We identify in-context robotic manipulation as a capability that emerges from explicit goal conditioning. With the scene and instruction held fixed, a new global goal image elicits a different subtask decomposition and a correspondingly reorganized action sequence, specifying out-of-distribution task compositions at deployment without any parameter update. ViGAR outperforms strong baselines on both simulation benchmark and real-robot compositional manipulation tasks, and exhibits strong in-context learning ability on unseen global goals, confirming the validity of our approach. Sec: related works VLAs for Compositional Robotic Manipulation. Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to continuous action trajectories, and have demonstrated strong generalizability across objects, scenes, and tasks~ brohan2023rt, black2024pi_0, intelligence2025pi_,rdt2,ZhaiX-RSS-26,internvla,fu2026stablevla,qu2025spatialvla . For compositional manipulation, however, a direct instruction-to-action mapping is often insufficient due to increased complexity, and recent systems introduce subtask information as an explicit planning interface, where a VLM or a pretrained world model synthesizes subtask information that conditions a VLA policy~ intelligence2025pi_, cai2026tau_0, intelligence2026pi, long2026scaling . World Models for Robotic Manipulation. World models learn the structure and evolution of physical environments by predicting future states, and world-action models (WAMs) extend this paradigm by jointly modeling future observations and actions. Recent studies have demonstrated that WAMs exhibit strong generalizability beyond the training domain, owing to their explicit modeling of geometric and temporal transitions~ li2026causal, ye2026world, agarwal2026cosmos,ma2026humanscaleegocentrichumanvideo . However, WAMs typically focus on local action generation and lack a mechanism for reasoning about the plan a compositional task requires. BagelVLA~ hu2026bagelvla and RxBrain~ liang2026rxbrain generate interleaved subtask text and subgoal images within a unified model, but these predictions either guide action generation implicitly through intermediate features or serve primarily as planning outputs, rather than acting as explicit subgoal conditions for the downstream policy. In-Context Learning for Robotic Manipulation. In large language models, a novel task can be performed simply by specifying it in the context without any parameter update, termed in-context learning (ICL)~ brown2020language, wei2022emergent, wei2022chain . Carried into robotic manipulation, this moves the acquisition of a new task out of training-time imitation and into inference time, bypassing the need for costly data collection and model fine-tuning. Zero-WAM~ zhou2026zero performs ICL by prompting a causal video-action model with human demonstration videos; HOST~ chen2026robots acquires a new skill from a single human video by predicting the robot's own future observations along the demonstrated progression; Skild S1~ skild2026s1 and GEN-1.5~ generalist2026gen15 likewise condition on a demonstration video or a short sensorimotor trajectory. In each case the context conveys how a task is performed, and the policy re-executes it under its own embodiment. We instead specify a task by its terminal world state: a global goal image constrains only what the scene should become, leaving the subtask decomposition to the model. title: FactorSplat: Appearance-Controllable Gaussian Proxies for Medical Volume Rendering
summary: Transfer functions (TFs) control color and visibility in medical volume rendering, but image-trained Gaussian proxies typically bake one transfer function into their appearance. We present FactorSplat, a per-scene N-dimensional Gaussian splatting (N-DGS) proxy that accepts region-specific intensity-to-RGBA curves at inference. A local lookup applies the authored color and opacity change, while a shared functional encoder and low-rank per-Gaussian factors learn the residual appearance response. Geometry and directional appearance remain shared across presets, with visibility control and TF-aware pruning preserving the ability to hide and reveal structures. On seven CT and MR scans, FactorSplat improves mean PSNR and changed-region error over region-aware VEG across validation, interpolation, unseen composition, and out-of-distribution (OOD) edits. Across these four splits, seven-scan mean PSNR gains over VEG range from 1.10 to 1.52 dB. One checkpoint per scan supports unseen edits without retraining. At $1600^2$, the cached fast renderer averages 524 FPS with 1.17 ms TF switches. Project page: https://gaozhongpai.github.io/FactorSplat/.

We present , a per-scene N-dimensional Gaussian splatting (N-DGS) proxy that accepts region-specific intensity-to-RGBA curves at inference. A local lookup applies the authored color and opacity change, while a shared functional encoder and low-rank per-Gaussian factors learn the residual appearance response. On seven CT and MR scans, FactorSplat improves mean PSNR and changed-region error over region-aware VEG across validation, interpolation, unseen composition, and out-of-distribution (OOD) edits. Across these four splits, seven-scan mean PSNR gains over VEG range from 1.10 to 1.52~dB. One checkpoint per scan supports unseen edits without retraining. At , the cached fast renderer averages 524 FPS with 1.17~ms TF switches. The project page is: . Introduction sec:intro Transfer functions (TFs) control the appearance of volume renderings by mapping measured intensity and derived attributes to color and opacity. They can suppress one material, expose another, or separate structures that overlap in a one-dimensional histogram~ kniss2002multidimensional . In the clinical renderer considered here, each segmented region has an authored intensity-to-RGBA curve (HU for CT). Segmentation selects the appropriate curve, whose resulting color and opacity govern volumetric transport. A preset change can therefore alter both which anatomy contributes to the image and how the visible anatomy occludes, shades, and transmits light in cinematic rendering~ dappa2016cinematic . Image-trained Gaussian proxies offer an efficient representation of such renderings. A proxy optimized from high-quality volume renderings is compact and rasterizes in real time ~ niedermayr2024application,gao2025renderfm . These fixed-appearance proxies encode the training appearance in per-Gaussian spherical-harmonic coefficients and opacities, so the TF is no longer an input. Supporting another preset then requires rebuilding or replacing the proxy. Moreover, training on one opaque preset may omit anatomy that a later preset should reveal. Making the TF an inference-time control poses three coupled problems. First, the condition is a function, not a categorical preset identifier: a model should respond to a new sampled curve without allocating new parameters. Second, the response is spatially heterogeneous. The same TF edit should affect a Gaussian according to the region curves and intensities it covers. Third, training and densification must preserve coverage across the condition family so that structures revealed by any supported preset remain represented. Because a TF changes optical appearance rather than anatomy, geometry should remain invariant to this control. We address these challenges with , a per-scene Gaussian proxy trained across TFs. Gaussian centers, covariances, and the N-DGS view response are shared. Local region--intensity samples drive two complementary appearance branches: a physical lookup applies the TF difference directly, while a shared pointwise encoder and low-rank per-Gaussian factors model the cinematic renderer's residual response. The lookup anchors the prediction to the authored edit; the learned branch corrects its image-space effect. Both branches modify only the view-independent (DC) color and opacity; directional SH coefficients remain TF-independent. Centering the branches on an authored base TF gives exact identity at that preset, and pruning by maximum opacity over the training bank protects primitives needed by different training TFs. Our main contributions are: Representation: FactorSplat conditions an N-DGS proxy on region-specific intensity-to-RGBA curves, rendering unseen TFs with shared geometry and no refitting. Appearance model: A hybrid model combines an interpretable local TF lookup, a low-rank DC-color/opacity residual, analytic visibility control, and TF-aware coverage preservation. Evaluation: Across seven scans, one checkpoint per scan improves mean PSNR and edit fidelity over region-aware VEG on unseen TFs. Related Work sec:related functions and learned visualization synthesis. Multidimensional TFs use intensity, gradients, or other attributes to classify overlapping volume structures and assign optical properties interactively~ kniss2002multidimensional . A complementary line of work helps users choose that mapping: differentiable direct volume rendering optimizes TF parameters against an image objective~ weiss2022diffdvr , and recent semantic systems derive mappings from selected structures or text prompts~ engel2024segmentationtf,jeong2024texttf . FactorSplat reproduces the rendering of an authored TF with a compact proxy. Image-space visualization surrogates condition neural generators on viewpoint and rendering parameters. berger2019generative encode color and opacity TFs into a view-invariant latent space, while DNN-VolVis~ hong2019dnnvolvis predicts volume-rendered images for interactive exploration. These models can learn the output of either local or global-illumination renderers, but an image generator has no explicit 3D primitive representation. ViSNeRF introduces a factorized radiance field for interpolation over TFs, isovalues, time, and simulation parameters ~ yao2025visnerf ; it retains ray-based field rendering rather than an explicit rasterizable proxy. Our functional encoder likewise keeps rendering controls explicit, but its output modulates a per-scene Gaussian field. proxies for volume rendering. 3D Gaussian proxies trained on multi-view volume renderings enable compact, real-time viewing of cinematic anatomy~ niedermayr2024application ; Render-FM amortizes proxy construction across scans by predicting an N-DGS representation feed-forward~ gao2025renderfm . Both target a fixed rendering appearance. iVR-GS instead trains editable basic models for disjoint intensity ranges and composes them to control color, opacity, and Blinn--Phong lighting~ tang2025ivrgs . Its cost and representational size grow with the number of basic models. ECoNGS shares parameters and compresses anchors across basic scenes, reducing redundancy while retaining the composition model~ tang2026econgs . VEG is the closest transfer-function-agnostic Gaussian representation ~ dyken2026veg . It initializes Gaussians from structured or unstructured volume data, stores scalar values rather than baked color and opacity, and trains under a set of opacity maps that covers the scalar range. At inference, it directly applies unseen one-dimensional color and opacity mappings under an emission--absorption renderer with Blinn--Phong shading. This factorization directly links Gaussian appearance to the scalar field. Our setting instead uses region-specific intensity TFs and cinematic-rendering supervision. We combine direct lookup with an image-trained N-DGS proxy whose residual learns the TF-dependent appearance response. Section~ sec:experiments describes our region-aware VEG extension. explicit Gaussian fields. N-dimensional Gaussian splatting has conditioned primitives on viewing direction and time~ gao20246dgs,gao20257dgs,liu2025universal . uses the opacity-only N-DGS formulation as its view-dependent backbone and adds a separate TF axis only to appearance. Concurrent scientific visualization systems also condition Gaussian attributes. GS-Surrogate learns sequential simulation- and visualization-parameter deformations and disables geometry heads for its opacity-only TF experiment~ li2026gssurrogate ; ParticleGS maps global particle radius and opacity controls to Gaussian scale and opacity~ jiang2026particlegs . These methods condition Gaussian fields on low-dimensional controls. DeepONet~ lu2021deeponet encodes input functions for a separable output representation. FactorSplat instead grounds function-valued TF inputs in each Gaussian's local support, with per-primitive factors mapping local codes to appearance offsets rather than generating full weights with a hypernetwork~ ha2017hypernetworks . title: Keep the Effect, Drop the Actor: Programmable Effect-to-Execution World-Action Models
summary: A robot demonstration records two things in the same frames: what happened to the objects, and how one particular arm made it happen. We condition on the first. A demonstration is compiled into an effect program: the 3D keypoint trajectories of the objects that moved, two points marking where each was held, and the configuration the scene ends in, with the demonstrator removed. PEWAM, a 71.5M-parameter world-action model, generates effect, robot execution, action and terminal state as four streams with independent flow-matching times, so clamping a program and sampling the execution turns inference into programming, re-solved closed loop from the live scene. On held-out LIBERO-Goal tasks, one demonstration's program completes 40 of 90 episodes, where the same backbone given a goal image or language, and published demonstration-conditioned methods, complete at most 19; on three of Meta-World's held-out classes it exceeds the best published results, though not on the five-class mean. Because a program is a set of coordinates, a person can edit it: the placement follows a shifted terminal state and the grasp turns with rotated contact points. The same program runs on four robot arms without retraining, and after a push, re-solving completes 23 of 60 episodes where replaying the demonstration completes 6. On a Franka arm, fine-tuned on real demonstrations of other tasks, programs compiled from single human videos complete 36 of 40 trials, against 22 for the same backbone conditioned on the video's last frame as a goal image.

Introduction sec:intro Showing a robot what to do is often easier than describing it, and a single demonstration is a direct way to specify a new manipulation task~ instantpolicy,kat,osviwm,vivla . A demonstration, however, records two things in the same frames: what happened to the objects, and how one particular arm made it happen. Watch someone put a bowl on a stove and you learn where the bowl should end up, roughly how it travels and where it can be held; you do not learn to bend your elbow the way they bent theirs. Most systems that learn from demonstrations keep the two together. Policies that transfer the demonstrator's motion keep the body and treat the world as context~ demodiffusion,atm,pointpolicy , and video-action models prompted with a demonstration predict both at once, as one pixel-level future~ hydra0,zerowam . The task is then entangled with one body's motion: no variable states it on its own, so it can be neither edited nor given to another robot. This viewpoint exposes a limitation of both dominant formulations. Conditioning on the demonstrator's trajectory or video~ uwm,atm,instantpolicy ties the task to one execution, which is valid only for the arm, the grasp and the layout that produced it. Methods built on object motion do separate the object from the actor~ im2flow2act,generalflow,track2act,dream2flow , but they generate that motion from language or video and execute it with a planner, a controller or a per-task policy. What is missing is a task interface that leaves the actor out, that one multi-task model accepts with no parameter update, and that a person can edit. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser , our key observation is that the change in the world is the task, and the demonstrator's motion is one of many ways to produce it. We therefore compile a demonstration into an effect program: keypoints of each relevant object tracked over time, two contact points recording where the object was held, and the configuration the objects end in. Nothing in the program refers to the robot. Based on this view we propose , a world-action model that describes effect, end-effector execution, native action and terminal state as four streams with separate flow-matching times unidiffuser,flowmatching,uwm , so that every conditional is a query of the same weights. Clamping the program and sampling the execution poses the question of how to make the effect happen, which turns inference into programming. At deployment the unfinished part of the program is re-solved from the live scene every few control steps. Because a push moves an object just as a grasp does, progress through the program is counted only for effects the robot has caused, and a disturbance becomes a new observation. We evaluate on LIBERO, Meta-World and RLBench, on four arms, under pushes, from pixels and on a real Franka arm programmed by human videos. Where the demonstrator's motion stays valid, copying it is stronger; the program pays off where copying breaks: after a push, on another arm, and from a person's hand. We summarize our contributions as follows: (i)~we formulate the task carried by a demonstration as an actor-free effect program of object keypoints, contact points and a terminal state, and propose , a world-action model whose independently noised streams let one set of weights both execute and predict; (ii)~we show that the program is an interface a person can edit and hand to another body: its terminal state moves the placement, its contact points turn the grasp, and one program runs on four simulated arms and, from a human video, on a real arm; (iii)~we treat progress as an effect the robot causes and gate the program on engagement, so that re-solving absorbs pushes that defeat replay; and (iv)~we show that editability needs contact written as points, not weights, and training data with several executions of one effect. Related Work sec:related World-action models and imitation from one demonstration World-action models learn video and action jointly, so that one network can both predict and act. UWM uwm couples video and action diffusion with independent timesteps, JOPAT jopat adds a point-track stream, and Hydra-0 and Zero-WAM condition multi-billion-parameter video models on flow or on a human video; generalist policies and pretrained world-action models specify the task with a sentence openvla,openwam . Methods that imitate one demonstration at test time read it as point-cloud graphs instantpolicy , as keypoint and action tokens kat , through demonstration-to-scene correspondences matchingpolicy or as the video itself osviwm,vivla , or they retarget the demonstrator's trajectory demodiffusion ; each carries the demonstrator's motion. We keep independent timesteps but condition on an actor-free program that a person can read and edit. Object motion as the task interface Several methods drop the actor and pass the object's motion to the robot. Most generate that motion, as 2D or 3D flow from language, images, point clouds or generated video im2flow2act,track2act,generalflow,avdc,partflow,novaflow,dream2flow or as a trajectory from a per-task model spot,motionfield3d , and execute it with a flow-conditioned policy, a controller or trajectory optimisation. Others reproduce the motion in one human video by optimisation, retargeting or a policy trained for that demonstration orion,rsrd,human2sim2robot . Keypoints and trajectories also serve as task specifications kpam,rekep,transporter,rttrajectory , ATM and Point Policy atm,pointpolicy condition on point tracks cotracker that include the actor's motion, and demonstration editing adapts recorded demonstrations to new layouts to synthesise data mimicgen,demogen . We share the premise that the object's motion is the task. Closest to us, Im2Flow2Act im2flow2act also carries a task from human video to a robot through object flow, but generates the flow with a separate model and executes it with a flow-conditioned policy; we read the effect from the demonstration itself, add contact points and a terminal state, and sample the execution from one multi-task world-action model that also answers forward queries of the same program. title: A Simulation-Grounded Agentic VLM Framework for Wildfire Monitoring and Reporting
summary: Effective wildfire monitoring requires relating visual evidence to physical fire dynamics, yet real videos with synchronized physical annotations are scarce and high-fidelity 3D simulation is costly. We present a simulation-grounded vision-language model (VLM) framework that automatically converts 2D wildfire simulations into labeled video episodes. A fixed Blender mapping produces low-detail 3D proxies aligned with simulator terrain, fuel layout, fire activity, and wind cues; controllable video generation supplies richer appearance. The proxies are intermediate representations rather than finely rendered final scenes. Generated videos and simulator labels form reusable multimodal memory for a training-free multi-agent VLM system that retrieves reference episodes, reconciles visual and memory-based predictions, and produces structured wildfire reports. On held-out generated episodes, video memory achieves 51.5% exact four-tag accuracy, compared with 22.6% for direct VLM querying and 16-17% for text-only memory; the complete system achieves 77.3% accuracy on six simulator-derived report fields. Component ablations, cross-generator tests, and three real-UAV evaluations assess retrieval, reporting, generator changes, and observable monitoring tasks. The framework connects automatic simulation-to-proxy conversion with memory-based VLM reasoning under scarce real-world physical annotations.
