On held-out generated episodes, video memory achieves exact four-tag accuracy, compared with for direct VLM querying and -- for text-only memory; the complete system achieves accuracy on six simulator-derived report fields. Component ablations, cross-generator tests, and three real-UAV evaluations assess retrieval, reporting, generator changes, and observable monitoring tasks. The framework connects automatic simulation-to-proxy conversion with memory-based VLM reasoning under scarce real-world physical annotations. Introduction Wildfire monitoring and reporting are fundamentally about connecting what is seen to what is happening physically in the wildland. Fire-spread simulators (e.g., mandel2011coupled,finney1998farsite,mallet2009modeling,Doyle_SimFire_2024 ) encode how fuel, slope, moisture, and wind shape propagation, and satellite, aerial, and UAV measurements provide partial visual observations of active incidents. Modern vision-language models (VLMs) need a framework to align two forms of evidence in a shared representation. Real wildfire videos are visually rich, yet labels for wind, moisture, slope, fuel condition, burn extent, and severe-fire behavior are usually absent. Simulators expose these variables directly, yet their native outputs are grid states, masks, and fire fronts, which differ from the aerial-view videos that VLMs are expected to interpret. Though existing wildfire VLM work has advanced fire and smoke recognition, UAV monitoring, satellite risk analysis, and VLM-guided planning~ du2025wildfire,wu2025fireclip,seidel2025advancing, ayanzadeh2026wildfirevlm,webb2026fire,xie2025marsha,sandeep2026context , temporally rich videos paired with physical fire-state labels remain scarce. Collecting synchronized wind, moisture, slope, fuel, and fire-behavior annotations is hazardous, expensive, and hard to control. Available UAV datasets provide valuable detection and segmentation annotations~ shamsoshoara2021aerial, kularatne2024fireman,pesonen2025boreal , but the annotations used here do not jointly describe these drivers. Fire-spread simulators expose such conditions without providing camera-view observations, while full 3D fire simulation~ kokosza2024scintilla,hadrich2021fire incurs costs that limit coverage across fuels, terrains, weather, and cameras. We therefore study a scalable middle ground: efficient 2D simulations over real terrain and fuel maps are automatically lifted into lightweight Blender proxies, translated into controlled videos, and stored as physics-labeled memory for VLM reasoning. Recent developments such as Code World Model~ chen2026codeworldmodel and Blender scene authoring with GPT-6 Astra highlight the potential of executable representations for visual world construction. We explore this direction in a simulation-grounded VLM framework for wildfire monitoring and reporting (Figure~ fig:placeholder ). Each episode starts with a 2D simulation over real LANDFIRE terrain and fuel data spanning approximately \(3\, \). A fully automatic Blender procedure maps evolving simulator fields into terrain, vegetation, flame, and wind-driven smoke cues. This lightweight proxy is an intermediate representation: fixed conversion rules maintain simulator-to-scene correspondence, while depth, scribble, and prompt controls guide richer video appearance. Generated clips retain their prompts, simulator parameters, environmental tags, and fire-behavior labels as reusable multimodal memory. Retrieved episodes then complement direct visual reasoning for interpreting new wildfire videos without updating VLM weights. Section~ sec:discussion further discusses the connections to code-based world construction and general-purpose scene authoring. Generated videos with known simulator labels provide controlled evaluation targets. We use 500 geo-disjoint locations: 400 episodes populate memory and 100 are held out for evaluation (Appendix~ sec:downstream_tasks ). For each query, retrieved references complement direct visual reasoning, and a judge resolves reporter disagreements. Video memory achieves 51.5 exact four-tag accuracy versus 16--17 for text-only memory and 22.6 for direct VLM querying; reporting reaches 77.3 on six simulator-derived fields. Structured records retain predictions, evidence, and reasoning. Cross-generator and real-UAV tests additionally assess generator changes, smoke/fire detection, and visible fire-area assessment. Our contributions are: Automatic simulation-grounded visual evidence. We connect efficient 2D wildfire simulation to controllable video generation through a fully automatic Blender proxy. A fixed mapping expresses terrain, fuel layout, fire activity, and wind cues as lightweight 3D controls, constructing labeled visual episodes under scarce real-world physical annotations. Memory-augmented agentic reporting. We organize generated videos and simulator context as reusable multimodal memory, and combine retrieval and reranking with complementary VLM reporters and selective disagreement adjudication. The training-free system produces environmental-driver estimates and structured wildfire reports without updating model weights. Controlled evaluation with complementary real-UAV tests. Video memory achieves 51.5 exact four-tag accuracy versus 22.6 for direct VLM querying and 16--17 for text-only memory; the full reporter reaches 77.3 on six simulator-derived fields. Ablations, cross-generator tests, and real-UAV perceptual evaluations examine the framework's components and transfer beyond the primary generated-video setting. Related Work Wildfire modeling and observation. Wildfire prediction combines spread models with sensing. Rothermel~ rothermel1972mathematical underlies FARSITE~ finney1998farsite ; level-set methods handle fire-front topology changes~ mallet2009modeling ; WRF-SFIRE couples spread with atmospheric dynamics~ mandel2011coupled . MODIS and VIIRS provide broad-area fire observations~ justice2002modis,giglio2016collection,schroeder2014new , complemented by UAV smoke/fire detection and front tracking~ bailon2022real,raoufi2025fire,fan2025real . Rather than replacing simulators or sensors, we automatically translate simulator states into visual reference episodes for VLM monitoring and reporting. VLMs for scientific and wildfire understanding. Scientific VLM benchmarks show that general-purpose multimodal models can be useful but struggle with domain-specific visual structure, terminology, and evaluation protocols~ esparza2025automated, roberts2024scifibench,wu2024scimmir,kuckreja2024geochat,li2023llava . Wildfire VLM systems have been studied for scene recognition~ du2025wildfire , smoke/fire detection~ wu2025fireclip,qi2026smokebench , UAV situational awareness~ seidel2025advancing , satellite-image risk reasoning~ ayanzadeh2026wildfirevlm , and VLM-guided reinforcement learning in wildfire digital twins~ webb2026fire . These works motivate VLM-based decision support, but they also highlight the need for physically grounded video data and task-specific evaluation. Code world models and simulation-conditioned video. WorldCoder~ tang2024worldcoder constructs executable world models through interaction, while Code World Model~ chen2026codeworldmodel connects coding-agent-driven state evolution to proxy-conditioned video generation. PhysGen~ liu2024physgen combines rigid-body simulation with generative video refinement, and Cosmos-Transfer1~ nvidia2025cosmostransfer1 supports spatially controlled generation. Together, these approaches motivate separating structured dynamics and spatial controls from visual appearance. We examine this separation for simulation-grounded wildfire memory; Section~ sec:discussion discusses its relationship to coding-agent world models and scene authoring. Memory-augmented multimodal reasoning. Retrieval-augmented generation supplies external evidence without updating model weights~ lewis2020retrieval . Agent memories support long-horizon reasoning~ packer2023memgpt,park2023generative , while multimodal RAG and video retrieval access visual, textual, and scene-level evidence~ jeong2025videorag,luo2024videorag,gia2025vrag,zeng2026scenerag,fu2026videostir using video--text embeddings~ xu2021videoclip,luo2022clip4clip,wang2022internvideo,ma2022xclip . WorldMem~ xiao2025worldmem and PhysStream~ chen2026physstream use memory for consistent visual generation. Our memory instead pairs reference videos with simulator-controlled conditions and fire-behavior labels for inference across episodes, complementing direct observations and historical-data or context-aware wildfire systems~ xie2025marsha,sandeep2026context . Method Figure~ fig:placeholder gives the overall workflow. The framework has two main components: a simulation-grounded visual evidence construction method and a memory-augmented multi-agent VLM system for monitoring and reporting. The subsections below follow this order. Simulation-Grounded Visual Evidence Construction sec:sim_to_video The first stage constructs labeled visual episodes to reduce reliance on scarce real footage with synchronized physical annotations. We retain the scalability and annotations of 2D wildfire simulation while making its outputs visually accessible to VLMs: diverse episodes over real terrain and fuel maps are lifted into procedural 3D proxies and translated into aerial-view clips. Here, simulation-grounded refers to the simulator-derived labels and controls linking each episode to its originating scenario; visual and temporal cue alignment is evaluated separately in Section~ sec:simulation_alignment . Physics-Grounded 2D Wildfire Simulation sec:2d_simulation To balance physical grounding and generation throughput, we use SimFire~ Doyle_SimFire_2024 as our 2D wildfire simulation platform. SimFire follows the classical Rothermel fire-spread model~ rothermel1972mathematical detailed in Appendix~ sec:rothermel_app , allowing us to generate large numbers of wildfire episodes with meaningful macroscopic spread behavior. For each episode, we randomly sample a geographic location specified by latitude and longitude, and query the LANDFIRE database to obtain real U.S. fuel and terrain information. Fuel types are represented using the Anderson 13 fuel model anderson1982aids , while terrain elevation is used to derive slope and support later 3D proxy construction. Wind direction, wind-related parameters, and fuel-moisture settings are randomized to increase scenario diversity. Each simulation covers a region of approximately \(3\, \) in spatial extent. We refer readers to Appendix~ sec:firemodel_app and sec:implementation_details for implementation details. Each episode is summarized using four physically meaningful factors: wind speed, moisture, slope angle, and vegetation density. Each factor is discretized into low and high levels, yielding a compact set of simulator-derived tags. These tags provide coarse environmental regimes for retrieval-based state estimation and agent reasoning, rather than continuous measurements of a query incident. title: World Action Modeling with Progressive Visual Planning
summary: World action models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic control by jointly predicting future visual dynamics and actions from an initial observation and instruction. However, existing WAMs struggle with long-horizon prediction, as generating dense video rollouts is highly inefficient. Some recent WAMs address this by predicting a single future frame without generating the full video, but this approach neglects how to progress toward the goal. We present ProWAM, a progressive world action model that jointly predicts actions and an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals, providing explicit visual guidance to anchor action generation throughout task execution. This design scales naturally, as sub-goal prediction can be learned from large-scale action-free videos, allowing the video backbone to offload complex visual planning from the action policy. For efficient action generation, ProWAM executes a single video-backbone forward pass to cache sparse sub-goal features, eliminating iterative full-video generation and requiring only lightweight action denoising during replanning. Across extensive evaluations, ProWAM achieves superior out-of-distribution robustness. On simulation benchmarks, it sets new state-of-the-art results on LIBERO-Plus (85.8%) and randomized RoboTwin (75.7%), outperforming the strongest baseline with relative gains of up to +35.9%. On RoboCasa365, ProWAM achieves a 48.1% success rate and 18.2% on the challenging Composite-Unseen split, ranking 4th overall. Crucially, in zero-shot real-world experiments, ProWAM achieves 70.0% success, outperforming the strongest baseline by +15.0 (from 55.0% to 70.0%, a +27.3% relative gain) in novel scenes. These results demonstrate the value of progress-indexed visual foresight for closed-loop control. Our program is in https://sii-ferenas.github.io/ProWAM-page.
full_text: Introduction sec_intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models primarily inherit semantic knowledge from vision-language pretraining but remain data-hungry due to their reliance on large, costly collections of robot demonstrations~ kim2024openvla,24pi0,25pi0.5 . In contrast, world action models (WAMs) introduce a complementary source of transferable knowledge: visual-dynamics priors learned by video generation models from large-scale video datasets~ blattmann2023svd,yang2024cogvideox,wan2025wan . Recent WAMs have shown that incorporating such predictive visual knowledge can improve data efficiency and out-of-distribution generalization in robotic control~ pai2025mimic,ye2026dreamzero,yuan2026fastwam,zhang2026imagewam,li2026lingbotva . Existing WAMs differ in how they utilize future visual prediction to guide action generation. Full-imagination WAMs~ pai2025mimic,ye2026dreamzero,li2026lingbotva leverage dense future rollouts that provide detailed near-term guidance but are inefficient as they require multiple denoising passes through a large video backbone. Alternatively, zero-imagination WAMs~ yuan2026fastwam,ye2026gigaworldpolicy generate actions without predicting future visual states. Between these extremes, ImageWAM~ zhang2026imagewam conditions control on an action-horizon endpoint frame without explicitly representing intermediate visual states. These designs reveal a fundamental trade-off: dense visual rollouts provide short-horizon dynamics at high computational cost, whereas other efficient alternatives lack explicit intermediate-progress guidance over the full task. To reconcile this trade-off, we introduce ProWAM, a progressive world action model that extends a single fixed-state prediction into an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals. Each sub-goal is indexed by normalized progress relative to the current state, where denotes the current observation and denotes the trajectory endpoint. This relative parameterization dynamically re-anchors sub-goals to the current observation, enabling consistent guidance across arbitrary task stages and varying trajectory lengths. Consequently, these sparse targets efficiently guide action generation without requiring dense video rollouts or separate high-level planning modules. Specifically, ProWAM adopts a vision-action mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architecture consisting of a video generation expert and a lightweight diffusion-based action expert for policy generation. Each visual sub-goal is represented as a latent slot associated with a normalized progress value. The video expert jointly predicts near-term future transitions and progress-conditioned sub-goals, while the action expert attends to current observations and sub-goals to generate low-level action chunks. Asymmetric attention prevents action information from altering the visual prediction pathway. This design preserves the generative prior of the video expert, enabling video-only pretraining on large-scale action-free videos followed by joint fine-tuning on task-specific robot demonstrations to couple visual planning with action generation. At inference, ProWAM reuses cached sub-goal features to eliminate repeated video-backbone computation, enabling efficient closed-loop control. Overall, our contributions are threefold: [label= , leftmargin=1.5em, itemsep=2pt, topsep=2pt] We introduce progressive sub-goal imagination (Figure~ fig:teaser ), a new visual planning paradigm for WAMs that represents long-horizon futures as an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals indexed by normalized task progress. This representation provides explicit intermediate guidance without requiring dense video rollouts during inference or an external planner. We instantiate this paradigm in ProWAM, a WAM that natively integrates progress-conditioned visual sub-goal prediction with action generation for long-horizon control. By embedding sub-goal slots into the video pathway and coupling them via asymmetric attention, ProWAM enables scalable action-free video pretraining followed by joint vision-action fine-tuning. At inference, cached sub-goal features guide action denoising without repeated video-expert computation. title: GeoScaffold: Learning Compact Geometric Latents via Reconstruction for Efficient Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Recent vision-and-language navigation (VLN) systems increasingly adopt streaming Video-LLM policies that map egocentric RGB observations and instructions directly to low-level actions. Yet these policies inherit weak 3D geometric priors from 2D pretraining. Existing geometry-aware extensions charge a persistent inference-time price: depth sensors, 3D encoders, or per-step perception tool calls. We propose GeoScaffold, a geometric supervision framework that pays this price once, at training time, by internalizing geometry into the policy itself. It first learns a compact depth tokenizer on depth maps from the training trajectories and freezes it. It then fine-tunes the policy with a handful of learnable geometry query tokens, training their hidden states to reconstruct navigation-critical geometry such as depth, connectivity, and traversability. This supervision turns the query states into compact geometric latents for action decoding, and through the shared weights also internalizes geometry into the backbone's own representations. Like a scaffold, the tokenizer, target generators, and reconstruction heads are discarded after training, leaving the backbone and action interface unchanged. Extensive experiments show that GeoScaffold consistently outperforms leading vision-only navigators on continuous VLN benchmarks, offering a practical paradigm for lightweight edge deployment of spatially aware embodied navigation models.

Yet these policies inherit weak 3D geometric priors from 2D pretraining. Existing geometry-aware extensions charge a persistent inference-time price: depth sensors, 3D encoders, or per-step perception tool calls. We propose GeoScaffold, a geometric supervision framework that pays this price once, at training time, by internalizing geometry into the policy itself. It first learns a compact depth tokenizer on depth maps from the training trajectories and freezes it. It then fine-tunes the policy with a handful of learnable geometry query tokens, training their hidden states to reconstruct navigation-critical geometry such as depth, connectivity, and traversability. This supervision turns the query states into compact geometric latents for action decoding, and through the shared weights also internalizes geometry into the backbone's own representations. Like a scaffold, the tokenizer, target generators, and reconstruction heads are discarded after training, leaving the backbone and action interface unchanged. Extensive experiments show that GeoScaffold consistently outperforms leading vision-only navigators on continuous VLN benchmarks, offering a practical paradigm for lightweight edge deployment of spatially aware embodied navigation models. Introduction sec:intro Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow natural-language instructions while moving through a previously unseen environment anderson2018vision,ku2020room,krantz2020beyond . Recent progress has increasingly moved VLN toward an end-to-end vision-language-action (VLA) paradigm, in which a Video-LLM policy maps egocentric RGB observations and the instruction to navigation actions step by step zhang2024navid,cheng2024navila,wei2025streamvln,zhang2025navfom,xin2026decovln . However, the backbones underlying these policies are pretrained almost entirely on internet-scale 2D data, which makes them strong at semantic recognition yet weak at metric and topological reasoning chen2024spatialvlm,fu2024blink,yang2025thinking . Navigation demands exactly these abilities. Beyond recognizing objects and matching them to linguistic landmarks, an agent must reason about free space, relative scale, doorway structure, and route connectivity. These policies therefore struggle with depth-sensitive decisions, such as judging whether a landmark is nearby, whether a passage is traversable, or whether to continue exploring rather than stop prematurely. Existing methods compensate for this weakness with additional machinery at inference time. Geometry-enhanced methods give the policy explicit spatial support, running a frozen 3D encoder alongside the backbone zeng2025janusvln,fan2026prospect,liu2026dygeovln or lifting RGB-D observations into geometry-aware BEV maps yang2026gavln . As shown in (b), these components remain active at deployment, with depth sensors adding hardware requirements and 3D encoders increasing GPU memory usage and inference latency. Other methods restructure the system, adopting dual-system designs in which a slow reasoning module guides a fast controller wei2025dualvln,internrobotics2025internvla,xue2026omninav or zero-shot pipelines of LLM planners, perception, and path-planning components zhou2024navgpt,long2024instructnav,chen2025aoplanner . Such designs require coordination among multiple modules, complicating system integration and deployment. By contrast, humans act with rich spatial awareness from visual experience alone, without explicit depth sensing at every step. For navigation, such spatial awareness should help the agent judge distances, identify traversable regions, and recognize passages that connect spaces. We therefore ask whether geometric supervision can equip an end-to-end VLA navigator with these abilities during training, while requiring only RGB observations and language instructions at deployment. To this end, we propose GeoScaffold, a training-only geometric enhancement framework for streaming VLN. GeoScaffold supervises the policy with three geometric targets. Depth captures metric scale, while connectivity and traversability mark route-relevant passages and free space, respectively. The supervision enters through a small set of learnable geometry query tokens carion2020detr,li2023blip2,mu2023gist,lai2024lisa , inserted before each action block, one dedicated group per target. Each group learns to reconstruct its own target from its hidden states. Training proceeds in two stages. Stage I learns a compact depth tokenizer offline. Stage II then fine-tunes the policy with the navigation objective unchanged plus the auxiliary reconstruction losses. This pressure compresses scene geometry into the query hidden states, which act as compact geometric latents for action decoding. After training, all auxiliary modules are discarded. The deployed policy runs on RGB and text alone, with only the learned geometry tokens remaining in the prompt. Our contributions are threefold: 3pt 2pt 0pt We introduce GeoScaffold, a lightweight, removable geometric enhancement framework for efficient end-to-end streaming VLN that requires no depth sensors, 3D encoders, or reconstruction modules at inference time and deploys on edge hardware. We design a query-token reconstruction objective whose dedicated depth, connectivity, and traversability groups shape their hidden states into compact geometric latents. We present an empirical study of training-only geometric supervision for VLN, showing consistent success-rate gains across different backbones and in real-world deployment, with only the learned geometry tokens retained at inference. Related Work sec:related VLA Model for Navigation sec:rw_vln Recent VLN research has increasingly reformulated navigation as an end-to-end vision-language-action problem. Navigators of this kind fine-tune a multimodal language model to map visual observations and the instruction to navigation decisions zhang2024navid,cheng2024navila,zheng2024navillm,zhang2025uninavid,zhang2025navfom , inheriting rich visual priors and the commonsense knowledge of the backbone. To run over long trajectories, other work turned the interaction into a streaming multi-turn dialogue whose cached context and compact memory keep the cost of each step bounded wei2025streamvln,xin2026decovln . Building on these policies, dual-system designs add a slow reasoning module above a fast controller wei2025dualvln,internrobotics2025internvla,xue2026omninav . However, their backbones are pretrained almost exclusively on 2D web images and videos, so the resulting policies inherit little sense of metric scale or 3D structure, precisely the abilities that navigation requires. Geometry-Enhanced VLN sec:rw_geometry A broad line of VLN research addresses this spatial weakness by injecting depth or 3D structure into the agent. These methods make geometry an input to the policy at deployment time, whether through RGB-D or stereo observations liu2025navid4d,wang2026stereonav , 3D-language feature fields and tokens wang2025g3dlf,wang2025dynam3d , map-like memories wang2023gridmm,zhang2025mapnav,zhang2026spatialnav,yang2026gavln , frozen 3D foundation models zeng2025janusvln,fan2026prospect,liu2026dygeovln such as VGGT wang2025vggt , or agentic perception tools that query occupancy, LiDAR, or depth on demand xin2026agentvln,yue2026spatialvln . These designs improve spatial understanding, but the sensors, encoders, maps, or tool calls that supply geometry must stay active at deployment and add latency, memory, or hardware to the robot. GeoScaffold instead uses geometry only as a training-time supervision signal, so the policy learns geometric representations from RGB alone and carries them into deployment as compact latents, with no geometry module on the inference path. Auxiliary Perception Supervision and Query Tokens sec:rw_query Auxiliary perception supervision enriches visual representations through prediction and reconstruction tasks. Early navigation methods explore depth prediction mirowski2017learning and self-supervised reasoning zhu2020auxrn . Recent approaches extend this idea to multimodal LLMs and VLAs: ROSS wang2025ross , 3DRS huang2025threedrs , and Spatial Forcing li2025spatialforcing use visual reconstruction or 3D feature alignment, while DreamVLA zhang2025dreamvla predicts future world knowledge for manipulation. Query-based aggregation and special-token readouts, as in DETR carion2020detr , BLIP-2 li2023blip2 , and LISA lai2024lisa , provide compact interfaces for visual prediction. Perception Tokens bigverdi2025perception and Perceptio li2026perceptio also explore autoregressive perception-token generation. GeoScaffold uses dedicated query states to reconstruct current-frame depth, connectivity, and traversability during training, learning compact geometric latents for RGB-only streaming navigation. Method sec:method Preliminaries sec:prelim We study vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE) krantz2020beyond , in which an agent follows a natural-language instruction using egocentric RGB observations and predicts actions from the action space . Streaming end-to-end VLN is commonly formulated as a multi-turn dialogue with a Video-LLM: each user turn provides the current observation with the instruction and the retained history, and each assistant turn emits an action before the next observation arrives. A Video-LLM navigation policy comprises a vision encoder that tokenizes the retained RGB observations, a projector that maps visual tokens into the LLM embedding space, and an autoregressive language model that processes the joint vision-language-action sequence. Let denote the visual window retained at turn , let denote the corresponding RGB observations, which are encoded into visual tokens, and let denote the text tokens containing the instruction, dialogue markers, and previous actions. The hidden states for action generation are Model Architecture sec:model_arch Prior geometry-enhanced navigators consume geometry through dedicated spatial encoders and fusion modules that make it usable to the LLM zeng2025janusvln,yang2026gavln . This machinery then stays resident at inference. We therefore reverse the interface. Rather than consuming geometry as an input, the navigator learns to predict it, compressing scene geometry into a small set of geometric latents that action decoding can attend to. The latents are supervised with discrete depth tokens and binary connectivity and traversability masks. Such classification-style targets are the kind of supervision the backbone is already trained on, in contrast to dense regression signals. Geometry query tokens. We add new vocabulary tokens , partitioned into three groups dedicated to depth, connectivity, and traversability, respectively. title: AdaTempo: Learning Shared Relative Tempo from Demonstrations for Faster Robot Manipulation
summary: Visuomotor policies trained via imitation learning often inherit the unnecessarily slow timing of teleoperated demonstrations. Yet uniform speedup is unreliable because different phases of a manipulation task tolerate acceleration differently. In this work, we introduce AdaTempo, a self-supervised method that accelerates visuomotor policies by exploiting shared relative-tempo structure in demonstrations. AdaTempo establishes phase correspondence, aggregates the aligned relative tempo into a consensus, and maps it to a continuous speedup profile used to resample demonstrations into accelerated training trajectories. Training standard policies such as ACT or Diffusion Policy on these resampled trajectories directly embeds the desired tempo in the learned behavior, without runtime tempo selection or online retiming. Extensive evaluations show that AdaTempo achieves up to a $3.57\times$ speedup and yields a stronger success--speed trade-off than the original policies and representative acceleration baselines.

AdaTempo exploits this structure to enable non-uniform acceleration across task progress. Right: On a fast conveyor-belt task, AdaTempo keeps pace with the production line and successfully grasps fast-moving objects that the ACT baseline frequently misses. fig:teaser Visuomotor policies trained via imitation learning often inherit the unnecessarily slow timing of teleoperated demonstrations. Yet uniform speedup is unreliable because different phases of a manipulation task tolerate acceleration differently. In this work, we introduce AdaTempo, a self-supervised method that accelerates visuomotor policies by exploiting shared relative-tempo structure in demonstrations. AdaTempo establishes phase correspondence, aggregates the aligned relative tempo into a consensus, and maps it to a continuous speedup profile used to resample demonstrations into accelerated training trajectories. Training standard policies such as ACT or Diffusion Policy on these resampled trajectories directly embeds the desired tempo in the learned behavior, without runtime tempo selection or online retiming. Extensive evaluations show that AdaTempo achieves up to a speedup and yields a stronger success--speed trade-off than the original policies and representative acceleration baselines. Introduction sec:introduction Visuomotor imitation learning has become a practical paradigm for acquiring complex manipulation skills from teleoperated demonstrations~ zhao2023act,chi2023diffusion,ze2024dp3 . Recent large-scale policies have further improved generalization across tasks and robot embodiments~ ghosh2024octo,kim2025openvla,black2024pi0 . Yet standard imitation objectives optimize what actions to reproduce, not how quickly they should be executed. Since teleoperated demonstrations are often slow and cautious, the resulting policies tend to inherit this conservative execution timing~ guo2025demospeedup,arachchige2025sail, yuan2025speedtuning,kim2026race . Removing this inefficiency is not as simple as downsampling the demonstrated trajectories by a constant rate. Different phases of a manipulation task tolerate acceleration differently. Uniform acceleration can skip important intermediate states, alter the closed-loop state distribution, or request motions that the controller cannot track over the shortened time horizon~ arachchige2025sail,kim2026race,nam2025speedaug . Effective speedup therefore requires determining both how much to accelerate a task and how to distribute that acceleration over its progress. Recent work has made substantial progress in accelerating learned manipulation policies beyond demonstration speed~ guo2025demospeedup,yuan2025speedtuning,arachchige2025sail, kim2026race,nam2025speedaug . However, existing methods typically determine how acceleration should vary using policy-derived proxies, interaction-based optimization, or additional runtime mechanisms, requiring auxiliary machinery during training or deployment. This motivates a central question: can demonstrations themselves provide a direct and fine-grained supervisory signal for phase-dependent speedup? As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:teaser , our key observation is that demonstrations may differ in absolute speed yet tend to exhibit similar relative-tempo patterns over task progress, consistent with prior observations of approximate relative-timing invariance in skilled movement~ schmidt1985invariance . Rather than absolute speed, we focus on relative tempo: within each demonstration, which phases are executed relatively faster or slower? When corresponding phases exhibit similar relative tempo across demonstrations, this consistency suggests phase-specific task characteristics. Phases consistently executed more cautiously, such as grasping or insertion, may tolerate less temporal compression, while relatively fast phases such as free-space transport offer greater acceleration potential. Based on this insight, we introduce AdaTempo, a self-supervised method for learning cross-demonstration relative tempo to accelerate visuomotor policies. AdaTempo aligns demonstrations with different durations, constructs episode-relative tempo profiles at corresponding task phases, and aggregates them into a cross-demonstration consensus while downweighting phases with high disagreement. It maps this consensus to a continuous speedup profile used for smooth virtual-time resampling of the original trajectories. A standard visuomotor policy, such as ACT or Diffusion Policy (DP), is then trained on the accelerated trajectories. The desired tempo is thus embedded directly in the learned behavior, requiring no runtime tempo-selection module, online retiming, or changes to the control interface at deployment. Extensive simulation and real-world evaluations show that AdaTempo achieves up to a speedup over demonstrations and yields a stronger success--speed trade-off than the original policies and representative acceleration baselines. Our contributions are: We identify shared relative tempo across demonstrations as a self-supervised cue for phase-dependent speedup, revealing recurring phase-wise timing structure beyond demonstrator-specific absolute speed. We develop AdaTempo, which phase-aligns demonstrations, converts their relative-tempo consensus into a continuous speedup profile for offline virtual-time resampling, without auxiliary models or additional mechanisms at deployment. We validate AdaTempo across 11 simulated and real-world manipulation tasks with ACT or DP, achieving up to a \(3.57 \) speedup and a stronger success--speed trade-off than representative acceleration baselines. Related Work sec:related-work Visuomotor Imitation Learning Modern visuomotor policies learn temporally coherent manipulation behaviors through action chunking, generative sequence modeling, and increasingly large-scale multi-task training~ shridhar2022peract,zhao2023act, chi2023diffusion,ze2024dp3,brohan2022rt1,zitkovich2023rt2,ghosh2024octo, kim2025openvla,liu2025rdt,black2024pi0,oneill2024openx, khazatsky2024droid . These methods typically train on the temporal sampling provided by demonstrations and can therefore reproduce not only demonstrated motions but also their execution tempo~ guo2025demospeedup, arachchige2025sail,yuan2025speedtuning,kim2026race . Orthogonal work reduces policy inference latency through distillation, efficient generative modeling, or asynchronous action generation~ prasad2024consistency, lu2024manicm,pertsch2025fast,black2025rtc . AdaTempo instead targets physical task execution time by temporally resampling demonstrations before policy training. Acceleration of Imitation Learning Execution Existing approaches accelerate manipulation policies either by modifying policy execution at runtime or by altering demonstrations and training targets before deployment. Runtime policy-execution acceleration Runtime methods advance within action chunks, select speed multipliers, or retime commands based on motion complexity, tracking error, latency, or physical reachability~ park2024pte,yuan2025speedtuning, arachchige2025sail,kim2026race,wu2026speeduppatch . Related approaches expose speed explicitly through variable-frequency conditioning or continuous action parameterizations that can be adjusted at deployment~ masuya2025vfil,jing2026tempovla,han2026bspline . While effective for adapting frozen policies or enabling on-demand speed control, these approaches require additional mechanisms to select execution speed at runtime. Some, such as SpeedTuning, further learn speed selection through reinforcement learning and environment interaction~ yuan2025speedtuning . Demonstration- and training-side acceleration Another family of methods accelerates policy execution by modifying the temporal structure of demonstrations or training targets before deployment. DemoSpeedup estimates conditional action entropy with a proxy generative policy and assigns different downsampling factors to the resulting trajectory segments~ guo2025demospeedup . Semantic approaches instead use vision--language reasoning, gripper--object relations, or propagated stage labels to identify regions that can be accelerated, while motion-frequency cues have been used to remove temporally redundant frames~ kim2025espada,sanchez2026volt,dai2026skip . AutoSpeed optimizes over smoothly speed-transformed action targets using a prediction-error and horizon criterion, whereas SpeedAug combines variable-tempo augmentation with reinforcement-learning refinement~ hu2026autospeed,nam2025speedaug . However, these methods typically rely on auxiliary signals or objectives to determine where and how much to accelerate. In contrast, AdaTempo derives a continuous speedup signal directly from relative-tempo structure shared across demonstrations and incorporates it through temporally resampled training data. Temporal Correspondence and Relative Tempo Temporal alignment enables comparison between demonstrations that follow similar task progress with different durations. Dynamic time warping (DTW) constructs a monotone correspondence between sequences~ sakoe1978dtw and has been used to align demonstrations before extracting or transferring skill structure~ braglia2024arclength . In acceleration work, ESPADA uses DTW to propagate semantic stage labels from an annotated trajectory to other demonstrations~ kim2025espada . Complementary evidence from motor-control studies indicates that skilled movements can retain relative timing and normalized velocity structure under changes in execution speed~ schmidt1985invariance,summers1975timing,shapiro1981gait, atkeson1985kinematic . This observation motivates comparing demonstrations in a normalized temporal coordinate rather than by their absolute execution speeds. AdaTempo uses DTW not to propagate predefined labels, but to establish correspondences across demonstrations, enabling relative tempo to be compared at matched task progress. Recurring cross-demonstration relative-tempo structure is then used to derive a continuous speedup profile. AdaTempo sec:method Let be a set of collected demonstrations, where denotes a trajectory of observations and action targets recorded at a fixed control frequency. AdaTempo transforms into an accelerated dataset while preserving the demonstrated task ordering. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:pipeline , the method first expresses tempo relatively within each demonstration and aligns the resulting profiles to a canonical phase. It then converts their cross-demonstration consensus into a continuous speedup profile, which is used to resample the demonstrations before standard policy training. From these smoothed targets, we construct a progress descriptor and an alignment descriptor . The progress descriptor retains the continuous arm-motion components, while the alignment descriptor additionally includes event landmarks such as the gripper state. Each continuous motion channel is normalized by a robust dataset-level percentile range. We parameterize an episode by its normalized cumulative motion arc length, Unlike elapsed time, measures the fraction of cumulative demonstrated motion completed. title: Imagine the Future, Internalize the Gist: Efficient VLA Reasoning via Internalized Spatiotemporal Imagination
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate intermediate reasoning to improve robotic manipulation, yet existing approaches primarily reason about observed states without explicitly anticipating future scene evolution. Extending such reasoning to explicit future rollouts at every inference step, however, introduces substantial computational overhead. We propose IG-VLA, a VLA reasoning framework that enables models to imagine the future and internalize the gist. Our Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning learns to imagine task-relevant future scene evolution directly in visual representation space, guiding action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation. To further reduce inference overhead, we introduce Scene Gist Memory, which internalizes reasoning-derived scene-behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token, preserving the benefits of future reasoning while bypassing explicit future imagination at inference. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of IG-VLA. On the LIBERO-Plus Language suite, both the reasoning and gist policies outperform the strongest baseline by nearly 6% in success rate. The gist policy also achieves up to 6.38x speedup over baselines, reducing inference latency from 1081ms to 169.5ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. These results demonstrate that future spatiotemporal reasoning can be effectively internalized for efficient VLA deployment.

Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable general-purpose robotic manipulation by mapping multimodal observations and language instructions to actions guan2025efficient,li2025vla,li2025comprehensive,sapkota2025vision,wang2025vision . However, learning an effective end-to-end mapping from multimodal perception to robotic actions requires extensive, high-quality demonstration data liu2025aligning,ma2026survey . To address this challenge, recent VLA models adopt a ``think-before-acting'' paradigm through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning guo2025vla,ye2025vla,yin2025deepthinkvla .By reasoning over task goals, visual observations, and object relations before execution, these models decompose complex instructions and adapt action plans to environmental feedback. Existing VLA paradigms include language-based reasoning zawalski2024robotic,lee2025molmoact,qu2508eo,huang2026fast , which carry out reasoning in language domain and reasoning in vision, exemplified by CoT-VLA's decomposition of predicted goals into visual subgoals zhao2025cotvla and VLA-Thinker's repeated incorporation of intermediate state images~ wang2026vla . As shown in Figure fig:compare (a), language-based reasoning loses fine-grained visual details and achieves lower success rates. In contrast, incorporating updated visual information during reasoning can mitigate drift from the actual environment wang2026vla (Figure fig:compare (b)). In general, existing approaches face two limitations: (i) reliance on observed states rather than future predictions, and (ii) substantial computational overhead from repeated reasoning rollouts. Specifically, existing approaches primarily reason over observed states and plan subsequent actions based on the current environment, without explicitly anticipating how the environment may evolve under different decisions. Meanwhile, reasoning in VLA models need to perform full spatiotemporal reasoning rollouts repeatedly at every inference step, introducing substantial computation overhead. To address these issues, we propose a visual reasoning framework for VLA models with two core mechanisms: latent spatiotemporal reasoning and scene gist memory. Latent spatiotemporal reasoning enables the model to imagine future scene evolution in visual representation space, exploring plausible action trajectories and their potential outcomes. These imagined futures guide action selection, as shown in Figure fig:compare (b). It is inspired by human reasoning process, which imagines how a scene might unfold under different candidate actions and makes decisions based on expected consequences atance2001episodic . For example, when crossing a street, we consider multiple possible futures conditioned on our own actions such as crossing, waiting, or speeding up, then choose the safest action. This anticipation evaluates candidate behaviors through the imagined consequences rather than merely extrapolating scene evolution independently of actions conti2021harnessing . To reduce computational overhead, our proposed Scene Gist Memory internalizes reasoning-derived scene--behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token. This token captures general scene context and corresponding action patterns rather than preserving the complete future reasoning trajectory. During inference, the gist encoder predicts the Scene Gist directly from the current context, allowing the model to bypass the explicit future-reasoning pathway while retaining reasoning-derived behavioral guidance (Figure fig:brain ). It's inspired by human behavioral psychology that repeated experience in familiar environments helps consolidate learned behaviors into procedural memory involving the basal ganglia~ wulf2010motor,wood2016psychology . This memory supports rapid responses with less deliberation, reducing cognitive effort and decision time. For example, familiarity with a home allows a person to head directly to the kitchen for coffee without searching the entire house. Repeated experience reinforces the association between the familiar scene and the corresponding navigation behavior. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: Our framework incorporates Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning, enabling VLA models to learn to imagine task-relevant scene evolution in visual representation space. These anticipated scene dynamics guide action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation. We further introduce Scene Gist Memory, which internalizes reasoning-derived scene--behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token. It enables the model to reuse this knowledge in corresponding scenarios, preserving reasoning benefits while bypassing explicit future imagination and full reasoning rollouts at inference. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our framework. For example, IG-VLA achieves an 85.6 success rate on LIBERO-Plus's challenging Language suite, outperforming the strongest baseline by nearly 6 . Meanwhile, the gist policy requires only 169.5\,ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000, achieving , and speedups over FastWAM-IDM (1,081\,ms), FastWAM (1-step) (302\,ms) and ImageWAM (263\,ms), respectively. Related Work VLA Models. Recent advances in embodied AI have shifted robot learning toward foundation VLA models that directly map visual observations and language instructions into executable actions brohan2022rt,mees2024octo,nvidia2025gr00t,yang2025magma,pertsch2025fast,driess2026knowledge . OpenVLA kim2024openvla adopts an end-to-end policy learning framework for language-conditioned robotic manipulation. black2024pi_0 extends this paradigm with scalable policy learning across more diverse robotic tasks. HAMSTER li2025hamster strengthens spatial reasoning through structured visual representations, while TraceVLA zheng2025tracevla further incorporates 2D visual trajectories to enhance the alignment between perception and action. VLA Reasonings. CoT improves LLM performance in mathematical reasoning, code generation, and question answering wei2022chain,yeo2025demystifying , motivating explicit reasoning in VLA models huang2026thinkact . Existing approaches mainly follow several directions. Prompting-based methods such as EcoT zawalski2024robotic use supervised reasoning traces to decompose tasks into intermediate subgoals before action execution. Data-centric methods, including RAD clark2025action , combine human videos with LLMs to construct reasoning-action demonstrations for policy learning. Another line of work, represented by CoT-VLA zhao2025cot , replaces textual reasoning with visual subgoal representations to better align planning with robot perception. Recently, reinforcement learning shao2024deepseekmath,guo2025deepseek has been adopted to optimize reasoning policies under verifiable rewards, where GRPO encourages more effective reasoning trajectories feng2026video,tan2025reason,liu2025visual . However, current methods often require costly reasoning supervision and sophisticated reward engineering huang2026fast . Methodology In this section, we present IG-VLA, a VLA framework that incorporates two core mechanisms, reasoning over possible future predicted trajectories to improve robustness and task success in long-horizon embodied tasks, and scene gist token to capture a coarse-grained scene-behavioral impression for efficient inference, as shown in Figure fig:framework . Our model builds upon a conventional VLA architecture, and incorporates spatiotemporal reasoning modules and gist modules. Vision Encoder and Vision-Language Backbone. A pretrained vision encoder maps the current visual observation to visual tokens: . These tokens compactly encode scene semantics and spatial structure, supporting subsequent spatiotemporal reasoning. A pretrained vision-language backbone jointly processes and the tokenized language instruction : , where encodes the current observation and task instruction, providing multimodal context for future-scene reasoning and action generation. Rather than autoregressively generating pixel-level frames, predicts future states directly in visual representation space: where denotes the predicted scene representation at the subsequent -th future step. Together, these latent states form a compact trajectory of anticipated spatiotemporal dynamics. Our framework consists of a reasoning policy that predicts the future actions based on the current multimodal representation and the predicted latent future representation: where denotes predicted action at the future step. It explicitly exploits anticipated scene evolution to determine future actions and provides reasoning-informed action guidance in training. Gist Compressor, Gist Encoder, and Gist Policy. We introduce a gist compressor and a gist encoder to summarize reasoning-derived information and predict it directly from the current context, respectively. After the complete latent spatiotemporal reasoning rollout, the implicit action reasoner fuses the current visual--language context with all predicted future representations to obtain a reasoning-enhanced representation . title: RoboBridge: A Self-Evolving Embodied Agent Framework for Sim-to-Real Transfer
summary: A key challenge in bringing embodied intelligence into the real world is transferring capabilities from simulation to reality and enabling agents to continually adapt after deployment. End-to-end vision-language-action policies provide strong manipulation capabilities, but their transfer to physical environments typically relies on calibrating simulated visual and dynamical conditions, collecting additional target-domain demonstrations, and optimizing the policy through further training. Tool-using embodied agents offer flexible task orchestration, yet existing systems primarily emphasize task execution and experience reuse within a given environment, with limited support for transferring procedural knowledge and continuously adapting it across simulation and reality. We propose RoboBridge, a framework that treats sim-to-real transfer as the continued adaptation of executable task skills. The agent represents task knowledge as procedures connecting task intent, observations, tool operations, and outcome verification. Interaction feedback is used to generate candidate skill revisions, which are evaluated before being persisted or rejected. A pretrained vision-language-action policy is exposed as a reusable action tool and enhanced with inference-time guidance, enabling fine-grained execution without retraining the underlying policy. RoboBridge grounds transferable skills in task semantics and interaction interfaces shared across simulation and reality. This representation preserves reusable task structure while allowing environment-dependent operations to be selectively revised through real-world execution feedback. We evaluate the framework on LIBERO-PRO and corresponding physical tasks, studying both skill evolution and post-transfer adaptation. Our framework provides a route from one-shot policy deployment to continual procedural learning across environments.

Introduction Reliable sim-to-real transfer requires robotic systems to preserve task performance across differences in visual observations and physical dynamics zhao2020sim2real . End-to-end vision-language-action models provide fine-grained manipulation capabilities by mapping visual observations and language instructions to action sequences kim2024openvla,black2024pi_0 . The policy-centered pathway illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser includes adapting simulation conditions using real-world experience chebotar2018closing . For pretrained VLA models, adaptation to new robotic settings commonly involves target-domain demonstrations and policy fine-tuning kim2025oft . In this formulation, task knowledge is largely embedded in model parameters and learned action distributions. This makes it difficult to isolate a reusable task procedure and selectively revise it when execution conditions change, tying procedural adaptation closely to policy optimization. Tool-using embodied agents offer a way to make task procedures explicit singh2022progprompt,rana2023sayplan . An agent harness provides the observation and tool interfaces through which the agent organizes subtasks, invokes operations, and verifies their outcomes liu2026guava . Successful procedures can then be retained as skills for subsequent execution wang2023voyager,lu2026aspire . Feedback-based memory updates and skill refinement extend this reuse across interactions shinn2023reflexion,wang2026self , and recent robotic systems further incorporate repair validation and validation-gated skill updates lu2026aspire,ding2026zetta . Sim-to-real deployment requires these mechanisms to govern which parts of a transferred procedure remain applicable and how the others should be refined using target-environment feedback. Meanwhile, task decomposition and tool selection still require an underlying capability to execute continuous, fine-grained manipulation yu2023language . Recent harnesses address this execution requirement by exposing frozen VLA policies as reusable manipulation primitives zhang2026harness . This perspective motivates a framework that combines revisable task knowledge with the manipulation capabilities of pretrained policies. We propose RoboBridge, a self-evolving embodied agent framework for sim-to-real transfer of procedural skills. RoboBridge incorporates a pretrained VLA policy as a reusable action tool within an agent harness. The policy supplies short manipulation segments, while the agent determines how these operations are organized, when they should be invoked, and whether their outcomes satisfy the task. Task knowledge is stored as procedural skills connecting intent, observations, tool operations, and outcome verification. This organization preserves pretrained execution capabilities while exposing task procedures for revision through interaction. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser , skills evolved in simulation are reused in reality through aligned task semantics and interaction interfaces, with action tools instantiated for each environment. Real-world execution feedback then supports continued skill adaptation. Effective transfer requires both reliable revision of the transferred procedures and accurate execution of their local operations. Reliable execution presents a complementary challenge: even a suitable task procedure can fail when a frozen policy produces actions that do not meet the current subtask requirements liu2026vls . Prior work has explored adapting pretrained policy behavior during inference through external guidance or verification wang2024steering,wu2025foresight,liu2026vls . RoboBridge therefore augments the policy tool with inference-time guidance. The agent determines whether guidance is needed and configures a reward specification from the subtask objective, execution constraints, and observed feedback. This reward steers action generation toward the intended operation while keeping the policy parameters fixed. Skill evolution thus adjusts the procedure across episodes, while inference-time guidance adapts action generation within an invocation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: A self-evolving framework for procedural sim-to-real transfer. We integrate pretrained action capabilities with explicit task skills, enabling procedures evolved in simulation to be reused through aligned interaction interfaces and further adapted from real-world feedback. Controlled skill evolution. We develop a feedback-driven process for adding, revising, and deleting procedural knowledge, with validation governing which updates are persisted and which are rejected or rolled back. Adaptive policy-tool orchestration. We enable the agent to determine when to invoke the pretrained policy, when to activate inference-time guidance, and how to configure subtask rewards, supporting context-dependent execution with frozen policy parameters. Related Work End-to-End Embodied Models End-to-end embodied models learn to map visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions. Early systems such as RT-1 brohan2022rt and RT-2 brohan2023rt established this paradigm, while later models expanded its scope through embodied multimodal reasoning, multi-robot datasets, and generalist policies, including PaLM-E driess2023palm , Open X-Embodiment o2024open , Octo team2024octo , OpenVLA kim2024openvla , and black2024pi_0 . These models improve generalization by increasing the diversity of training tasks, observations, robot embodiments, and demonstrations, but their behavior remains primarily encoded in a fixed policy. To address the gap between simulation and physical deployment, existing approaches increase the diversity of simulated observations tobin2017domain , perturb simulated dynamics peng2018sim , or adapt the simulator distribution using informative variations and posterior estimation mehta2020active, muratore2022neural . Recent data-centric methods further scale simulated experiences and adaptation data to improve transfer across tasks and robot embodiments~ liu2025dexscale , while inference-time steering adjusts a frozen policy during execution~ liu2026vls . These approaches use a single end-to-end policy to map observations and instructions to actions, leaving adaptation coupled to the policy itself. Our framework instead uses an agent to organize reusable skills and invoke action tools, so the transferred procedure can be revised in the target environment without retraining the entire policy. Embodied Agents Embodied-agent research introduces explicit reasoning, tool use, and feedback into robotic execution. Early systems grounded language in executable affordances and used environment feedback for closed-loop planning ahn2022can, huang2022inner , while program-based approaches synthesized control logic or composed spatial value functions for manipulation liang2023code, huang2023voxposer . Subsequent work explored skill bootstrapping, lifelong skill libraries, and open-vocabulary adaptation through interaction and memory zhang2023bootstrap, tziafas2024lifelong, zhao2025vla . Recent systems have further studied workflow reasoning, self-directed skill acquisition, feedback-based repair, and continual adaptation in simulated or physical environments lu2026aspire, ding2026zetta, wang2026self, nie2026teach, liu2026guava, lei2026ace, zhang2026playful . These studies show that explicit procedures, persistent memory, and execution feedback can extend embodied reasoning beyond direct policy execution. Their primary focus, however, varies between workflow planning, skill discovery, memory expansion, and runtime self-improvement. Our work focuses on the migration process itself: a skill is treated as a revisable task hypothesis, and feedback from the target environment determines which parts of the transferred procedure should be retained, modified, or removed. Method RoboBridge integrates skill-guided execution, inference-time action guidance, and feedback-driven skill evolution into the closed loop illustrated in Figure~ fig:method_main . During task execution, the agent consults the active skill and current observations to select tool operations, then uses task checks and program outputs to guide subsequent decisions. When invoking the pretrained end-to-end action model, the agent can construct a reward function to steer action refinement during denoising while keeping model parameters fixed. Execution logs from the rollout provide evidence for adding, deleting, or replacing skill content. Candidate skills are evaluated through task execution, and validated improvements are retained to guide subsequent rollouts while unsuccessful revisions are rejected. This loop allows execution experience to improve reusable procedures and updated procedures to guide future actions. With aligned task semantics and compatible observation and tool interfaces, skills evolved in the simulator can initialize real-world execution and continue to adapt through physical feedback. Each task is specified by an instruction and a completion condition . title: CHASE-VLA: Post-Training Quantization Framework for Vision-Language-Action Models with Chunk-Aware Scale Estimation
comment: Accepted at ACCV 2026. 22 pages, including references and supplementary material
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to continuous robot actions, but a diffusion-based action expert (AE) poses a key challenge for low-bit post-training quantization (PTQ). The AE is repeatedly invoked across denoising steps and policy queries, where fixed calibration scales can be mismatched with activation ranges that vary with denoising progress and intended motion. We propose CHASE-VLA, a chunk-aware PTQ method that exploits a VLA-specific signal readily available from the policy: the generated action chunk, including its unexecuted future suffix. Rather than relying only on static scale matching for AE layers, CHASE-VLA combines the previously generated chunk as causal action context with denoising step group information to adapt AE activation scales. This enables W4A4 quantization of both MLP and attention projections in the repeated AE without modifying the pretrained policy. On LIBERO, CHASE-VLA achieves 97.3% average success rate on $π_{0.5}$ when both MLP and attention projections in the AE are quantized to W4A4, restoring FP16-level performance. CHASE-VLA also reduces the weight storage of the quantized AE linear layers by 73.4% and their single-chunk memory traffic by 70.9% and 71.2% on $π_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.6, respectively, with a predictor overhead of at most 1.26% of the saved storage.

The AE is repeatedly invoked across denoising steps and policy queries, where fixed calibration scales can be mismatched with activation ranges that vary with denoising progress and intended motion. We propose CHASE-VLA, a chunk-aware PTQ method that exploits a VLA-specific signal readily available from the policy: the generated action chunk, including its unexecuted future suffix. Rather than relying only on static scale matching for AE layers, CHASE-VLA combines the previously generated chunk as causal action context with denoising step group information to adapt AE activation scales. This enables W4A4 quantization of both MLP and attention projections in the repeated AE without modifying the pretrained policy. On LIBERO, CHASE-VLA achieves 97.3 average success rate on when both MLP and attention projections in the AE are quantized to W4A4, restoring FP16-level performance. CHASE-VLA also reduces the weight storage of the quantized AE linear layers by 73.4 and their single-chunk memory traffic by 70.9 and 71.2 on and GR00T N1.6, respectively, with a predictor overhead of at most 1.26 of the saved storage. Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a foundation for embodied intelligence by connecting vision-language understanding with executable robot control brohan2023rt1,brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,li2024cogact,black2024pi0,bjorck2025gr00t . By integrating visual perception, language understanding, high-level reasoning, and action generation within a single policy, these models allow robots to interpret natural language instructions, ground them in visual observations, and produce control commands for manipulation tasks brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,team2024octo,li2024cogact,black2024pi0,kim2025openvlaoft . Previous VLA systems typically treat action generation as a lightweight output interface, where robot actions are discretized into language-compatible tokens and predicted through the Vision-Language Model (VLM) output head rather than a dedicated action-generation module brohan2023rt1,brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,bu2025univla,wang2025vqvla . In contrast, recent VLA architectures increasingly preserve the perception and reasoning capability of the VLM branch while introducing a specialized diffusion-based action expert (AE) for continuous trajectory generation chi2023diffusionpolicy,team2024octo,li2024cogact,liu2024rdt1b,black2024pi0,wen2025dexvla,wen2025diffusionvla . This transition makes the AE a central component of modern VLA policies, because it directly determines trajectory smoothness, temporal consistency, and control robustness during robot execution li2024cogact,black2024pi0,wen2025dexvla,zhang2026quantvla,xu2026qvla,xu2026daptq . Fig.~ fig:example1 summarizes this architectural trend: the VLM branch provides vision-language grounding, while a separate diffusion-based AE repeatedly refines continuous action chunks for robot control. Unlike action-token decoders, a diffusion-based AE generates action chunks through iterative refinement, repeatedly processing transformer blocks across denoising steps chi2023diffusionpolicy,peebles2023scalable,li2024cogact . This computation recurs at every replanning step throughout a rollout, so weight reads and activation movement accumulate over the entire trajectory zhang2026quantvla . The AE is therefore a primary target for deployment-oriented quantization because it directly affects both memory traffic and control fidelity in repeated action generation xu2026qvla . Among compression options, post-training quantization (PTQ) is a practical approach for pretrained policies because it avoids the robot data collection, rollout validation, and iterative action generation required by quantization-aware training nagel2020adaround,jacob2018quantization,wang2025bitvla . This makes low-bit PTQ attractive for deployment, but the quantized AE must still preserve continuous-control precision across repeated denoising and replanning throughout the executed trajectory xu2026qvla,zhang2026quantvla . Low-bit PTQ for the AE therefore differs from language-model quantization in both sensitivity and execution pattern xiao2023smoothquant,frantar2023gptq,lin2024awq,ashkboos2024quarot,zhang2026quantvla . Previous VLA PTQ methods keep sensitive attention projections in floating point and quantize only the MLP projections zhang2026quantvla,xu2026daptq , leaving a large fraction of the repeated AE cost unquantized. This limitation stems from a mismatch between static calibration scales and the dynamic activation behavior of the repeatedly executed AE ptq4dit,qdit,viditq,zhang2026quantvla . As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:action_expert_distribution (a), the AE is invoked in two nested loops: it refines each action chunk over multiple denoising steps and regenerates a new chunk at every replanning step throughout a rollout chi2023diffusionpolicy,black2024pi0,li2024cogact . Across denoising steps, the AE produces physical control values through iterative refinement, so its activations change with the denoising step rather than following a fixed forward-pass distribution zhang2026quantvla . The activation range also changes with the action context. Each policy query is conditioned on a different observation, instruction, and robot state, so the generated motion, and therefore the required activation scale, can vary substantially from one chunk to the next black2024pi0,li2024cogact,xu2026daptq . Fig.~ fig:action_expert_distribution (b) shows this behavior within individual AE linear layers, where the maximum absolute activation varies across both denoising steps and action contexts. A single calibration-derived scale cannot accommodate these variations without either clipping broad activations or losing resolution for fine control zhang2026quantvla,zheng2026dyqvla . Across repeated denoising and replanning, the resulting local errors can accumulate into trajectory-level control errors xu2026daptq . Addressing this mismatch requires activation scales that depend on both the denoising step and the motion being generated ptq4dit,qdit,zheng2026dyqvla . However, the action context of the current chunk is not causally available before the AE produces that chunk, making direct current-chunk scale selection impractical. Chunk-based VLA execution provides a causal source of action context for resolving this causality constraint. Modern VLA policies predict short action chunks at each policy query instead of a single immediate action chi2023diffusionpolicy,li2024cogact,black2024pi0, bjorck2025gr00t . Each chunk constitutes a short-horizon plan conditioned on the current observation, language instruction, and robot state. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:example1 , the robot executes only an initial prefix of the chunk and then replans after receiving a new observation chi2023diffusionpolicy,black2024pi0, bjorck2025gr00t . The remaining suffix is not executed because the next policy query generates a new chunk based on the updated observation. However, this suffix is still the policy's predicted continuation of the same trajectory whose prefix is executed. Thus, it provides an accessible signal of the intended near-future motion without additional rollouts or task-specific annotations. We propose CHASE-VLA, a chunk-aware PTQ method for low-bit quantization of diffusion-based VLA AEs. Instead of using fixed calibration scales, CHASE-VLA modulates calibrated activation scales with action-conditioned factors that are shared within groups of denoising steps. The conditioning signal is the previously generated action chunk, which compactly summarizes the intended near-future motion and enables scale selection to reflect both action context and denoising progress without modifying the AE architecture. Through adaptive scaling, CHASE-VLA supports 4-bit weight and activation quantization (W4A4) and mitigates the scale mismatch that typically arises from static PTQ. Unlike previous VLA PTQ methods, which keep sensitive attention projections in floating point for stability, CHASE-VLA extends W4A4 coverage beyond MLP layers to the attention projection layers within the repeated AE. By including these repeatedly invoked projections in the low-bit quantization target, CHASE-VLA achieves further reductions in memory traffic compared to MLP-only AE quantization. Our contributions are summarized as follows. We identify activation-scale mismatch across denoising steps and action contexts as a central barrier to low-bit PTQ for diffusion-based VLA AEs. CHASE-VLA expands the W4A4 AE target from MLP projections to both MLP and attention projections while keeping the pretrained policy and the AE architecture unchanged. Experiments on LIBERO across , GR00T N1.6, and CogACT show that this design largely preserves task success under the expanded W4A4 target, while an efficiency analysis on and GR00T N1.6 quantifies reductions in quantized AE linear weights and single-chunk memory traffic with modest predictor overhead. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models Diffusion Policy demonstrated that modeling robot actions as a conditional denoising process is effective for generating smooth and multimodal action trajectories chi2023diffusionpolicy . Following this direction, recent systems such as CogACT, , GR00T, and RDT employ diffusion-based action generation modules to couple high-level vision-language reasoning with low-level continuous control li2024cogact,black2024pi0,black2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t,liu2024rdt1b . These AE architectures are attractive because they predict action chunks rather than isolated actions, allowing temporally correlated future controls to be generated as a coherent trajectory chi2023diffusionpolicy,black2025pi05, bjorck2025gr00t . The chunk-based formulation enhances trajectory smoothness and execution reliability, which are critical for contact-rich manipulation and long-horizon robotic tasks chi2023diffusionpolicy,li2024cogact,liu2024rdt1b,bjorck2025gr00t . However, this property introduces a substantial deployment burden as the AE repeatedly evaluates action chunks during multiple denoising steps. The AE is therefore a major determinant of continuous-control quality and a key target for low-bit deployment zhang2026quantvla, xu2026daptq . Efficient VLA Inference and Compression Recent studies have explored several approaches to reducing the inference cost of VLA models without sacrificing their embodied control capabilities. VLA-Cache further improves runtime efficiency by reusing cached key-value features for static visual tokens, and MoLe-VLA dynamically skips non-essential computation through mixture-of-layers routing in the language backbone xu2026vla,molevla . Most of these efforts primarily modify the model architecture or inference execution path, while the numerical precision of VLA policies remains less explored. For lightweight deployment under tight memory and bandwidth budgets, this leaves quantization as an important requirement beyond architectural or execution-level optimization. This requirement is particularly relevant to diffusion-based AEs, where low-bit inference must preserve action-chunk-dependent activation distributions and denoising step dynamics. Post-Training Quantization for LLMs, VLMs, DiTs, and VLAs For VLA AE quantization, a central distinction is not only quantization scope but also the information used for activation-scale selection during iterative action generation. title: SimpleTouch: Can Vision-Language-Action Models Master Contact-Rich Manipulation Without Tactile Policy Pretraining?
summary: Tactile sensing provides essential contact information for robotic manipulation, yet incorporating it into pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models remains challenging. A common concern is that simply introducing touch during task-specific fine-tuning may fail to bridge the cross-modal gap, yielding limited gains or even reduced success. Consequently, existing methods often rely on large-scale tactile policy pretraining or separate visuotactile alignment, adding data requirements and training stages. We introduce SimpleTouch, a simple VLA extension that augments $π_{0.5}$ with a tactile expert, to test whether these additional stages are necessary. Leveraging all tokens from a frozen pretrained tactile encoder, the expert learns from action supervision and multi-horizon prediction of future tactile latents. This single-stage training uses only task demonstrations, without additional tactile policy pretraining or separate alignment. With 50 demonstrations per task, SimpleTouch achieves the highest success rate among evaluated methods on all six UniVTAC tasks. Its average success rate reaches 77.5%, compared with 45.2% for FTP-$π_{0.5}$ and 66.7% for FTP-1, corresponding to gains of 32.3 and 10.8 percentage points, respectively. Across four real-world tasks, it averages 71.3%, exceeding FTP-1 by 8.8 percentage points. These results demonstrate that, given pretrained VLA and tactile representations, additional tactile policy pretraining is not a prerequisite for strong performance on these tasks, offering a simpler route to contact-rich manipulation.
