Project page: Introduction Robot manipulation has made substantial progress through learned policies~ zhao2023act,chi2023diffusionpolicy and pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) models~ kim2025openvla,black2024pi0 . Much of this progress has relied on visual perception as the primary interface for scene understanding. However, visual observations do not fully determine contact-rich interaction: two manipulation states can appear visually similar while requiring different actions because their contact geometry, deformation, or slip state differs~ li2014gelsight,yuan2017gelsight . Tactile sensing supplies local feedback about these otherwise hidden contact states, motivating policies that learn from touch and use it during manipulation~ xue2025rdp,huang2025tactilevla,lou2026dreamtac . However, adding touch to a pretrained policy does not automatically make it useful. Tactile observations lie outside the pretraining modalities of many VLA backbones, and directly incorporating them during fine-tuning can yield limited gains or even reduce success~ niu2026trex,li2026atvla,zhang2026tacvla . The central challenge is therefore not merely obtaining tactile features, but presenting them to a pretrained VLA in a form that preserves contact information while allowing the policy to learn their task-specific use from limited demonstrations. Representative responses include large-scale tactile policy pretraining, as in FTP-1~ yuan2026ftp , and separate visuotactile representation alignment, as in VITaL~ george2024vital . These routes provide useful priors but introduce additional data requirements and training stages. Meanwhile, pretrained tactile encoders already offer reusable contact representations~ zhao2025t3 . This distinction between acquiring tactile representations and learning a tactile policy motivates our question: given a pretrained VLA and tactile encoder, can a policy learn strong contact-rich manipulation from task-specific tactile demonstrations without additional tactile policy pretraining or a separate alignment stage? We introduce , a simple recipe that augments ~ intelligence2025pi05 with one tactile expert, without additional tactile policy pretraining or a separate alignment stage. Its design follows two principles. First, it preserves the pretrained tactile representation: we freeze the tactile encoder and retain all current tokens, including global and spatial features, as a stable source of contact information. Second, it learns the task-specific use of that representation through a tactile expert. The tactile expert processes current tactile features separately from the visual-language backbone, and the action expert reads them through layerwise attention. During joint training, the expert learns from both action supervision and multi-horizon prediction of future tactile latents through latent flow matching~ lipman2023flow . This task-trained pathway gives action generation direct access to high-fidelity tactile features. During task-level training, we jointly optimize the pretrained policy, including its visual-language backbone and action expert, together with the tactile expert, while keeping the tactile encoder frozen. With 50 demonstrations per task, achieves the highest success rate among the evaluated methods on all six UniVTAC~ chen2026univtac tasks. Its mean success rate of 77.5 exceeds those of FTP- and the pretrained FTP-1 policy by 32.3 and 10.8 percentage points, respectively. Across four real-world tasks, averages 71.3 , surpassing FTP-1 by 8.8 points and showing improvements in real-world experiments as well. At deployment, the tactile expert processes the current observation once, and its layerwise cache is reused throughout action-flow integration; future tactile prediction is used only as training supervision. Together, these results show that, given strong pretrained VLA and tactile representations, a frozen tactile representation and task-trained tactile expert can achieve strong performance without additional tactile policy pretraining or explicit alignment. Related Work sec:related Generalist Policy Learning. Generalist policy learning converts broad visual and language priors into continuous robot control across diverse tasks. The series couples pretrained vision-language backbones with flow-matching action experts~ black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05 . Other VLA systems investigate large-scale data, efficient fine-tuning, execution, generalization, and modular policy development~ oneill2023openx,khazatsky2024droid,bjorck2025groot,pertsch2025fast,kim2025oft,cai2026xiaomi,chen2025internvla,community2026starvla . Complementary world-action models incorporate predictive visual or feature dynamics into action learning, including Video Prediction Policy, LingBot-VA, Motus, DreamZero, LaWAM, and Fast-WAM~ hu2024vpp,li2026lingbot,zhang2026lingbot2,bi2025motus,ye2026dreamzero,chen2026lawam,yuan2026fastwam . These directions establish strong reusable architectures and priors for action generation, but their observation interfaces are primarily built around vision, language, and proprioception rather than local tactile contact feedback. Tactile Policy Learning. Tactile policy learning can be organized by where contact-sensitive priors are acquired. One route first learns how tactile observations participate in control through large-scale tactile policy pretraining or tactile-grounded mid-training, as in FTP-1, the -TWAM/ -VTLA family, and T-Rex~ yuan2026ftp,neote2026n0twam,neote2026n0vtla,niu2026trex . A second route aligns tactile and visual representations before policy learning, including VITaL, UniTouch, and VT-MUSE~ george2024vital,yang2024unitouch,xu2026vtmuse . Both front-load resources beyond task-level learning. Other methods explore task-level tactile reasoning, adaptive fusion, or reactive feedback~ yu2023mimictouch,huang2024threedvitac,heng2025vitacformer,liu2025vitamin,huang2025tactilevla,bi2025vlatouch,li2026atvla,xue2025rdp , while predictive approaches model future contact or multimodal dynamics~ lou2026dreamtac,niu2026touchdreaming,zheng2026omnivta . Across these settings, simply adding tactile input during fine-tuning does not consistently improve success~ yuan2026ftp,niu2026trex,li2026atvla . An open question is whether strong contact-rich control instead requires an additional tactile policy-learning or alignment stage once pretrained VLA and tactile representations are available. Pretrained Tactile Encoders. Pretrained tactile encoders address representation acquisition rather than action generation. Early work such as T-Dex learns self-supervised tactile embeddings from robotic play for downstream dexterous control~ guzey2023tdex . Sparsh and Sparsh-X learn general-purpose representations from self-supervised vision-based and multisensory touch data, respectively~ higuera2024sparsh,higuera2025sparshx ; the AnyTouch series models static and dynamic tactile signals across sensors and downstream tasks~ feng2025anytouch,feng2026anytouch2 . T3 combines sensor-specific encoders with a shared Transformer trained across sensors and tasks~ zhao2025t3 . Such encoders provide reusable contact-sensitive features across tasks and sensing configurations. This differs from tactile policy pretraining: encoders supply sensory representations, whereas policy pretraining also learns how touch influences action generation. Existing encoder work does not prescribe the downstream action interface or establish whether a separate tactile policy-training stage remains necessary. A detailed review of related work is provided in Appendix~ app:extended_related_work . title: Skill2Real: Agentic Skill Learning for Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Robot Manipulation
summary: Transferring robotic skills from simulation to reality requires task knowledge that remains usable across differences in perception, dynamics, and embodiment. We introduce Skill2Real, an agentic policy framework that learns executable skills through a shared application programming interface (API). A Proposer-Verifier-Governor (PVG) loop uses privileged simulation evidence to diagnose outcomes and validate updates, while keeping learned skills grounded in public observations and API semantics. The Cerebellum first acquires local manipulation skills; the Brain then learns task-level composition with the Cerebellum frozen. Both memories transfer to the real robot without task-policy fine-tuning or skill-memory updates. As GPT-5.6 Sol learns skills on LIBERO-90, evaluating each frozen checkpoint with GPT-6 Astra raises LIBERO-Pro Long success from 2.0% to 56.3%, without training on Pro Long. Independent Robosuite training reaches 85.1% and 89.4% mean success with Sol and Opus 5 across seven tasks, respectively. Frozen Sol-trained LIBERO-90 skills achieve 78.75% mean completion across four real-world manipulation tasks with Astra. Removing the Verifier or Governor during LIBERO-90 training lowers final Pro Long success by 17.3 and 13.3 percentage points, respectively. These results support learning and transferring a hierarchy of executable skills through a common robot interface.
full_text: 0pt Sim-to-real learning commonly adapts policies or representations to domain variation, often directing the learning budget toward task-agnostic low-level representations at the expense of task-level knowledge. Skill2Real builds on cross-domain grounding from foundation vision-language models (VLMs) to acquire validated, reusable skills in simulation through a shared code-based policy interface. In its asymmetric Proposer--Verifier--Governor (PVG) loop, the Proposer acts from public observations and API returns, the Verifier diagnoses outcomes with privileged simulation evidence, and the Governor admits updates supported by validation rollouts. A Cerebellum learns reusable local manipulation skills; a Brain then composes the frozen library into long-horizon programs with planning and recovery. At deployment, this hierarchy is grounded in real observations through the same interface. On unseen LIBERO-Pro Long, frozen LIBERO-90 skills raise success from 2.0 to 56.3 with Astra and from 0.5 to 49.0 with Opus 5. Robosuite success reaches 85.1--89.4 across seven tasks. On a real UR5e, the same agent's mean completion rises from 27.50 to 78.75 across four tasks with Skill2Real, a controlled gain that, with cross-model improvements, shows Skill2Real adds a capability orthogonal to the foundation model by learning transferable task knowledge in simulation. Project page: skill2real.github.io . =-1 Introduction section:introduction Zero-shot sim-to-real robot manipulation aims to convert experience acquired in simulation into behavior that can be executed by a physical robot without real-world task training. Simulation provides a scalable environment for learning such behavior, but discrepancies in appearance, dynamics, contact, and embodiment can prevent policies learned in simulation from transferring reliably to reality~ 8202133,8793789 . For long-horizon manipulation, the challenge extends beyond transferring individual actions: a robot must reliably execute local manipulation skills, compose them into task-level behavior~ pmlr-v100-gupta20a,pmlr-v267-shi25d , and recover when intermediate actions fail. =-1 Existing methods leave a central bottleneck unresolved: learning reusable, composable task knowledge from privileged simulation evidence without spending the learning budget on task-agnostic low-level representations. Randomization and asymmetric actor--critic methods improve transfer by adapting neural policies or representations~ 8202133,Pinto-RSS-18 . Appearance-heavy domain randomization can therefore spend much of the learning budget modeling task-irrelevant variation in lighting and texture rather than acquiring reusable manipulation knowledge. Code-generation methods make behavior composable, but assemble supplied primitives rather than acquire local skills and task strategies from experience~ codeaspolicies2022 . Representative skill-library systems accumulate programs through human guidance or real-world execution feedback~ 2ddda900980a441888ee44f0cdee4b2e,lu2026aspire . Skill2Real instead relies on foundation VLMs for cross-domain grounding and directs simulation learning toward validated, hierarchical executable knowledge. =-1 We introduce Skill2Real, an agentic policy framework that learns executable robot skills through a shared code-based policy interface. The key idea is to separate the information used to supervise skill learning from the information required to execute learned skills: simulator privilege can evaluate and improve behavior, while persistent skill knowledge is expressed entirely through public observations and API semantics. The shared interface defines the transfer boundary: programs invoke operations with common semantics, while each backend provides its own perception, calibration, and low-level execution. This separation lets task knowledge be reused across simulation and reality without incorporating simulator-only state into the deployed policy. =-1 Skill2Real realizes this idea with an asymmetric Proposer--Verifier--Governor (PVG) loop that learns a two-level skill hierarchy. The Proposer executes programs from public observations and proposes reusable updates; the Verifier turns privileged simulation outcomes into publicly grounded diagnoses; and the Governor aggregates evidence across validation rollouts to admit supported updates into memory. Stage I learns Cerebellum skills for reusable local manipulation. Stage II freezes this library and learns Brain skills that compose it into long-horizon task programs with planning and recovery. At deployment, the Proposer grounds both frozen memories in current observations through the real code-based policy interface. =-1 Our experiments test whether frozen hierarchical knowledge generalizes across task suites, Proposers, and the real robot. As frozen LIBERO-90 libraries~ NEURIPS2023_8c3c6668 progress from no memory through the Cerebellum to the full hierarchy, success on unseen LIBERO-Pro Long tasks~ zhou2025liberopro rises from 2.0 to 35.3 to 56.3 with Astra and from 0.5 to 29.3 to 49.0 with Opus 5, showing that both skill levels transfer across Proposers beyond the source tasks. Across seven single-arm and bimanual Robosuite tasks~ zhu2020robosuite , independently learned libraries raise mean success from 16.6 to 85.1 with Sol and from 19.4 to 89.4 with Opus 5, demonstrating consistent gains across Proposers. On the real UR5e, the full Brain--Cerebellum hierarchy reaches 78.75 mean task completion versus 56.25 with local skills alone, confirming the value of task-level composition for long-horizon behavior. =-1 Our main contributions are: [leftmargin=*] We introduce Skill2Real, an agentic policy framework that learns executable robot programs in simulation and transfers frozen skill knowledge through a shared code-based policy interface using only public observations at deployment, without real-world task-policy adaptation. We develop an asymmetric Proposer--Verifier--Governor scheme: the Proposer acts on public observations, the Verifier translates privileged execution evidence into public feedback, and the Governor admits updates supported by validation rollouts. We develop a hierarchical policy learning strategy in which the Cerebellum learns reusable local manipulation skills and the Brain learns long-horizon compositions conditioned on the frozen Cerebellum library, enabling task-level planning and recovery. Related Work section:related_work Sim-to-Real Robot Learning. Classical sim-to-real methods primarily bridge visual, dynamics, and execution gaps by learning policies or representations that are invariant to domain shift. Domain randomization~ 8202133 and dynamics randomization~ Sim2Real2018 expose the learner to controlled variation, while privileged critics~ Pinto-RSS-18 , real-world adaptation~ 8793789 , and active randomization~ pmlr-v100-mehta20a provide additional training signals or target-domain experience when the gap is difficult to model. Foundation vision-language-action models instead bring broadly pretrained representations that can reason across heterogeneous observations, tasks, and embodiments: RT-2~ pmlr-v229-zitkovich23a and Open X~ OpenX24 scale such learning, while Octo~ Ghosh-RSS-24 and OpenVLA~ pmlr-v270-kim25c make generalist policies more accessible. Building on the cross-domain reasoning capability of foundation VLMs, Skill2Real learns transferable task-level knowledge in the form of validated, executable skills and task programs, without learning a new representation from scratch. The frozen skills are deployed through a shared code-based policy interface: privileged state and evaluation are used only during simulation training, while the real backend supplies perception, calibration, and low-level execution. =-1 Language Agents and Code Policies. Language-conditioned policies provide a natural interface for composing robot behavior. Code as Policies~ codeaspolicies2022 and ProgPrompt~ 10161317 generate executable programs, while SayCan~ pmlr-v205-ichter23a grounds language plans in physically feasible affordances. Recent agentic systems expand beyond fixed skill sets: Agentic Skill Discovery~ zhao2024agentic bootstraps skills and success criteria, CaP-X~ fu2026capx studies feedback-driven coding-agent improvement, and ASPIRE~ lu2026aspire executes, diagnoses, repairs, and validates robot programs. Playful Agentic Robot Learning~ zhang2026playful and ENPIRE~ xiao2026enpireagenticrobotpolicy further investigate autonomous exploration and real-world policy evolution. Zetta~ ding2026zetta evolves code-based runtime critics and recovery skills around frozen base policies, combining action-level monitoring with validation-gated harness updates. It also demonstrates zero-shot transfer of learned recovery skills. Skill2Real is a multi-agent decision-making system in which the Proposer generates executable robot programs, the Verifier diagnoses their outcomes using privileged simulation evidence, and the Governor decides which validated updates enter persistent skill memory. Together, the agents learn a two-level hierarchy of local skills and task programs that is deployed as frozen, publicly grounded knowledge through the shared interface. =-1 Robot Skill Learning and Hierarchical Policies. Hierarchical reinforcement learning separates short-horizon control from long-horizon decisions. Options~ sutton1999between , MAXQ~ dietterich2000hierarchical , and HIRO~ NEURIPS2018_e6384711 establish temporal abstraction through subpolicies, value decompositions, and subgoal-conditioned control. Relay Policy Learning~ pmlr-v100-gupta20a and SPiRL~ pmlr-v155-pertsch21a show that reusable stages or skill priors can improve long-horizon manipulation. More recent systems build semantic or persistent skill libraries, including Lifelong Robot Library Learning~ 2ddda900980a441888ee44f0cdee4b2e , AtomSkill~ zhu2025learning , and Hi Robot~ pmlr-v267-shi25d ; MemoryVLA~ shi2025memoryvla , MemoryVAM~ jiang2026memoryvam , RoboHarness~ huang2026roboharness , RoboHiMan~ chen2025robohiman , RoboPARA~ duan2026roboparadualarmrobotplanning , and RigPI~ he2026rigpidynamicparameteridentification study memory, policy routing, hierarchical evaluation, task planning, or dynamics identification for manipulation. Their transfer units are typically policies, latent skills, fixed stages, or episodic records. Skill2Real instead learns a two-level hierarchy of reusable skills. The Cerebellum acquires and freezes validated local manipulation skills, while the Brain learns task-level skills that compositionally recombine the local library into long-horizon programs. Reuse and composition at both levels support generalization across tasks, scenes, and deployment domains through the shared interface. =-1 Method section:method Skill2Real transfers a frozen hierarchy of executable Cerebellum and Brain skills learned in simulation, rather than model parameters. This transfer builds on the premise that foundation VLMs provide representations capable of zero-shot generalization from simulated to real-world visual domains, while the shared code-based policy interface gives learned skills a common executable form in both. The Cerebellum learns reusable local manipulation skills, while the Brain learns task-level skills that compose them into long-horizon programs. =-1 Shared Code-Based Policy Interface subsection:agentic_policy The central intuition is to make learned robot knowledge executable and reusable across domains by representing it as programs over a public interface with common semantics. title: ManiPhysicsBench: Physics-Based Assessment of Object Preservation in VLA Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models aim to perform diverse manipulation tasks, but task success in existing rigid-body benchmarks does not indicate whether they preserve objects. We introduce ManiPhysicsZoo, which consolidates literature-supported material properties, 3D meshes, and supporting references into reusable object assets. Using these assets, a solver-based assessment computes grasp-specific damage thresholds from object geometry, material properties, and recorded grasp conditions and compares them with recorded contact forces to assess potential deformation and fracture. Building on these components, ManiPhysicsBench evaluates object preservation in LIBERO and SimplerEnv across three physics axes and three difficulty levels. Public VLA checkpoints show a substantial gap between task success and safe success, defined as task completion while preserving the object. Their gripper commands concentrate near full opening and closure, with largely similar aggregate distributions across objects, consistent with binary gripper supervision. We examine how object-specific continuous gripper labels change model behavior by retraining a VLA model. The retrained model shows more object-dependent gripping and higher safe success, but lower task success and limited generalization of object-preserving behavior.
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models aim to perform diverse manipulation tasks, but task success in existing rigid-body benchmarks does not indicate whether they preserve objects. We introduce , which consolidates literature-supported material properties, 3D meshes, and supporting references into reusable object assets. Using these assets, a solver-based assessment computes grasp-specific damage thresholds from object geometry, material properties, and recorded grasp conditions and compares them with recorded contact forces to assess potential deformation and fracture. The retrained model shows more object-dependent gripping and higher safe success, but lower task success and limited generalization of object-preserving behavior. Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models aim to perform a wide range of manipulation tasks from visual observations and language instructions. Their recent performance and generality across tasks and embodiments have made them a major paradigm in robot learning~ rt2, openvla, pi0, gr00t . This capability has been evaluated through manipulation tasks in simulation and in the real world, which serve as a standard protocol for VLA evaluation~ libero, simplerenv . However, task completion alone does not establish whether a policy handles objects without damaging them. In real-world deployment, VLAs may need to grasp and move objects with diverse physical properties, such as fragile eggs and rigid wooden boxes. Humans take these properties into account by holding fragile objects firmly enough to prevent slipping but gently enough to avoid damage, while using a stronger grip when handling rigid objects. In this sense, physical properties determine which actions are appropriate, and a genuinely generalist policy should be able to complete a task while preserving the object. We therefore ask: Can current VLAs account for objects’ physical properties to complete manipulation tasks without causing damage? The direct way to evaluate this ability is to conduct real-world experiments. However, fractured or permanently deformed objects cannot be reused under the same conditions, so repeated trials incur object replacement costs. Moreover, damaged objects and fragments may pose safety risks to the robot and its surroundings. Therefore, a simulation-based framework is needed to assess object preservation under repeatable conditions. Yet widely used simulation benchmarks do not account for object damage when evaluating task success~ libero, simplerenv . Because objects are modeled as rigid bodies, a policy can receive the same success score regardless of whether it handles the object carefully or uses gripping that would damage it in the real world. Adjacent lines of work, including physical understanding benchmarks, robot safety benchmarks, and tactile and force-aware VLAs, leave this gap open, as none of them judges a policy's actions against a physically grounded criterion for object preservation~ physbench, manipbench, safevla_bench, oopsieverse, tactile_vla, taf_vla . These limitations highlight the need for a common evaluation protocol that assesses whether policies complete tasks while respecting each object's physical constraints. Developing such an evaluation protocol requires defining preservation criteria for each object and reliably assessing how policy-applied forces affect its state during a rollout. This entails two challenges. First, defining physically grounded preservation criteria requires object-specific material properties, geometric meshes, and supporting references, but these resources are not readily available in a unified, verifiable form. Second, evaluating object preservation requires translating the forces applied during a rollout into predictions of deformation or fracture, but the rigid-body simulators used in standard manipulation benchmarks do not model these outcomes. To address the first challenge, we propose , an object library that consolidates object-specific material properties, 3D meshes, supporting references, structural information, and validation status into reusable assets. These assets can be reused for evaluating new policies, robots, and objects across simulation environments. The supporting references justify the material properties and preservation criteria, making their physical basis traceable and verifiable. To address the second challenge, we introduce an assessment method that uses physics solvers to determine whether contact forces recorded during a manipulation rollout could cause object deformation or fracture under the corresponding grasp conditions. After each rollout is completed, the physics solver combines the recorded grasp information with the material properties and 3D mesh from to compute a damage threshold for each grasp. We compare the recorded contact forces with the corresponding thresholds and judge an interaction to be potentially damaging if its force exceeds the threshold. We justify each threshold using material properties and damage criteria supported by the literature, and document the modeling assumptions to make the resulting evaluation traceable and verifiable. Building on these two components, we construct , a physics-based benchmark for evaluating object preservation during manipulation. constructs manipulation tasks in LIBERO~ libero and SimplerEnv~ simplerenv using objects selected from our . Solver-based assessment enables object-preservation evaluation on these platforms, even though their simulators model objects as rigid bodies. The benchmark is organized into three physics axes: brittle fracture, soft object deformation, and thin-walled container deformation. Each axis includes high, medium, and low difficulty levels, with higher difficulty corresponding to a narrower range of gripping forces that allow the object to be lifted without damage. We evaluate public VLA checkpoints~ openvla_oft, cogact, pi05, molmoact2 on and observe a substantial gap between task success and safe success, defined as task completion while preserving the object. To investigate this gap, we analyze the policies' gripper commands to examine whether they adapt their gripping behavior to objects' physical properties. We find that these commands concentrate near fully open and fully closed states, with largely similar aggregate distributions across objects. This pattern motivates examining the role of gripper supervision. Standard VLA pipelines often binarize gripper labels into open and close, which may limit the learning of object-dependent gripper control~ bridgedata_v2, openvla . We therefore replace binary labels with continuous labels derived from object-specific physical constraints and evaluate how retraining with these labels affects gripper behavior and safe success. Retraining yields more object-dependent gripping and higher safe success. However, task success decreases, and the resulting object-preserving behavior shows limited generalization. Our contributions are summarized as follows. [leftmargin=1.5em, itemsep=0pt] . An object library that consolidates object-specific meshes, properties, and supporting references into reusable assets for physically grounded preservation assessment. Physics solver-based assessment. A solver-based pipeline that computes damage thresholds for each grasp from object geometry, material properties, and grasp conditions. . A benchmark that evaluates across three physics axes and three difficulty levels whether VLA models manipulate objects while respecting their physical constraints. Evaluation and behavioral analysis. An evaluation of public VLA checkpoints, reporting the gap between task success and safe success. We analyze gripper behavior and examine the effects of object-specific continuous gripper supervision, identifying improvements in safe success alongside reduced task success and limited generalization of object-preserving behavior. Related Work sec:related_work Benchmarks. Manipulation benchmarks evaluate policies across diverse tasks, objects, and environments. LIBERO~ libero studies knowledge transfer across manipulation tasks, while SimplerEnv~ simplerenv provides simulation-based evaluation of real world robot policies. CALVIN~ calvin evaluates language-conditioned task sequences, and RLBench~ rlbench provides a diverse task suite with demonstrations. Because these benchmarks model objects as rigid bodies and do not track whether an object is damaged, task success alone does not indicate object preservation. r 0.52 Comparison with representative related work. Simulation: policies are evaluated on manipulation tasks in simulation. Preservation: damage to the object is judged. Physics: the verdict rests on the objects' own physical response, either computed from its material properties with a physics model or observed in real tests. Physical understanding benchmarks evaluate VLMs' knowledge of physical properties and interactions through question answering. PhysBench~ physbench assesses understanding of object properties and physical dynamics, while ManipBench~ manipbench evaluates low-level manipulation reasoning through multiple-choice questions on interaction keypoints and action trajectories. We share their interest in connecting physical knowledge to manipulation. However, in these benchmarks' question-answering evaluations, models answer questions without executing manipulation actions, so object preservation during task execution is not directly assessed. Even PhysBench's force test relies on VLM-specified gripping forces, while its simulator treats all objects as rigid bodies and does not simulate grasp-induced damage. Our work complements these evaluations by assessing whether contact forces recorded during policy rollouts exceed physically grounded damage thresholds for each grasp. Deformable manipulation environments aim to simulate objects that change shape. SoftGym~ softgym provides tasks with cloth, rope, and fluids, while PlasticineLab~ plasticinelab focuses on shaping elastoplastic materials. However, deformation is the goal of these tasks, so object preservation is neglected and the damage criterion is absent. DefGraspSim~ defgraspsim computes the stress and deformation of an object under a grasp with the finite element method (FEM). However, its material parameters are assigned from a fixed set rather than sourced from the object's own material, so the computed response is hypothetical. Moreover, in DefGraspSim a gripper is placed at candidate poses produced by a sampler and closes on the object, without an arm and a manipulation task. Therefore, grasping as part of manipulation falls outside its concern. Safety Benchmarks. Robot safety benchmarks assess hazards and harmful interactions during policy execution. title: SARI: Phase-Split Sim-Real Co-Training for Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models often require costly real-world demonstrations to adapt to contact-rich manipulation tasks, particularly when generalization across object placements is needed. We propose SARI (Simulated Approach, Real Interaction), a phase-split sim-and-real co-training framework built on a simple insight: spatial coverage and contact physics should be acquired from the domains best suited to them. Specifically, free-space approaches require spatial diversity but tolerate modest simulation gaps, making them ideal for synthetic generation; conversely, contact interactions demand accurate physics but vary little across object placements, allowing a few real demonstrations to generalize across the workspace. SARI generates diverse simulated approaches in a photorealistic digital twin while collecting real contact interactions at only a few placements. Post-trained on these phase-segmented demonstrations, a single policy seamlessly stitches simulated approaches with real contact interactions using visual appearance alignment and a shared camera-relative action representation--without explicit phase labels or hand-coded switches. Across five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, SARI reduces real-data collection time by 34.3% and achieves 27.5% success at unseen placements, where all full-task sim-real baselines fail completely (0%).
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models often require costly real-world demonstrations to adapt to contact-rich manipulation tasks, particularly when generalization across object placements is needed. We propose SARI (Simulated Approach, Real Interaction), a phase-split sim-and-real co-training framework built on a simple insight: spatial coverage and contact physics should be acquired from the domains best suited to them. Specifically, free-space approaches require spatial diversity but tolerate modest simulation gaps, making them ideal for synthetic generation; conversely, contact interactions demand accurate physics but vary little across object placements, allowing a few real demonstrations to generalize across the workspace. SARI generates diverse simulated approaches in a photorealistic digital twin while collecting real contact interactions at only a few placements. Post-trained on these phase-segmented demonstrations, a single policy seamlessly stitches simulated approaches with real contact interactions using visual appearance alignment and a shared camera-relative action representation—without explicit phase labels or hand-coded switches. Across five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, SARI reduces real-data collection time by 34.3 and achieves 27.5 success at unseen placements, where all full-task sim-real baselines fail completely (0 ). INTRODUCTION sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong and increasingly general manipulation capabilities, but this progress has been enabled by human-collected robot data at a formidable scale. Recent VLAs, including ~ pi05 , GR00T N1.7~ gr00tn1 , and GEN-1.5~ gen15 , are trained on large and diverse collections of robot, human, and synthetic data. Yet adapting these models to a new, contact-rich task still commonly requires many task demonstrations, and long-horizon tasks amplify this demand because errors and distribution shifts accumulate over time. An important cause is the limited spatial generalization of VLA policies. Although visual encoders are pretrained on broad data, post-trained policies can still overfit an action sequence to the specific object placements observed in their demonstrations, rather than reliably extrapolating across the workspace~ demogen,r2rgen . Consequently, achieving workspace-wide coverage requires the redundant repetition of near-identical free-space approaches, rather than focusing effort on contact-rich supervision. Simulation offers an effective route to alleviate this human collection burden. Recent advances, including MimicGen~ mimicgen , DemoGen~ demogen , Real2Render2Real~ real2render2real , and others~ robosplat,simandreal , synthesize additional demonstrations by transforming a small set of source demonstrations, generating trajectories in reconstructed scenes or combining simulated and real data for policy training. These methods can efficiently expand workspace coverage, diversify trajectories, and eliminate redundant teleoperation of identical free-space approaches. However, existing synthetic-data pipelines commonly assume that simulation is reliable throughout an entire task or require accurate modeling of contact dynamics~ dexmimicgen,demogen,robosplat,simandreal . In contact-rich manipulation, unmodeled friction, compliance, object resistance, and visual sim-to-real discrepancies can make synthetic contact data unreliable. To bridge this gap, straightforward sim-and-real co-training mixes full-task simulated and real demonstrations; yet, this still wastes costly real-world effort on free-space approaches and allows the spatially narrow real-data distribution to override and dilute the broad spatial coverage provided by simulation. To address these challenges, we propose SARI (Simulated Approach, Real Interaction), a phase-split co-training framework built on a simple insight: spatial coverage and contact physics should be acquired from the domains best suited to them. Simulation can cheaply provide broad spatial coverage for free-space approaches, while a few real demonstrations suffice to teach contact interactions that generalize across placements. Specifically, the approach phase requires broad spatial diversity but tolerates modest simulation gaps, making it ideal for synthetic generation. Conversely, the interaction phase demands accurate contact dynamics but varies little across object placements, allowing a modest number of real demonstrations at a few placements to generalize across the workspace. Figure~ fig:teaser contrasts this phase-split allocation with full-task sim-real co-training. We instantiate this phase-specific allocation using a Gaussian-Splatting~ gaussiansplatting digital twin that generates simulated approaches across all placements, while collecting real contact interactions near the pre-contact boundary at only a subset. To enable a single policy to learn seamlessly from both sources without phase labels or a hand-coded switch, we align visual appearances and express actions in a shared camera-relative representation. Across five real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, SARI reduces real-data collection time by 34.3 and achieves 27.5 unseen task completion, whereas all baselines achieve 0 . Our core contributions are: We introduce SARI, a phase-split sim-and-real co-training framework that decouples workspace-wide spatial reaching from contact interactions, allocating data collection to the domain best suited for each phase. We present a sim-to-real alignment pipeline, enabling a single policy to seamlessly stitch simulated approaches with real contact interactions without explicit phase labels or switching heuristics. We evaluate SARI on a Franka robot across five contact-rich manipulation tasks, demonstrating that our camera-relative action representation serves as the key mechanism to unlock zero-shot spatial generalization to unseen placements while reducing real-world collection time. RELATED WORKS sec:related-work Synthetic data generation. Reconstructed scenes and digital twins are increasingly used to reduce robot-data collection cost. Gaussian Splatting enables photorealistic robot-workspace rendering and has recently supported simulation, memory, and reactive control~ gaussiansplatting,splatctrl,gaussmemory ; related systems synthesize demonstrations from few real examples or reconstructed workspaces~ mimicgen,dexmimicgen,demogen,real2render2real,robosplat,robosimgs,gsworld . However, these pipelines often require full-task demonstrations or assume that synthetic rollouts are reliable throughout the task, including contact regimes where friction, compliance, and object resistance are hard to model. We therefore restrict reconstruction-based synthesis to the phase where geometric fidelity is sufficient: generating appearance-aligned free-space approaches across placements, while reserving contact-rich interaction for real data. Sim-and-real co-training. Sim-to-real and mixed-domain training combine simulation scalability with real-world deployment fidelity. Existing methods typically co-train policies on full-task simulated and real data~ simandreal,cotrainmechanistic , introduce online corrections or real-world residuals for contact-rich transfer~ transic,sparr , or study robust assembly in simulation prior to deployment~ industreal,cips . However, these approaches generally assume full-task trajectory in both domains or require extra adaptation machinery when simulated physics fails. In contrast, SARI exploits a fundamental task-phase asymmetry: simulation provides workspace-wide coverage for free-space approaches, while real demonstrations supply accurate contact dynamics at a sparse subset of placements. A single policy is post-trained on their union without phase labels, residual controllers, or phase-specific losses. VLA post-training. Large robot datasets and VLA policies have made post-training a practical mechanism for adapting pretrained robot models to new tasks~ rt1,rt2,openxembodiment,octo,openvla,pi0,pi05,droid . Recent work improves VLA action generation, pretraining sources, obstacle-aware imitation, and world-model conditioning~ imlevla,huro,obstadiff,wmcraftnet , while contact-rich variants introduce force-aware modules or curricula~ forcevla,craft . Yet adapting VLAs to a new workspace usually still requires full task demonstrations covering both approach and interaction, and specialized contact signals add assumptions beyond standard behavior cloning. We keep the recipe plain: a pretrained VLA, a shared camera-relative action representation, and phase-specific sim-real data. Together, these ingredients enable a single policy to seamlessly stitch simulated approach trajectories with real contact interactions, supporting spatial generalization to placements without real interaction demonstrations using only standard behavior cloning. PRELIMINARIES sec:problem Task setting and pre-contact boundary We consider single-object manipulation tasks whose demonstrations have two segments. In the free-space segment, the robot moves from its deployment home toward the object without making contact. In the contact segment, it presses, pulls, or pushes the object to complete the task. The segments meet at a pre-contact pose: a pose near the object that serves as the end of the simulated approach and the starting region for real contact collection. Figure~ fig:pipeline illustrates this setup: the robot travels from home, through free space, to this pre-contact pose, and then executes the contact interaction. To transfer a single calibrated pre-contact pose across the candidate object placements, we anchor it to five coordinate frames spanning the robot, table, object, and cameras. The task uses the robot-base frame , the table frame , the object's canonical body frame , the physical end-effector flange frame , and the wrist camera optical frame . The table has a fixed pose , and each nominal placement keeps the object at its canonical yaw. We select one object-relative pre-contact transform at a reference placement and transfer it to the others: We assume that the same object-relative pre-contact pose is suitable at each placement. With the fixed wrist camera mounting, this also preserves the nominal object pose in the optical frame: We compare our phase-split the end-effector--object relationship, the wrist camera encounters similar local views of the object just before contact across placements. This geometric consistency does not imply identical backgrounds, lighting, or contact dynamics. Segmented, partially real dataset Let be the subset of placements where real contact demonstrations are collected. The training set contains two sources: : simulated free-space episodes from the home region to , for every ; : real contact episodes starting near and completing the interaction, only for . Both sources use the same language instruction for a given task and the same action convention. Neither source contains a home-to-contact full-task demonstration. We post-train one policy on their union, without supplying a phase label or an intermediate-goal instruction. We categorize object placements based on real-world demonstration coverage: seen placements ( ) contain both simulated approaches and real contact demonstrations, while unseen placements ( ) are covered strictly by simulated approaches. The key evaluation question is whether contact behaviors can generalize to unseen placements without any real interaction demonstrations. METHODS sec:method

title: FastOPD: On-Policy Distillation for Lightweight VLA Deployment
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models have scaled rapidly to enhance manipulation performance and generalizability, but this scaling incurs high computational costs that render real-world deployment increasingly challenging. Existing approaches typically mitigate this issue by designing smaller architectures or reducing the iterative denoising steps in flow-based policies. In this work, we propose FastOPD, a foundation-to-lightweight VLA framework that enables the practical deployment of large-scale VLAs through efficient on-policy distillation. Specifically, FastOPD adapts a flow map for single-state teacher supervision and combines it with a self-consistency objective to construct a compact student that learns the teacher dynamics. Furthermore, we theoretically demonstrate that minimizing this objective allows the distilled student to recover a distribution on par with that induced by an ideal few-step teacher model. We evaluate FastOPD across diverse foundation policies in simulation and real-world experiments. On LIBERO, FastOPD retains 84% of the performance of $π_{0.5}$ with only two inference steps, reducing inference latency by 78.1% while outperforming existing few-step distillation baselines in average success rate. With LingBot-VLA as the teacher, FastOPD improves the single-step success rate over the base student by 15.9 percentage points on RoboTwin 2.0. We further demonstrate its applicability to a World Action Model (WAM) and deploy a compact student distilled from MolmoAct2 on a real robot.

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models have scaled rapidly to enhance manipulation performance and generalizability, but this scaling incurs high computational costs that render real-world deployment increasingly challenging. Existing approaches typically mitigate this issue by designing smaller architectures or reducing the iterative denoising steps in flow-based policies. In this work, we propose FastOPD, a foundation-to-lightweight VLA framework that enables the practical deployment of large-scale VLAs through efficient on-policy distillation. Specifically, FastOPD adapts a flow map for single-state teacher supervision and combines it with a self-consistency objective to construct a compact student that learns the teacher dynamics. Furthermore, we theoretically demonstrate that minimizing this objective allows the distilled student to recover a distribution on par with that induced by an ideal few-step teacher model. We evaluate FastOPD across diverse foundation policies in simulation and real-world experiments. On LIBERO, FastOPD retains 84 of the performance of with only two inference steps, reducing inference latency by 78.1 while outperforming existing few-step distillation baselines in average success rate. With LingBot-VLA as the teacher, FastOPD improves the single-step success rate over the base student by 15.9 percentage points on RoboTwin~2.0. We further demonstrate its applicability to a World Action Model (WAM) and deploy a compact student distilled from MolmoAct2 on a real robot. Introduction Recent progress in robot learning has moved toward large-scale foundation policies, ranging from Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ o2024open,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_,bjorck2025gr00t,wu2026pragmatic,fang2026molmoact2actionreasoningmodels to emerging World Action Models (WAMs)~ kim2026cosmos,ye2026world,yuan2026fast . In particular, recent methods such as DreamZero~ ye2026world and Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmos leverage pretrained video generation models to capture rich visual dynamics and achieve strong generalization and manipulation performance. However, these powerful foundation priors also lead to increasingly large policy backbones and high computational cost, creating a tension between model capability and deployment efficiency on physical robots. Lightweight VLA models such as SmolVLA~ shukor2025smolvla address the efficiency side of this trade-off by directly designing smaller policies with less than 0.5B parameters. A complementary direction is to transfer the capability of a powerful foundation policy into a compact student through knowledge distillation. Knowledge Distillation (KD)~ hinton2015distilling, mansourian2025comprehensive has been widely studied for transferring the capability of a large teacher model into a smaller student. Specifically, On-Policy Distillation (OPD)~ agarwal2024policy supervises the student using teacher predictions on its own generated trajectories, reducing distribution mismatch and compounding errors from offline distillation. OPD also provides dense supervision along the student trajectory, in contrast to the sparse rewards commonly used in reinforcement learning. While OPD has been actively explored in LLM post-training, recent works have extended it to diffusion and flow models~ li2026diffusionopd,fang2026flow . However, directly applying OPD to flow-based policies is computationally inefficient. It requires rolling out the student's denoising trajectory and repeatedly evaluating the teacher at the visited timesteps, resulting in high training cost for large foundation teachers. In this work, we revisit few-step flow-map models through the lens of on-policy distillation (OPD) and introduce FastOPD, a foundation-to-lightweight VLA framework for efficient policy distillation. Our goal is to transfer the capabilities of a large-scale VLA into a compact student while substantially reducing both training and inference costs, without sacrificing policy performance (see Fig.~ fig:figure1 ). To reduce the training cost of conventional OPD, FastOPD combines on-policy teacher supervision of the student's velocity field with a self-consistency objective~ frans2025one . Rather than querying teacher supervision throughout an entire generation trajectory, the self-consistency objective propagates local velocity supervision to finite-interval shortcut transitions, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:conceptual-figure . This allows the student to approximate the teacher dynamics without explicitly constructing or evaluating a teacher flow map over each shortcut transition. We further show theoretically that FastOPD implicitly recovers the distribution induced by the teacher's ideal shortcut model, providing a distributional justification for few-step distillation. Importantly, the same self-consistency formulation naturally induces an any-step flow map~ boffi2024flow,song2023consistency,kim2024consistency,geng2025mean,sabour2025align , allowing the distilled student to operate with substantially fewer sampling steps at inference. FastOPD therefore compresses the foundation VLA along two complementary dimensions: model capacity and sampling complexity, enabling deployment on resource-constrained, consumer-grade hardware. The proposed formulation also enables stable training in the challenging few-step regime without adversarial objectives or costly higher-order derivative computations. A concurrent work, VLA-OPD~ zhong2026vla , also studies on-policy distillation for VLA models, but primarily uses expert supervision to improve policy performance. In contrast, FastOPD focuses on transferring a foundation policy into a lightweight few-step student. We evaluate FastOPD on two simulation benchmarks and one real-world manipulation task, using diverse foundation teachers with 3B--6B parameters~ intelligence2025pi_,yuan2026fast,fang2026molmoact2actionreasoningmodels . To maximize both architectural and inference efficiency, we adopt SmolVLA as the lightweight student policy. We compare against representative few-step distillation methods, including CTM, DMD, and iMF. Across these settings, FastOPD enables the compact student to recover up to 84 of the performance of teacher models that are more than larger, using only one or two sampling steps. This substantially reduces inference cost while retaining a large fraction of the foundation policy's performance. To the best of our knowledge, FastOPD is the first OPD framework for VLAs that jointly reduces both model size and the number of sampling steps while retaining the capabilities of a large-scale foundation policy. Background Flow-based Models. Diffusion and flow-based models~ song2021scorebased,ho2020denoising,esser2024scaling,lipman2023flow generate high-quality samples through iterative denoising. Let be a Gaussian prior and the context-conditioned data distribution over actions. Flow matching~ lipman2023flow, esser2024scaling defines a stochastic interpolant , with , , and learns the marginal velocity field via Sampling integrates the probability-flow ODE from to , for example, with Euler steps, where . While these models capture high-quality multimodal action distributions, accurate integration typically requires many denoising steps, motivating few-step distillation for faster inference. Vision-Language-Action Models. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ o2024open,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_, bjorck2025gr00t,wu2026pragmatic,liu2024rdt,team2024octo couple a pretrained vision-language backbone with an action decoding head to map an observation and a language instruction to a distribution over robot actions, most commonly via a flow or diffusion action expert~ chi2023diffusionpolicy,black2024pi_0 trained with flow matching loss. Recent foundation VLA models illustrate the scale required for strong multi-task generalization, typically exceeding 2B parameters and trained on over 10 , 000 hours of multimodal robot data spanning multiple embodiments~ black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi_,wu2026pragmatic , but remain expensive to deploy. Several works~ team2024octo,shukor2025smolvla,wen2024tinyvla,reuss2025flower instead train smaller VLAs; SmolVLA~ shukor2025smolvla , for example, reduces model size to 450 million parameters by using a small VLM and layer skipping. However, it still requires denoising steps per action chunk and does not benefit from the capabilities of larger foundation policies. Flow Map Models. A wide range of few-step generative methods aim to reduce iterative sampling cost. Distillation-based approaches~ sabour2025align, boffi2024flow , including Consistency Models (CM)~ song2023consistency , and Consistency Trajectory Models (CTM)~ kim2024consistency , distill a pre-trained multi-step teacher into a few-step student, while score-distillation methods directly match teacher and student distributions~ yin2024one,yin2024improved . Distillation-free approaches, such as MeanFlow (MF)~ geng2025mean and Shortcut Models~ frans2025one , instead train from scratch using self-consistency constraints. A flow map model parameterizes the state-to-state transition over an arbitrary interval , so that a single jump at the interpolant replaces an entire sequence of Euler substeps. For example, frans2025one combines flow matching loss with the self-consistency constraint at the midpoint time : The first term enforces standard flow matching, while the second encourages the direct transition from to to agree with two shorter transitions composed through . In robot manipulation, these ideas have been adapted to accelerate diffusion- and flow-based policies such as Diffusion Policy~ chi2023diffusionpolicy . Consistency Policy (CP)~ prasad2024consistency adapts CTM~ kim2024consistency ; OneDP~ wang2024one and SDM Policy~ jia2024score use distribution matching for one-step action generation; and recent methods learn average velocity fields~ geng2025mean,geng2026improved,sheng2026mp1,guo2026reactvla or shortcut objectives~ frans2025one,luan2026snapflow,yan2025maniflow,li2026one regularized by flow matching. For instance, SnapFlow~ luan2026snapflow constructs its target from two Euler steps but trains only on fixed endpoints, while OFP~ li2026one derives its target from nested sub-intervals with a self-guided regularizer. Despite these advances, few-step policies often suffer from training instability and degraded quality as the number of denoising steps decreases. This trade-off is particularly critical in robot manipulation, where low latency must be achieved without sacrificing the precision and stability required for physical execution, and still remains insufficiently addressed~ shukor2025smolvla . On-policy Distillation. Given a pretrained teacher diffusion model, on-policy distillation (OPD) supervises the student to match the teacher's one-step transition kernel along the student's own rollout , by minimizing the reverse KL objective~ li2026diffusionopd . Since the student and teacher share the same diffusion coefficient, resulting in identical covariance, its per-step KL reduces to a closed-form squared distance between the means, . Despite providing dense supervision, this objective necessitates evaluating the teacher at every single denoising step, resulting in computational inefficiency. FastOPD circumvents this training bottleneck by supervising the student at a single on-policy state per trajectory. title: PointWAM: 3D World Action Modeling for Dexterous Robotic Manipulation
summary: World action models jointly learn to forecast world dynamics and predict robot actions, such that the learned internal world dynamics guide accurate actions. Existing approaches typically represent the world as RGB frames or latent counterparts while predicting actions as end-effector poses or joint angles, but they often struggle to capture the 3D spatial structure and contact geometry central to dexterous manipulation. We introduce Point World Action Model (PointWAM), a 3D world action model that decomposes the world into a scene (i.e., environment) and hands (i.e., actor), and jointly forecasts both as 3D point trajectories within a shared space-time coordinate frame. This explicit, disentangled representation enables effective pre-training on large-scale human demonstration videos without requiring any task-specific object or keypoint selection. Given a colored point cloud and a language instruction, PointWAM predicts how the scene and hands co-evolve in 3D space over time, then retargets the forecast hand motion to robot actions. Pre-training on human videos improves average DexJoCo success by 56.9 percentage points, and scene-trajectory supervision adds 10.9 points over forecasting the hands alone. With both, PointWAM surpasses the prior state of the art on ten DexJoCo tasks by 11.7 points and outperforms strong VLAs on a real robot.

Project page: Introduction sec:intro Dexterous robotic manipulation requires multiple fingers to precisely coordinate their 3D motion relative to object surfaces~ salisbury1982articulated,okamura2000dexterous , enabling robots to perform a wide range of tasks from grasping objects of varied shapes to tool use~ bicchi2000hands,dexilsurvey2025 . Conventional Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs)~ pi05_2025,groot_n1_2025 map observations to motor commands without explicitly forecasting how the scene evolves. World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative by treating world and action modeling as deeply intertwined: they jointly learn to forecast how the world will change and what actions cause those changes~ uva2025 . Many existing WAMs build on video generation backbones and represent the world as RGB frames~ unipi2023 or their latent counterparts~ uva2025,genieenvisioner2025 . These representations are limited in their ability to capture key aspects of physical interaction, including 3D spatial structure and causal relations between the actor and the environment. Point-based policies~ pointpolicy2025,dexpointpolicy2026 address the 3D action prediction problem by forecasting trajectories of 3D points, but do not model how the environment evolves. They also rely on humans or external perception models to select task-relevant objects for their scene inputs. Conversely, action-conditioned 3D world models forecast dense 3D scene trajectories, yet treat robot actions as inputs rather than quantities to be predicted~ pointworld2026 . In this work, we introduce Point World Action Model ( ), a 3D world action model that decomposes the world into a scene ( , environment) and hands ( , actor), and represents both as three-dimensional point trajectories within a shared space-time coordinate frame (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). This explicit, disentangled world representation enables effective learning of cause-and-effect relations between the environment and the actor by modeling how their points co-evolve in 3D space over time. Given a colored point cloud and a language instruction, forecasts trajectories for every observed scene point and hand keypoint in a common coordinate frame. Its action retargeter then converts the forecast hand trajectories into the corresponding robot actions. The proposed approach offers three additional advantages. First, modeling both the scene and hands in a shared 3D space enables effective pre-training on human demonstration videos from EgoDex~ egodex2026 and VITRA~ vitra2025 . Second, no task-specific objects or scene keypoints need to be selected in advance, so scene forecasting is not restricted to a predefined set of target objects. Third, by decoupling hand-point trajectories from the scene, the forecast hand motion is amenable to effective retargeting onto robot hands for action prediction. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows. 1.2em We introduce , which jointly forecasts the 3D trajectories of scene points and hand keypoints in a shared space-time coordinate frame, unifying world and action modeling. We demonstrate that 3D world modeling benefits dexterous manipulation. Scene-trajectory supervision improves average DexJoCo success by 10.9 percentage points over the same model without it, and our 3D encoder outperforms lifted image features by 5.4 percentage points. We show that pre-training on human demonstrations from EgoDex and VITRA improves average DexJoCo success by 56.9 percentage points over training from scratch. With this pre-training, surpasses the prior best multi-task success rate on DexJoCo by 11.7 percentage points and outperforms robot-pre-trained VLAs on a real robot by up to 25 percentage points. Related Work sec:related We discuss the closest work here and provide a broader review in Appendix~ app:related . World action models (WAMs). WAMs unify predictive world modeling with action prediction; unlike conventional VLAs, which map a visual observation straight to a motor command, a WAM is trained to forecast how the world will change and predict what actions the robot must perform ~ unipi2023,vpp2025,genieenvisioner2025,cosmospolicy2026,uva2025 . Existing WAMs typically forecast future visual representations in the latent space of pretrained video models while predicting robot actions as end-effector poses. These models must therefore learn how changes in latent visual features correspond to robot motion, rather than explicitly modeling both scene and hand motion as 3D trajectories. Closest to ours, EgoWAM~ egowam2026 , PointWorld~ pointworld2026 , and PointZero~ pointzero2026 forecast dense 3D scene motion. EgoWAM jointly learns scene forecasting and action prediction but maps human hand motion to the actions of parallel-jaw grippers, a 6-DoF pose and a gripper state per hand, which lacks individual finger motions. Pri4R~ pri4r2026 likewise targets grippers, adding a training-only 3D point-trajectory head to a VLA fine-tuned on robot demonstrations. PointWorld forecasts scene motion with a 3D point-cloud network~ wu2024ptv3 conditioned on future robot trajectories, so it needs a separate planner that selects them with a task cost.
