title: MixVLA: Adaptive Mixing of Non-Invariant Information for Generalizable Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved remarkable advances in robotic manipulation, yet their zero-shot generalization under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions remains limited. These models often entangle task-relevant invariant structure with environment-specific non-invariant factors, causing policies to rely on spurious appearance cues during action prediction. In this work, we propose \textbf{MixVLA}, a model-agnostic training framework that improves the generalization of VLA models without requiring additional OOD data or architectural modifications. The key component of MixVLA is \textbf{Adaptive Mixing of Non-Invariant Information (AMI)}. AMI stochastically mixes non-invariant representations to regularize distribution-specific variability while preserving complementary predictive cues. The mixed non-invariant features are then fused with invariant representations for final action prediction, resulting in improved robustness without sacrificing policy expressiveness. Extensive experiments across challenging manipulation settings, including LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, the RoboTwin perturbation suite, and real-world tasks, demonstrate that MixVLA improves overall zero-shot robustness while retaining strong in-domain performance.
full_text: Experiment sec:exp Our experiments assess whether regularizing, rather than discarding, non-invariant information improves zero-shot robustness to distribution shifts while retaining strong in-domain performance. Beyond overall performance, we investigate the role of non-invariant information in generalization, the applicability of MixVLA across policy architectures and real-world settings, and the potential to reduce training requirements while preserving robustness gains As outlined in Figure~ fig:setup , our experiments address the following four questions: 1. Robust Generalization. Can MixVLA improve zero-shot robustness to unseen distribution shifts while retaining strong in-domain performance? 2. Representation Analysis. What does regularized non-invariant information contribute beyond invariant features alone? 3. General Applicability. Do the robustness gains extend across policy architectures and to real-world manipulation? 4. Training Cost. Can MixVLA retain its robustness benefits using a single Invariant Net training run, without training a separate standard policy? . We evaluate MixVLA across simulation and real-world manipulation settings. For simulation, we train on LIBERO~ liu2023libero and evaluate both in-domain performance and zero-shot robustness under distribution shifts using LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025libero . We further conduct clean-to-clean (C2C) and clean-to-randomized (C2R) evaluations on RoboTwin~ chen2025robotwin , where policies are trained only with clean demonstrations to assess generalization to unseen randomized environments. Finally, we deploy policies on real robots and evaluate robustness. details. We implement MixVLA on two representative VLA architectures: OpenVLA-OFT~ kim2025fine , which predicts continuous action chunks through parallel decoding, and ~ Intelligence202505AV , which generates continuous actions through flow matching. For the main simulation experiments, the Normal Net and the Invariant Net are each trained for 100K steps on LIBERO or clean RoboTwin demonstrations. In Stage~2, we perform AMI training for 1K steps on LIBERO and 10K steps on RoboTwin. Detailed training configurations are provided in the Appendix~ sec:more implementation . Robustness to Unseen Distribution Shifts sec:exp_robustness from LIBERO to LIBERO-Plus. We build MixVLA on OpenVLA-OFT and train it on LIBERO, evaluating on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus. As shown in Table~ tab:libero_plus_compare , MixVLA achieves the highest overall success rate of 76.2 among the compared methods, surpassing OpenVLA-OFT by 6.6 . However, its lower performance under camera perturbations suggests that non-invariant feature mixing alone may be insufficient to address viewpoint-induced geometric shifts. On LIBERO, MixVLA retains strong in-domain performance, achieving an average success rate of 96.7 compared with 97.1 for OpenVLA-OFT (Table~ tab:libero_compare ), with a decrease of only 0.4 . -to-randomized generalization on RoboTwin. We build MixVLA on and train it exclusively on clean demonstrations from RoboTwin 2.0. As shown in Table~ tab:robotwin_c2r , MixVLA improves C2R success from 46.0 to 62.4 (+16.4 ) over , while also increasing C2C success from 70.7 to 75.6 (+4.9 ). Taken together, these results support a positive answer to Q1: MixVLA improves robustness to a range of unseen distribution shifts while retaining strong in-domain performance. Understanding the Role of Non-Invariant Information sec:exp_noninvariant invariant representations. We compare the Normal Net, Invariant Net, and full MixVLA, using OpenVLA-OFT on LIBERO-Plus and on RoboTwin (Table~ tab:ablation ). IB-only (Invariant Net) improves overall OOD performance on both benchmarks, but reduces robustness under camera and language perturbations on LIBERO-Plus relative to the standard policy. This uneven behavior highlights the limitations of relying solely on invariant representations to handle diverse distribution shifts. Complementing invariant representations with AMI-regularized non-invariant features yields further gains of 4.0 on LIBERO-Plus and 2.8 on RoboTwin C2R over IB-only. MixVLA outperforms Invariant Net across all seven LIBERO-Plus perturbation categories while largely preserving clean-environment performance on RoboTwin. These results support our central premise that non-invariant information need not be discarded: when regularized, it can complement invariant features and improve OOD generalization. Additional analyses of mixing strategies are provided in the Appendix~ sec:more experiments . attribution under distribution shifts. Figure~ fig:att_vis presents Grad-CAM visualizations along the respective rollouts of the Normal Net, Invariant Net, and MixVLA on a LIBERO-Plus task. The Invariant Net exhibits localized responses around manipulation-related regions, whereas MixVLA highlights these regions together with broader nearby context at intermediate steps. Both the Normal Net and the Invariant Net fail to complete the task, while MixVLA succeeds. Figure~ fig:tsne further visualizes mean-pooled token features from eight RoboTwin tasks under clean and randomized conditions. The Normal Net forms predominantly task-homogeneous local clusters, whereas the Invariant Net projection exhibits a different organization with some regions still dominated by either clean or randomized samples. MixVLA retains task-associated neighborhoods alongside local clean--randomized interleaving, while the Non-Invariant Net exhibits substantial cross-task overlap. These projections illustrate changes in feature organization rather than establish complete domain alignment. Together with the ablations in Table~ tab:ablation , these qualitative observations support our answer to Q2: regularized non-invariant information can complement invariant features and improve OOD generalization. Generality across Policies and Real-World Deployment sec:exp_generality Applicability across policy architectures. As shown in Tables~ tab:libero_plus_compare and~ tab:robotwin_c2r , MixVLA improves robustness over the corresponding baselines for both OpenVLA-OFT and . These gains are obtained using the same two-stage training framework, despite their different action-generation mechanisms: parallel action decoding in OpenVLA-OFT and flow matching in . These results support the model-agnostic design of MixVLA, demonstrating its applicability beyond a single policy architecture. l 0.48 fig:realworld Robustness in real-world manipulation. We deploy and its MixVLA counterpart on a Franka robot. We collect 80 demonstrations for a bread-placement task with two instruction variants, requiring the robot to pick up the sixth slice of bread and place it on either the near or far plate, as specified by the instruction. We evaluate each policy over 10 trials under lighting perturbations, counting a trial as successful when the specified slice is placed on the instructed plate. As shown in Figure~ fig:realworld , MixVLA achieves a success rate of 60 , compared with 20 for . See Appendix~ sec:more experiments for videos of real-world executions. These results complement the cross-architecture simulation findings and provide preliminary evidence that MixVLA's robustness benefits extend to real-world manipulation, supporting a positive answer to Q3. Robustness from a Single Training Run sec:exp_single_run Reusing intermediate IB checkpoints. r 0.48 tab:single_run 3pt 1.1 @ l > X > X > X@ Method & C2C & C2R & Avg. \\ Self-MixVLA & 73.0 & 60.8 & 66.9 \\ MixVLA & 75.6 & 62.4 & 69.0 \\ We explore whether intermediate checkpoints from a single Invariant Net training run can eliminate the need to train a separate Normal Net. Our intuition is that Invariant Net training progressively favors invariant information, and differences between early and late checkpoints may provide a proxy for complementary non-invariant information. Motivated by this hypothesis, we introduce Self-MixVLA, which constructs a Self Non-Invariant Net from the 10K- and 100K-step checkpoints of the same IB training run: The resulting branch is paired with the 100K-step Invariant Net for subsequent AMI training, avoiding a separate Normal Net training run. These results support a positive answer to Q4: Self-MixVLA reduces training requirements by eliminating the separate Normal Net training run, while retaining robustness benefits with a modest performance reduction relative to full MixVLA (Table~ tab:single_run ). We regard this variant as a preliminary exploration of reusing a single IB training trajectory, with further opportunities to investigate checkpoint selection and extrapolation strategies for recovering complementary information.

title: DexJoCo-X: Benchmarking Action Representations for Multi-Hand Dexterous Manipulation
summary: As dexterous hands proliferate, collecting data and training policies separately for every morphology becomes increasingly impractical. Scalable cross-embodiment learning therefore requires a unified representation that captures shared manipulation structure while preserving morphology-specific control. Differences in hands, tasks, datasets, and control interfaces prevent existing studies from isolating the effects of representation, pretraining, and architecture. We introduce DexJoCo-X, a benchmark and toolkit for controlled comparison across seven representative dexterous hands, six single-arm and bimanual tasks, and 2,100 balanced demonstrations. DexJoCo-X provides a matched multi-hand, multi-task protocol with common scenes, success criteria, and execution interfaces, redesigned glove-to-hand mappings, and an automated pipeline that expands reviewed demonstrations across randomized scenes. Using $π_{0.5}$, Ego-Pi, and Being-H0.5, we examine whether a shared action interface is sufficient for multi-hand learning. Expanding $π_{0.5}$ to an 80-dimensional bimanual output yields near-zero success. Ego-Pi preserves the pretrained action head through interleaved prediction and supports per-hand multi-task learning, but remains ineffective for seven-hand joint training. By contrast, Being-H0.5 combines cross-embodiment pretraining, a unified action space, and embodiment-aware experts, enabling one policy to control all seven hands. Within this architecture, function-aligned action slots achieve 47.7% mean success, compared with 47.0% for native coordinates and 33.1% for DexLatent. These results show that cross-embodiment representation depends on the entire learning system: action coordinates, pretraining, and architecture must jointly separate shared manipulation structure from embodiment-specific control.
full_text: As dexterous hands proliferate, collecting data and training policies separately for every morphology becomes increasingly impractical. Scalable cross-embodiment learning therefore requires a unified representation that captures shared manipulation structure while preserving morphology-specific control. Differences in hands, tasks, datasets, and control interfaces prevent existing studies from isolating the effects of representation, pretraining, and architecture. We introduce DexJoCo-X, a benchmark and toolkit for controlled comparison across seven representative dexterous hands, six single-arm and bimanual tasks, and 2,100 balanced demonstrations. DexJoCo-X provides a matched multi-hand, multi-task protocol with common scenes, success criteria, and execution interfaces, redesigned glove-to-hand mappings, and an automated pipeline that expands reviewed demonstrations across randomized scenes. Using , Ego-Pi, and Being-H0.5, we examine whether a shared action interface is sufficient for multi-hand learning. Expanding to an 80-dimensional bimanual output yields near-zero success. Ego-Pi preserves the pretrained action head through interleaved prediction and supports per-hand multi-task learning, but remains ineffective for seven-hand joint training. By contrast, Being-H0.5 combines cross-embodiment pretraining, a unified action space, and embodiment-aware experts, enabling one policy to control all seven hands. Within this architecture, function-aligned action slots achieve 47.7 mean success, compared with 47.0 for native coordinates and 33.1 for DexLatent. These results show that cross-embodiment representation depends on the entire learning system: action coordinates, pretraining, and architecture must jointly separate shared manipulation structure from embodiment-specific control. Introduction Learning manipulation skills that can be shared across dexterous hands is essential for deploying general-purpose robots on diverse hardware. Diverse hand kinematics and actuation fragment demonstrations and policies, making separate training costly and limiting experience reuse. Multi-embodiment datasets and generalist policies, including Open X-Embodiment/RT-X, Octo, OpenVLA, HPT, and the series~ oxe,octo,openvla,hpt,pi0,pi05 , establish a foundation for sharing robot experience. RT-2~ rt2 transfers vision--language knowledge to control. RDT-1B~ rdt uses unified action coordinates, and X-VLA~ xvla addresses embodiment heterogeneity through soft prompts, while Being-H0.5~ being and Ego-Pi~ egopi connect human demonstrations with robot learning. Complementary approaches include diffusion policies with shared action latents~ lad,opfa and cross-hand reinforcement learning~ crossdex . These efforts motivate action representations that link shared skills to embodiment-specific execution. Recent dexterous foundation-model frameworks, including UniDex~ unidex2026 and XL-VLA~ xlvla2026 , report promising multi-hand learning capabilities through different representations. Yet results obtained with different hands, datasets, and task protocols do not establish which approach best supports cross-hand manipulation under a common evaluation standard. Existing benchmarks provide complementary capabilities: DexArt~ dexart studies articulated objects, Bi-DexHands~ bidex emphasizes bimanual control, DexJoCo~ dexjoco2026 supplies functional tasks and demonstration tools, and DexVerse~ dexverse2026 broadens task and embodiment coverage. These benchmarks expand task coverage, but leave open which action representations best support cross-hand learning under matched conditions. A fair comparison requires the same hands, tasks, demonstrations, policy backbone, and success criteria. A shared control interface is also needed to evaluate new representations without rebuilding the hand-control pipeline. These needs motivate a dedicated benchmark for fair and accessible cross-hand evaluation. To address these needs, we introduce DexJoCo-X, a unified benchmark and toolkit designed for fair comparison and straightforward integration of cross-hand policies (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Built on DexJoCo, it combines seven hand interfaces, six tasks, and 2,100 demonstrations with a reusable collection pipeline. We fine-tune ~ pi05 with the Ego-Pi protocol~ egopi as a per-hand multi-task reference, training one Native-action policy for each hand. Our central cross-hand comparison instead trains one Being-H0.5 policy~ being jointly on all seven hands under Native, FAAS, or DexLatent, and evaluates every hand on independent scenes. Our contributions are: A unified cross-hand benchmark. Seven hands and six tasks share evaluation scenes, success criteria, and control interfaces for fair comparison of action representations under matched training conditions. A reusable demonstration collection toolkit. Redesigned glove-to-hand mappings for all seven hands support human teleoperation, while automated scene expansion and trajectory verification scale demonstration collection. A balanced multi-hand demonstration dataset. We collect 2,100 demonstrations spanning six single-arm and bimanual tasks, with 50 trajectories for each of the 42 hand--task pairs. Related Work Manipulation Benchmarks and Dexterous Tasks RLBench~ rlbench , CALVIN~ calvin , and LIBERO~ libero benchmark arm--gripper manipulation; Robosuite~ robosuite and ManiSkill2~ maniskill2 provide broader simulation infrastructure. Arm--gripper tasks do not test independent finger coordination. Multi-finger hand benchmarks address bimanual coordination~ bidex , articulated objects~ dexart , deformable objects~ dexdeform , and trajectory tracking across hands~ pgdm . Grasp-focused resources evaluate pose generation~ dexgraspnet,gagrasp and functional or language-guided grasping~ dexfuncgrasp,dexvlg . DexJoCo~ dexjoco2026 evaluates complete functional tasks, while DexVerse~ dexverse2026 expands task and embodiment coverage. Building on DexJoCo, we enable fair comparison of cross-hand action representations through balanced seven-hand, six-task demonstrations, shared evaluation scenes and success criteria, and reusable control interfaces. Human Demonstrations and Automated Expansion Human-to-robot hand mapping spans joint, Cartesian, task-oriented, and reduced-dimensional formulations~ mappingreview . DexPilot~ dexpilot , Robotic Telekinesis~ telekinesis , AnyTeleop~ anyteleop , and DIME~ dime use human motion to teach dexterous control. ALOHA~ aloha and UMI~ umi broaden accessible demonstration capture, while LEAP Hand~ leap provides an affordable dexterous embodiment. DexMV~ dexmv and ViViDex~ vividex learn from human video demonstrations. CyberDemo~ cyberdemo augments simulated human demonstrations for real-world manipulation. MimicGen~ mimicgen expands demonstrations across contexts, and DexMimicGen~ dexmimicgen extends this approach to bimanual dexterity. Our toolkit supplies native demonstrations through seven glove mappings and verified scene expansion. Cross-Hand Learning and Action Representations Recent advances span action-chunking and diffusion policies~ aloha,dp,dp4,dp3,r3dp , vision--language--action models~ rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05,xvla,being,egopi , and world-model-based control~ unipi,robodreamer,crosshandworld . Cross-hand grasping shares contact points or maps~ unigrasp,gendexgrasp,cedex , interaction geometry~ drograsp,anydexgrasp , and morphology-conditioned eigengrasps~ machagrasp . For closed-loop cross-hand control, shared keypoint commands~ crosshand2024 , retargeted human-hand actions~ crossdex , morphology-aligned graphs~ dexgraspzero , and canonical hand descriptions~ canonicalhand connect common skills to different kinematics. Particle-based world models~ crosshandworld additionally share interaction dynamics. Shared action spaces also enable learning from heterogeneous demonstrations. LAD~ lad and OPFA~ opfa learn aligned action latents; AdvDex~ advdex aligns human and robot joints. UniDex~ unidex2026 uses functional slots, while XL-VLA~ xlvla2026 learns cross-hand codecs. DexJoCo-X compares these representation principles under matched data, backbones, scenes, and control interfaces across seven hands. DexJoCo-X Benchmark Embodiments and Task Scope The seven hands are XHand, Inspire, Wuji, LEAP, Sharpa Wave, LinkerHand, and Allegro. Each retains its native kinematics, actuation, coupling, and joint limits; state and actuator dimensions are recorded separately. Figure~ fig:tasks shows three single-arm tasks---bucket lifting, nail hammering, and Hanoi---and three bimanual tasks---microwave cooking, iPad unlocking, and photography. Together they require stable grasping, directed tool use, sequential placement, and coordination between support and operation. Task success is determined by task-specific geometric, contact, and temporal criteria. Tasks share initial scenes, objects, and success rules across hands, enabling paired comparisons of morphology and representation. Records retain successful and failed attempts. Common Learning Interface and Native Control To compare action representations without changing the underlying control problem, DexJoCo-X separates a common learning interface from each hand's native controller. At 20\,Hz, every episode synchronizes RGB observations, task instructions, proprioceptive states, and robot commands. Arm control follows a shared convention based on world-frame translation and rotation-vector increments, whereas hand states and commands retain each embodiment's native joint order, limits, actuation, and coupling. This design preserves the control structure of each hand instead of imposing an artificial joint correspondence. Native state and execution-command layouts are and , with masks for valid coordinates and active arms. Encoded policy outputs have representation-specific layouts and are decoded to native commands for execution. Up to five RGB streams provide front, side/ego, and wrist views, and each backbone comparison uses the same fixed view subset. Under this interface, Native, FAAS, and DexLatent share observations, arm commands, timing, and execution conditions, differing only in how hand actions are represented. Their performance can therefore be attributed more directly to the action representation and its interaction with the learning architecture. Training Data and Coverage The dataset contains 2,100 accepted demonstrations across seven hands and six tasks, with 50 trajectories per hand--task pair. All 2,100 demonstrations are used for policy training: each per-hand Ego-Pi policy receives 300 trajectories, while each joint Being-H0.5 policy receives the complete 2,100-trajectory set. Normalization statistics are computed from the corresponding training demonstrations. Policy performance is measured through separate closed-loop evaluation rollouts. Demonstration Collection Seven-Hand Teleoperation The capture setup follows DexJoCo~ dexjoco2026 : Rokoko gloves measure finger pose, and Vive trackers measure hand motion for arm control (Fig.~ fig:collection ). Each tracker attaches to the dorsal glove module through a printed connector. The operator observes the simulated task while the system records native robot states and commands. We redesign the glove-to-hand mappings for all seven embodiments, including Allegro. Each mapping respects digit correspondence, coordinate order, motion direction, actuator limits, and joint coupling. Four-finger and five-finger hands use their respective digit configurations; dependent joints follow the native coupling model. The capture interface is where indexes the hand embodiment and the control step; is the glove measurement, is the tracked wrist pose, and and are the calibrated hand and arm mappings. The outputs and are the native hand and arm commands. These mappings generate native demonstrations. Policy-action encoding is applied afterward, so all representations share the recorded trajectories. Reviewed Sources and Scene Expansion Figure~ fig:demonstration_e

title: HexVIO: Towards All-Day Stereo-Inertial Tracking Through Commodity DSPs
summary: The ability of a device to localize itself within its surroundings is a fundamental prerequisite for spatial computing. Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) has proven to be a cost-effective and accurate solution for this task. Robots, wearables, XR devices, and drones can benefit significantly from efficient implementations of VIO since they allow for cooler, lighter, and cheaper devices with longer battery life and a better user experience. In this work, we propose to enhance the efficiency of a VIO system by leveraging the Hexagon DSP, a commodity co-processor present in many modern smartphones and XR devices. Our approach offloads the visual frontend of a stereo-inertial odometry system to the DSP while keeping the backend on the main CPU. By optimizing the implementation for the DSP architecture, we achieve significant reductions in power consumption and latency compared to CPU-only execution. Our system, HexVIO, demonstrates a 67% reduction in power consumption or an 86% increase in throughput on a commodity smartphone, with the ability to sustain long-term real-time 30 fps tracking for 0.83 W, corresponding to ~18 hours of tracking on the testing device. These results highlight the potential of commodity DSPs for enabling all-day visual-inertial tracking in robotics and mobile devices.
full_text: The ability of a device to localize itself within its surroundings is a fundamental prerequisite for spatial computing. Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) has proven to be a cost-effective and accurate solution for this task. Robots, wearables, XR devices, and drones can benefit significantly from efficient implementations of VIO since they allow for cooler, lighter, and cheaper devices with longer battery life and a better user experience. In this work, we propose to enhance the efficiency of a VIO system by leveraging the Hexagon DSP, a commodity co-processor present in many modern smartphones and XR devices. Our approach offloads the visual frontend of a stereo-inertial odometry system to the DSP while keeping the backend on the main CPU. By optimizing the implementation for the DSP architecture, we achieve significant reductions in power consumption and latency compared to CPU-only execution. Our system, HexVIO, demonstrates a 67 reduction in power consumption or an 86 increase in throughput on a commodity smartphone, with the ability to sustain long-term real-time 30\,fps tracking for 0.83\,W, corresponding to 18 hours of tracking on the testing device. These results highlight the potential of commodity DSPs for enabling all-day visual-inertial tracking in robotics and mobile devices. INTRODUCTION 0 Recent advancements in robotics zitkovichRT2VisionLanguageActionModels2023,zhangHuBLearningExtreme2025 , computer vision wangVGGTVisualGeometry2025a,ICLR2026_e0982cbc,ICLR2025_bc8b2058,kerblImpactOutlook3D2025 , and foundation models capable of complex reasoning openaiGPT4TechnicalReport2024,guoDeepSeekR1IncentivizesReasoning2025,chowdheryPaLMScalingLanguage2023 have started to show the possibilities of perception engineering lavalleVirtualRealityEmerging2024a as a new discipline and of spatial computing delmericoSpatialComputingIntuitive2022 as the ever more common class of problems that require a computing device to understand its surroundings. Different instances of this problem arise in important applications like autonomous vehicles, drones, humanoid robotics, wearables like smartglasses, and VR headsets. A fundamental capability that allows much of this reasoning comes from the ability of the device to localize itself and its movements in space. Utilizing cameras and inertial measurement units (IMU) for visual-inertial odometry (VIO) and visual-inertial simultaneous localization and mapping (VI-SLAM) has shown to be a particularly good combination thanks to the low cost of these sensors, their reduced power consumption, and proven accuracy krishnanBenchmarkingEgocentricVisualInertial2025a,camposORBSLAM3AccurateOpenSource2021 . The field of VIO and VI-SLAM has made rapid progress in the previous decade enabling this technology to be deployed in commercial devices like VR headsets and smartphones. However, existing limitations in terms of accuracy per watt remain in the literature kumarHighSpeedStereoVisual2024 , driving research into highly specialized hardware accelerators suleimanNavion2mWFully2019,kuhneLEVIOLightweightEmbedded2026 . These accelerators reach their efficiency through custom silicon, so they only ship in devices designed around them. We instead use a co-processor that existing devices already carry. It is nowadays common to find systems, even low-end ones, that have a GPU alongside the CPU. DSPs have developed from fixed-function audio and modem processors into increasingly general-purpose compute units that run at a fraction of the energy cost of a CPU codrescuHexagonDSPArchitecture2014 . The Hexagon DSP is now present in a multitude of devices spanning smartphones, VR, AR, and robotics (e.g., Snapdragon 8, XR2, AR1, and RB5 respectively). The DSP provides very long instruction words with wide vector lanes coupled with fast local memory. When properly utilized, this results in significantly reduced power usage for certain tasks compared to using the CPU or GPU. This kind of co-processor allows robots, XR devices, and smartphones to do long-haul vision tasks thanks to the low power required to perform them on these accelerators. The low power not only extends operation, but can also directly improve the target application: smaller batteries for lighter and cheaper drones, lighter headworn devices for reduced neck strain, and cooler smartglasses for improved comfort. The goal we work towards is tracking that runs for a full day on a device's own battery. Even with all these benefits, very few works in the literature exploit it for the fundamental task of visual-inertial tracking and, to the best of our knowledge, none of them for the stereo-inertial sensor modality. In this work, we offload the frontend of a visual-inertial odometry system based on Basalt usenkoBasaltVisualInertialMapping2020 to the Hexagon DSP of a Samsung Galaxy S23 (Snapdragon 8 Gen 2, Hexagon V73). A direct port does not beat the CPU. Sparse tracking branches per feature and reads scattered pixels, the vector unit runs all lanes together and its gather reads only on-chip memory, and each DSP call costs hundreds of microseconds, so calling the DSP once per stage spends much of the gain on round trips. Most of the work is restructuring the frontend around these three constraints. The contributions of this work are: The first stereo-inertial odometry system in the literature leveraging the Hexagon DSP co-processor. An optimized open-source The source code will be released implementation of the VIO frontend providing insight into the DSP for vision tasks. A thorough power, latency, and performance analysis that shows HexVIO achieving an 86 increase of throughput or a 67 reduction of power (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). An energy-focused configuration that sustains real-time 30\,fps tracking for 0.83\,W, corresponding to 18 hours of tracking on the testing device. RELATED WORK Contemporary VIO and VI-SLAM pipelines generally decompose into a visual frontend, responsible for keypoint detection and feature tracking, an inertial integration stage, and a backend optimizer or filter tasked with fusing these modalities. A diverse set of representative systems has emerged in the literature, including optimization-based frameworks such as ORB-SLAM3 camposORBSLAM3AccurateOpenSource2021 , which augments feature-based pipelines with inertial measurements and map atlases, and VINS-Mono/VINS-Fusion qinVINSMonoRobustVersatile2018 or OKVIS leuteneggerKeyframebasedVisualInertial2015b , which rely on sliding-window nonlinear optimization. Filter-based approaches, notably ROVIO bloeschRobustVisualInertial2015 and MSCKF mourikisMultiStateConstraintKalman2007a , also remain widely adopted. In this work, we build upon Basalt usenkoBasaltVisualInertialMapping2020 , incorporating modifications from demayoMonadoSLAMDataset2025 . Basalt utilizes a fixed-lag smoother that couples patch-based Lucas-Kanade tracking Lucas-1981-15101,bouguet2001pyramidalf , implemented in its inverse-compositional form Baker-2002-8493 to keep reference-side linear algebra out of the iteration loop, with FAST corner detection rostenMachineLearningHighSpeed2006 , preintegrated IMU factors, and first-estimate-Jacobian marginalization. The open implementation of Basalt, along with its balance between performance and accuracy demayoMonadoSLAMDataset2025 , makes it a particularly strong target for frontend acceleration on embedded platforms. Mobile VIO systems must additionally sustain the camera frame rate within a strict thermal and power envelope, a dual constraint formalized in embedded VIO benchmarking practices that report tracking accuracy alongside per-frame computational cost on target hardware delmericoBenchmarkComparisonMonocular2018a . One established strategy to meet these constraints involves redesigning the estimator itself. For instance, LEVIO kuhneLEVIOLightweightEmbedded2026 achieves 20\,fps six-DoF tracking below 100\,mW on an ultra-low-power RISC-V SoC by employing a streamlined ORB-based frontend alongside a comprehensive hardware-software co-design. In contrast, this work preserves Basalt's complete pipeline and instead focuses on accelerating its execution. This is a reasonable approach given these SoCs are already widely adopted by different industries trying to leverage spatial computing. The visual frontend is a natural hardware acceleration target, as its per-feature computations are easy to parallelize and its backend interface reduces to sparse correspondences. Prior work has largely targeted GPUs: vilib nagyFasterFASTGPUAccelerated2020a and Jetson-SLAM kumarHighSpeedStereoVisual2024 accelerate FAST-based frontends in CUDA (KLT as in ours, and ORB, respectively), while FastTrack khabiriFastTrackGPUAcceleratedTracking2025a offloads portions of ORB-SLAM3 to the GPU. GLidE-SLAM desousaGLidESLAMGLAcceleratedIndirectDirect2026a employs OpenGL compute shaders to circumvent CUDA lock-in and augments indirect features with direct GPU tracking. In contrast, our DSP-based approach frees the GPU for concurrent workloads and sidesteps the thermal constraints and higher power draw typical of GPU acceleration, while still delivering low-power, high-frame-rate tracking. At the other extreme, custom silicon achieves the lowest reported energy per frame. Navion suleimanNavion2mWFully2019 integrates a complete VIO pipeline into a 2\,mW ASIC via algorithm-hardware co-design zhangVisualInertialOdometryChip2017 , albeit at the cost of fixing the algorithm. FPGA-based solutions offer a more flexible alternative: eSLAM liuESLAMEnergyEfficientAccelerator2019 accelerates only ORB extraction and matching, while ac2SLAM wangAc2SLAMFPGAAccelerated2021 accelerates both the ORB-SLAM2 frontend and backend, though neither incorporates inertial fusion. PX4Flow honeggerOpenSourceOpen2013 instead computes block-matching optical flow on a microcontroller inside the sensor. Compared to the Hexagon DSP, however, these custom accelerators lack broad availability on commodity platforms, and ASICs offer no post-deployment reprogrammability. Hexagon DSPs occupy a middle ground: they are programmable, widely deployed, and optimized for energy-efficient single-instruction multiple-data (SIMD) vector processing. The Hexagon architecture codrescuHexagonDSPArchitecture2014 combines a VLIW scalar core with the HVX wide-vector coprocessor and a software-managed scratchpad. Originally designed for audio and modem tasks, it now supports general-purpose workloads, including LLM inference haoScalingLLMTestTime2026 , while vendor CV/ML stacks (FastCV, SNPE, QNN qualcomm2024qnni ) and the Halide compiler ragan-kelleyHalideLanguageCompiler2013 already target it for dense image processing. Despite this ecosystem, academic use of Hexagon for visual-inertial tracking remains limited. The closest prior work is Muffang's thesis muffang2021slamh , which offloaded OpenVINS genevaOpenVINSResearchPlatform2020a frontend routines to a Snapdragon 845 via FastCV; it reduced CPU load but the offloaded kernels ran slower than their CPU equivalents, and no source code was released. An open Hexagon port of the ORB-SLAM3 feature extractor and matcher exists for the Lynx R1 headset lynx2025orbslam3g , but it lacks inertial fusion and requires a rooted device. Crucially, none of the prior efforts support stereo-inertial tracking, a ubiquitous modality in consumer XR and robotics. Relative to this body of work, our system is, to the best of our knowledge, the first to accelerate a multicamera VIO pipeline on the Hexagon DSP of a stock consumer smartphone. While LEVIO shares our energy efficiency goals, it fundamentally redesigns the estimator for minimal compute budgets sacrificing accuracy; approaches like vilib, FastTrack, Jetson-SLAM, and GLidE-SLAM target frontend acceleration but rely on higher-power GPUs; ASIC-, FPGA- and MCU-based solutions like Navion, eSLAM, ac2SLAM, and PX4Flow achieve high efficiency but require hardware that is unavailable on common platforms. title: MobiAgent: Dual-Loop Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Long-Horizon Mobile Manipulation
comment: Accepted at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026. Project page: https://kaiknower.github.io/mobiagent
summary: Long-horizon mobile manipulation presents significant challenges due to compounding execution errors and capacity interference between locomotion and arm control. While recent Vision-Language-Action models excel at short-horizon tasks, they lack the hierarchical reasoning required for multi-stage objectives. Furthermore, existing hierarchical agents suffer from rigid sub-task mapping, inflexible replanning, and a lack of continuous learning. To address these limitations, we introduce MobiAgent, a dual-loop agentic framework that bridges robust deployment execution and recursive policy self-improvement. During deployment, the Inner Loop decouples high-level reasoning from low-level control through highly composable atomic skills. It employs Vision-Language models for receding-horizon planning and visual reflection, dynamically composing skills to ensure robust error recovery. These skills are executed by specialized flow-matching experts that share a unified VLM backbone, maximizing reusability while mitigating capacity interference. Concurrently, the Outer Loop drives automated lifelong learning by autonomously segmenting and verifying deployment rollouts, clustering them to discover atomic skills, and continuously fine-tuning the skill library without human annotations. Evaluations on RoboCasa, BEHAVIOR-1K, and real-world tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of MobiAgent. It outperforms $π_{0.5}$-TA by 22.5 percentage points on BEHAVIOR-1K and enables robust recovery from execution failures. Through autonomous data recycling, success improves from 7.50% to 27.50% on RoboCasa and from 32.5% to 57.5% on Astribot S1.

Introduction sec:introduction Long-horizon mobile manipulation requires executing complex, multi-stage tasks to achieve global goals, necessitating the seamless interleaving of distinct behavioral modes including global navigation and precise prehension. This domain poses significant challenges due to compounding execution errors and the capacity interference inherent in jointly modeling disparate sensorimotor mappings for locomotion and arm control. Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, notably OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla , \( _ 0 \)~ physicalintelligence2024pi0 , and \( _ 0.5 \)~ physicalintelligence2025pi0_5 , have demonstrated exceptional proficiency in tabletop environments by directly mapping multimodal observations to continuous actions. Building on this foundation, systems like Mobi-\( \)~ yang2025mobipi and N2M~ chai2025n2m extend VLAs to mobile platforms, primarily optimizing the navigation-manipulation hand-off. Nevertheless, these monolithic architectures function predominantly as reactive policies tailored for short-horizon objectives. In long-horizon scenarios, they lack the hierarchical reasoning necessary for semantic task decomposition and struggle to maintain the long-term context required for closed-loop replanning, fundamentally limiting their autonomy and reliability. To transcend short-horizon reactive policies, recent research explores hierarchical agentic frameworks that layer Large Language Models (LLMs) or Vision-Language Models (VLMs) over low-level controllers~ yao2023react, liang2023codeaspolicies, huang2023voxposer, li2024manipllm, wu2024momallm, shi2025hirobot, zhao2025vla2, roboclaw2026 , typically adopting a plan-execute-verify paradigm. Beyond their confinement to stationary manipulation, these architectures exhibit three critical bottlenecks: 1) Constrained Planning via Sub-task Mapping: They typically assign an individual, isolated policy to each decomposed sub-task. High-level planning is then reduced to discrete selection from a predefined list rather than open-ended generation, inherently limiting scalability and increasing system overhead as the required sub-task repertoire expands. 2) Inflexible Verification and Replanning: Stemming directly from this rigid policy mapping, dynamically replanning after a verification failure becomes highly cumbersome. This inflexibility is particularly fatal in mobile manipulation, where reflection and error recovery demand complex, continuous spatial reasoning (e.g., dynamic navigation, distance and viewpoint adjustments) prior to interaction. 3) Absence of Data Curation and Policy Self-Improvement: The vast majority of these frameworks operate open-loop regarding lifelong learning. While rare exceptions like RoboClaw~ roboclaw2026 introduce automated data collection, the field still lacks a comprehensive pipeline for unconstrained data curation and recursive self-improvement. To bridge the gap between robust deployment execution and recursive policy self-improvement, we propose MobiAgent, a dual-loop agentic system tailored for long-horizon mobile manipulation, as shown in Fig. fig:teaser . MobiAgent decouples high-level reasoning from low-level control based on atomic skills, partitioning the system into a deployment-time Inner Loop and an offline-training Outer Loop. To overcome the bottlenecks of constrained planning and inflexible replanning, the Inner Loop shifts the execution paradigm from rigid sub-task policies to highly composable atomic skills within a receding-horizon control flow. First, a Task Planner dynamically composes these skills on the fly. By replanning after completing each plan, it swiftly adapts to environmental changes and enables open-ended plan generation, bypassing the scalability limits of predefined sub-task lists. Next, by breaking down traditional sub-tasks into finer-grained actions, the Skill Executor employs skill-specific flow-matching experts built upon a shared VLM backbone. This semantic partitioning allows diverse sub-tasks sharing the same underlying action to reuse a single action expert, maximizing reusability while avoiding capacity interference. Finally, a Reflection Critic provides continuous visual verification to trigger flexible replanning. Operating at this granular level allows the Critic to explicitly manage the complex spatial reasoning essential for robust error recovery. The Outer Loop drives the automated data curation and evolution of the skill library, eliminating the need for manual data curation. First, a VLM-powered Data Curator processes startup demonstrations and deployment rollouts to autonomously segment and verify trajectory clips with instruction captions. Next, an Skill Generator clusters these instructions to establish a discrete vocabulary of atomic skills, seamlessly standardizing new rollout data into this inventory. Finally, a Skill Trainer uses this curated data to instantiate and continuously fine-tune the skill policies. To evaluate MobiAgent on long-horizon mobile manipulation, we conduct experiments across the simulated RoboCasa~ robocasa2024,robocasa365 and BEHAVIOR-1K~ li2023behavior1k benchmarks, as well as four real-world tasks on Astribot S1. On BEHAVIOR-1K, MobiAgent achieves a 65.0 mean success rate, outperforming the task-specific -TA baseline~ larchenko2025behavior1ksolution by 22.5 percentage points, while component ablations demonstrate the importance of dynamic planning, skill-specific experts, and visual verification. Its critic-driven global replanning further enables recovery from failures such as object drops and pose misalignments. Finally, deployment-to-training updates improve success from 7.50 to 27.50 on RoboCasa and from 32.5 to 57.5 on Astribot S1, validating the Outer Loop's ability to drive continuous, annotation-free policy improvement through autonomous data recycling. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-language-action (VLA) policies for short-horizon manipulation. Recent foundation models have popularized VLA policies that directly map language and visual observations to short-horizon robot actions brohan2023rt2, kim2024openvla, octo2024, physicalintelligence2024pi0, physicalintelligence2025pi0_5, li2024cogact, zhen2025spatialvla, kim2025openvlaoft, li2024roboflamingo, zhang2026retrieval . To model these short-horizon action distributions, architectures typically adopt one of two paradigms: models like RT-2 brohan2023rt2 and OpenVLA kim2024openvla co-train web-scale VLMs to output discretized action tokens, whereas recent state-of-the-art approaches like physicalintelligence2024pi0 and physicalintelligence2025pi0_5 leverage flow matching to directly generate continuous action trajectories. Hierarchical agentic frameworks for long-horizon tasks. Hierarchical frameworks typically layer LLMs or VLMs over low-level controllers using a plan-execute-verify paradigm yao2023react, liang2023codeaspolicies, huang2023voxposer, li2024manipllm, wu2024momallm, shi2025hirobot, zhao2025vla2, pang2026scivla, guo2024doremi, liu2023reflect, duan2024aha, liu2026goal2skill . While effective, they often rely on fixed skill repertoires. For instance, CaP-X fu2026capx composes predefined primitives but cannot learn underlying continuous sensorimotor behaviors. MobiAgent instead employs a unified, skill-conditioned VLA for native vision-based control. Additionally, existing error recovery mechanisms are often rigid; RoboClaw roboclaw2026 , for example, requires explicitly paired forward and reset policies. Adaptive World Action Models use future--reality verification~ wang2026trust , whereas MobiAgent performs skill-level verification and task-level replanning. Finally, unlike most open-loop systems that leave failed behaviors unchanged, MobiAgent introduces a deployment-to-training pipeline to continuously refine its skills from curated rollouts. Mobile manipulation systems. Current mobile manipulation systems wu2023tidybot, xiong2024spotcompose, fu2024mobilealoha, fu2024humanplus, liu2024okrobot, wang2025mg, yenamandra2023homerobot , including recent VLA extensions like Mobi-\( \) yang2025mobipi and N2M chai2025n2m , excel at reactive control and navigation-manipulation hand-offs. However, they lack the closed-loop replanning, online verification, and deployment-driven refinement required for long-horizon execution. Furthermore, state-of-the-art approaches like \( _ 0.5 \)-TA larchenko2025behavior1ksolution (the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge winner) rely on isolated, task-specific models. Their use of time-indexed stages forces distinct behaviors to share a single prediction head, causing capacity interference. MobiAgent: A Dual-Loop Agentic System for Mobile Manipulation sec:method Task Definition Motivation. We address long-horizon mobile manipulation, where a robot must execute complex, multi-stage tasks specified by a global language instruction \( \). At each step \(t\), the robot maps multi-modal observations \(o_t\) to continuous base and manipulator actions \( _t\), requiring the seamless interleaving of distinct behavioral modes like global navigation and precise prehension. Since monolithic end-to-end policies often suffer from compounding execution errors and capacity interference when jointly modeling disparate sensorimotor mappings, we propose MobiAgent. By decoupling high-level semantic reasoning from low-level sensorimotor control, our system enables dynamic task decomposition, spatial-aware failure recovery, and continuous offline skill evolution. Dual-Loop Architecture. As shown in Fig.~ fig:method_overview , MobiAgent employs a dual-loop agentic architecture to separate deployment-time execution from offline policy evolution: Inner Loop (Deployment): Governs closed-loop execution. It consists of a Task Planner that dynamically decomposes \( \) into actionable sub-tasks, a Skill Executor that maps sub-task instructions and real-time observations to low-level action chunks, and a Reflection Critic that evaluates outcomes to trigger progression, retries, or spatial-aware replanning. Outer Loop (Offline Training): Drives automated policy evolution. It ingests collected rollouts, utilizing a Data Curator for VLM-powered trajectory segmentation, a Skill Generator for semantic skill clustering, and a Skill Trainer for continuous policy updates. title: Detect and Suppress: A Mechanistic Defense against Adversarial Patches in VLA Models
summary: Adversarial patches can disrupt Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models by manipulating visual observations, leading to failures in robot control. However, it remains poorly understood which internal mechanisms underlie these failures and how targeted interventions can mitigate them. In this work, we mechanistically analyze VLA representations using a sparse autoencoder (SAE) and identify a feature whose activation strongly correlates with the presence of an adversarial patch. Based on this analysis, we suppress the identified feature at inference time only when a linear probe detects an attack. This intervention improves robustness without the cost of fine-tuning the VLA. We evaluate our method against VLA adversarial patch attacks on LIBERO-10. Conditional intervention improves success rate under intermittent attacks, whereas continuously applying the same intervention substantially degrades policy performance. These results show that attack-related internal representations can provide useful targets for VLA adversarial defense and that controlling when to intervene is important for limiting disruption to nominal policy behavior.

Introduction sec:introduction Adversarial patches can disrupt vision-language-action (VLA) policies by altering the visual observations used for robot control~ wang2025exploring,xu2025model . Existing VLA defenses modify either the inputs, through image preprocessing~ wang2026partially , or the model parameters, through adversarial fine-tuning~ xu2025model . Adversarial fine-tuning, however, incurs the computational cost of additional policy training. We ask whether VLA robustness can instead be improved by directly targeting attack-related internal features at inference time, without fine-tuning the policy. Mechanistic interpretability provides a basis for investigating this question. Recent studies have identified internal directions and sparse autoencoder (SAE) features whose manipulation influences VLA behavior~ haon2025mechanistic,swann2026sparse,jin2026event,buurmeijer2026observing . These studies primarily examine nominal behavior, leaving the use of such features for adversarial defense underexplored. However, indiscriminately suppressing attack-related features may also disrupt nominal policy behavior. An effective defense therefore requires examining both which feature to target and when to suppress it. We investigate these questions through SAE-based analysis and conditional intervention in VLA representations. We identify an SAE feature associated with patch presence and train a linear probe to detect attacks from the VLA's internal state. At inference time, we suppress the feature's contribution only when the probe detects an attack, while keeping the VLA parameters fixed. On LIBERO-10~ liu2023libero under Untargeted Action Discrepancy Attack (UADA)~ wang2025exploring , this conditional intervention improves task success under intermittent attacks, whereas continuous suppression of the same feature substantially degrades performance. Our results suggest that internal features associated with adversarial patches can serve as targets for VLA defense, and that intervening only during detected attacks limits disruption of nominal behavior. r 0.45 SAE features associated with adversarial patch presence. fig:motivation Motivation: Attack-Related Features sec:motivating_analysis Before introducing our method, we examine how adversarial patches are reflected in VLA representations. We train an SAE on internal representations collected from clean trajectories on LIBERO tasks. We then repeatedly switch an adversarial patch generated by UADA~ wang2025exploring on and off during a rollout in order to examine how SAE feature activations respond to patch presence. Figure~ fig:motivation shows that several SAE features track patch presence over time, a pattern also observed across multiple episodes. These observations motivate us to investigate whether suppressing these features only when an attack is detected can improve policy robustness. Methodology: Conditional Feature Intervention sec:methodlogy Problem Setup. Our goal is to improve task success under adversarial patch attacks while limiting performance degradation under clean observations. A VLA policy generates an action \(a_t = (o_t, l)\) from a visual observation \(o_t\) and a language instruction \(l\). title: XGenAct: Geometry-Enhanced World Action Models through Cross-Task Generation
summary: World action models (WAMs) have advanced robot control by predicting how observations and actions evolve over time. Despite this progress, RGB and action based future prediction does not explicitly address the spatial understanding needed for robot manipulation. Existing efforts often add a limited set of spatial prediction tasks through specialized heads or branches, leaving both the range of spatial supervision and the model architecture fragmented. We introduce XGenAct, a world action model that represents RGB observations, robot actions, metric depth, surface normals, and functional role segmentation as RGB videos through deterministic codecs. By sampling perception and action tasks during training, XGenAct uses one video diffusion transformer and one objective to learn temporal prediction across these spaces without modality specific learned heads. On held out RLBench tasks, structured perception training improves average closed loop success over RGB only training, and XGenAct achieves 52% success in the five task external comparison, versus 26% for the strongest evaluated baselines. It also predicts future depth and segmentation more accurately than the evaluated pipelines that generate RGB first and then apply a frozen perception expert.

By sampling perception and action tasks during training, XGenAct uses one video diffusion transformer and one objective to learn temporal prediction across these spaces without modality specific learned heads. On held out RLBench tasks, structured perception training improves average closed loop success over RGB only training, and XGenAct achieves 52 success in the five task external comparison, versus 26 for the strongest evaluated baselines. It also predicts future depth and segmentation more accurately than the evaluated pipelines that generate RGB first and then apply a frozen perception expert. Introduction sec:intro World action models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for generative robot control by jointly predicting future RGB videos and robot actions ye2026world,zhu2025uwm,zhen2026action . Compared with vision language action models that directly predict actions, WAMs use video generation to explicitly model how a scene evolves over time. This generative objective provides dense supervision for visual dynamics and temporal context, which can in turn improve action prediction. WAMs therefore offer a direct way to address the temporal reasoning required for robot control. However, their progress has been primarily temporal rather than spatial. Robots operate in a three dimensional world that evolves over time, while most WAMs represent the predicted world only as two dimensional RGB video. Although RGB observations contain implicit geometric cues, appearance prediction alone does not explicitly capture metric depth, surface orientation, or other spatial structures required for physical interaction. This limited spatial understanding remains a major bottleneck to further improving WAMs. Recent work has begun to address this limitation by introducing spatial information into WAMs. One possible direction is to predict explicit three dimensional or four dimensional representations, such as point clouds or point trajectories. zhen2025tesseract, dharmarajan2025dream2flow While these representations provide rich geometric structure, incorporating dense reconstruction directly into a generative control model requires additional representations and decoding procedures, making efficient joint prediction with robot actions nontrivial. A more practical alternative is to supervise spatial understanding through image aligned signals, including depth, optical flow, geometric features, and semantic maps. Several recent WAMs have adopted this strategy to enrich RGB based future prediction ma2026geosem,yuan2026dreamwam,li2026wam4d,zhao2026rynnworld . However, these spatial signals are typically introduced through auxiliary prediction heads, gated residual modules, or modality specific branches, each with its own representation and training objective. Their coverage also remains fragmented. Depth receives the most attention, while few methods incorporate complementary information such as surface orientation and task dependent functional regions within a single model. We argue that spatial supervision should not remain an auxiliary component attached to an RGB based WAM. Instead, multiple geometric and semantic prediction tasks should be expressed within the same generative space used to model observations and actions, allowing structured spatial knowledge to directly shape the shared action generator. Inspired by ~ zhen2026action , which represents 7 DoF robot actions as multiview RGB videos, we consider image space as a common interface for both perception and control. This representation is particularly suitable for structured visual signals because metric depth, surface normals, and segmentation can also be expressed as decodable RGB images gabeur2026image,wang2026video . Based on this insight, we introduce , a geometry enhanced world action model that represents RGB observations, metric depth, surface normals, functional role segmentation, and 7 DoF robot actions as RGB videos through deterministic codecs. Every stream is encoded by the same frozen video VAE into a shared latent space. During training, each sample selects a perception action template that pairs one perception stream with the action stream, rather than combining all perception modalities simultaneously. All templates are processed by the same diffusion transformer, output head, and flow matching objective, without modality specific learned heads, auxiliary losses, or manually balanced loss coefficients. By varying the perception task across training samples, this cross task formulation exposes the shared action generator to complementary geometric and semantic supervision. Experiments on held-out RLBench tasks demonstrate that achieves the highest average closed-loop success among eight external policy baselines while retaining the ability to predict future RGB, depth, surface normals, and segmentation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: 2pt Geometry enriched image space. We extend image space world action modeling beyond RGB and actions by encoding depth, surface normals, and functional role segmentation in the same visual modality, adding complementary geometric and semantic information. Head free and extensible task interface. Task templates and conditioning plans enable all perception and action tasks to share the same frozen VAE, DiT, output head, and flow matching objective, without modality specific learned heads or auxiliary losses. Improved robot control through cross-task generation. Experiments on held-out RLBench tasks show that structured geometric and semantic generation improves average closed-loop success by up to 28.75 percentage points over RGB-only training at matched compute and action budgets, while retaining future RGB generation. Related Work sec:related Structured world prediction for action learning. World action models (WAMs) jointly learn structured visual future prediction and robot action generation, often using a shared video diffusion backbone~ ye2026world,zhu2025uwm,zhen2026action,zhou2026tauzero,chen2026flowwam . While most WAMs predict RGB futures, recent methods introduce geometric or semantic supervision. PAD~ guo2024pad extends joint image and action denoising to depth using separate modality encoders and decoders. GeoSem-WAM~ ma2026geosem , DreamWAM~ yuan2026dreamwam , WAM4D~ li2026wam4d , and X-WAM~ guo2026xwam incorporate geometry through auxiliary branches, residual modules, or training-only readouts. RynnWorld-4D~ zhao2026rynnworld generates RGB, depth, and optical flow using a three branch architecture, then predicts actions with a downstream inverse dynamics head. These methods demonstrate the value of structured future supervision, but rely on modality specific components, objectives, or action modules. SA-WAM~ lopetegui2026sawam is closest to our representation. It encodes RGB and metric depth with the same frozen video tokenizer and jointly denoises them with actions in one latent sequence. However, actions occupy dedicated latent positions, and the model uses a fixed RGB, depth, and action layout. In contrast, represents both structured perception and action as video streams and samples multiple perception action templates within one shared generative model. Perception as generation. A complementary line of work formulates visual understanding through image or video generation. Painter~ wang2023painter and DICEPTION~ zhao2025diception express multiple perception tasks in a common visual space. Vision Banana~ gabeur2026image and GenCeption~ wang2026video generate depth, segmentation, surface normals, and correspondence from task prompts. SUV~ yuan2026suv applies a similar formulation to driving, but retains a separate action expert. These methods establish generation as a common interface for perception, but do not examine whether a mixture of structured perception tasks can improve a robot action generator expressed in the same output space. Visual representations of action. RT-Trajectory~ gu2023rttrajectory and TraceVLA~ zheng2025tracevla augment observations with visual motion cues but still predict action tokens. PIVOT~ nasiriany2024pivot visualizes candidate actions for a vision language model to select. Action Images~ zhen2026action instead represents a 7-DoF end effector pose as multiview RGB canvases generated by a video model. extends this image space beyond RGB observations and actions by incorporating metric depth, surface normals, and functional role segmentation. This connects perception as generation with action as generation, allowing multiple geometric and semantic tasks to supervise one action generator without modality specific heads or auxiliary losses. Method sec:method Overview We build on the Action Images formulation~ zhen2026action using a Wan2.2-TI2V-5B video diffusion backbone~ wan2025 . Following Action Images, a 7-DoF robot action is projected into multiple camera views and rendered as an RGB video that can be decoded back into continuous control. We retain this action representation without modification. The video VAE remains frozen, and only the diffusion transformer is fine-tuned. Our key idea is to extend this shared video space with geometry-related perception tasks. RGB observations, metric depth, surface normals, functional role segmentation, and robot actions are converted into RGB videos through deterministic codecs and encoded by the same frozen VAE. This places appearance, geometry, semantics, and control in a common latent space without introducing modality specific learned encoders or output heads. For each training sample, we select one perception modality \(m\) and pair it with the action stream from two camera views: Thus, a sample contains one perception modality and action, rather than all perception modalities simultaneously. The template \( _m\) determines which streams the model processes, while a conditioning plan determines which frames are observed and which frames must be generated. All templates share the same diffusion transformer, output head, and training objective. Geometry Enriched Video Space Let \(x^ (m,v) \) denote a video stream of modality \(m\) from camera view \(v\). We define a deterministic codec \( _m\) that converts each stream into a three channel video accepted by the frozen video VAE: where \( \) is shared across all modalities. These codecs contain no learnable parameters. They preserve the information required to recover the original signal while producing videos that remain stable under VAE encoding and decoding. RGB and action. RGB observations use the identity mapping. Robot actions use the Action Images codec~ zhen2026action , which projects each 7-DoF end effector pose into the camera views and renders the resulting trajectories as RGB videos. We use this representation unchanged. Metric depth. Raw metric depth has an unbounded and highly nonuniform value distribution, making direct grayscale encoding inefficient. We first compress depth values with a monotonic power transform and then map the resulting scalar values onto a continuous path through the RGB cube. At decoding time, generated colors are projected back onto this path before the scalar transform is inverted. This encoding distributes metric depth across an RGB path instead of a single grayscale axis. Full definitions and decoding rules are provided in Appendix~ a

title: DR-IPC: Disturbance-Resilient Integrated Planning and Control for LiDAR-Based Quadrotor Navigation
summary: LiDAR-based quadrotor navigation in cluttered environments remains challenging under external disturbances, particularly when obstacle-aware motion generation and disturbance-rejection control are handled in separate layers. This article presents disturbance-resilient integrated planning and control (DR-IPC), which combines lightweight path guidance with nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) to directly generate angular velocity and thrust. An interconnected extended Kalman filter and nonlinear disturbance observer jointly provide filtered state estimates and reconstructed disturbances for NMPC prediction. The resulting formulation unifies nonlinear quadrotor dynamics, actuator constraints, local motion generation, and penalised safe-flight-corridor residuals without requiring a separate trajectory-optimization stage. Gazebo and MARSIM simulations, together with indoor and outdoor experiments, validate DR-IPC under wind, suspended payloads, narrow passages, ball impacts and reactive avoidance of a dynamic obstacle. In multi-goal navigation with disturbances, DR-IPC increases the number of completed missions from 1/10 to 9/10 in Gazebo and reduces the altitude RMSE from 0.34 to 0.01 m in experiments. The complete system operates onboard at 100 Hz. Supplementary videos are available on the project page https://drpp316.github.io/DR-IPC-Page/, and the source code will be released.
full_text: LiDAR-based quadrotor navigation in cluttered environments remains challenging under external disturbances, particularly when obstacle-aware motion generation and disturbance-rejection control are handled in separate layers. This article presents disturbance-resilient integrated planning and control (DR-IPC), which combines lightweight path guidance with nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) to directly generate angular velocity and thrust. An interconnected extended Kalman filter and nonlinear disturbance observer jointly provide filtered state estimates and reconstructed disturbances for NMPC prediction. The resulting formulation unifies nonlinear quadrotor dynamics, actuator constraints, local motion generation, and penalized safe-flight-corridor residuals without requiring a separate trajectory-optimization stage. Gazebo and MARSIM simulations, together with indoor and outdoor experiments, validate DR-IPC under wind, suspended payloads, narrow passages, ball impacts and reactive avoidance of a dynamic obstacle. In multi-goal navigation with disturbances, DR-IPC increases the number of completed missions from 1/10 to 9/10 in Gazebo and reduces the altitude RMSE from 0.34 to 0.01~m in experiments. The complete system operates onboard at 100 Hz. Supplementary videos are available on the project page , and the source code will be released. Integrated planning and control, nonlinear model predictive control, disturbance-aware navigation, interconnected observer, LiDAR-based quadrotor INTRODUCTION roviding onboard 3-D mapping and odometry, LiDAR-based quadrotors have become an important platform for autonomous navigation in cluttered and partially unknown environments ren2025survey , including inspection liu2025lidar,marshall2025redundant , search and rescue lim2024autonomous , precision agriculture su2023ai , and aerial transportation sun2025agile . However, LiDAR maps contain only geometric information and do not capture wind, payload-induced forces, or modeling errors. Odometry noise further degrades the state measurements used for feedback tian2015mechatronic . Consequently, these disturbances and uncertainties can drive the LiDAR-based vehicle away from the nominally collision-free path. Most LiDAR-based quadrotor systems use a hierarchical planning and control (HPC) architecture ren2025survey,marshall2021survey , where a planner generates collision-free motion from the LiDAR map and a downstream controller handles tracking separately zhou2020ego . This separation makes it difficult to adjust collision-avoidance motion and control actions together when disturbances cause path deviations. Integrated planning and control (IPC) reduces this gap by jointly optimizing local motion and control commands within a predictive backend liu2025slope, liu2023integrated, wu2025flying . However, existing LiDAR-based IPC methods provide only partial integration and limited (i.e., passive instead of active) robustness to external disturbances and noisy state measurements. To this end, on top of the classical IPC liu2023integrated , this paper presents DR-IPC, a Disturbance-Resilient Integrated Planning and Control algorithm for LiDAR-based quadrotor navigation. Unlike the original IPC, DR-IPC uses the reconstructed disturbance not only for feedback compensation but also within the NMPC prediction to jointly modify collision-avoidance motion and control inputs. The pipeline is shown in Fig.~ pipeline . The main contributions are: DR-IPC Algorithm: A DR-IPC algorithm is developed for LiDAR-based quadrotor navigation in cluttered, noisy, and disturbance-rich environments. The A* path references, soft SFC penalties, nonlinear quadrotor dynamics, input constraints, and reconstructed disturbances are jointly handled in a unified NMPC backend. Nonlinear Interconnected Observer: A nonlinear interconnected EKF+NDO is designed for simultaneous state filtering and disturbance reconstruction in the presence of noise, providing noise-attenuated state estimates and smoother disturbance estimates for NMPC. Comparative Multi-Scenario Validation: DR-IPC is validated in Gazebo and MARSIM, together with indoor and outdoor experiments covering wind disturbances, suspended-payload transportation, narrow-passage navigation, impacts from a throwing ball, reactive avoidance of a dynamic obstacle, wooded and factory flights. Vector inequalities are interpreted element-wise. RELATED WORK Obstacle-Aware Motion Generation and Predictive Control Hierarchical Planning and Control Conventional quadrotor navigation separates path planning, trajectory optimization, and tracking control. A front-end planner typically uses a geometric or simplified point-mass model, while a back-end optimizer converts the path into a smooth nominal trajectory. Representative methods include SFC-based polynomial optimization liu2017planning , minimum-snap generation mellinger2011minimum , EGO-Planner zhou2020ego , and hierarchical two-layer MPC benders2025embedded . A lower-level feedback controller then tracks the optimized trajectory. In this architecture, obstacle avoidance is handled only by the planner, typically using a simplified model without disturbance effects. The resulting path may be geometrically collision-free but not dynamically feasible under disturbances. At the control level, as illustrated in Fig.~ hpc_ipc (a), the tracking controller does not have obstacle information and continues to reduce the tracking error after the vehicle deviates from the reference. It may drive vehicles toward nearby obstacles without timely replanning. Consequently, the performance of HPC may degrade in cluttered environments under disturbances. Integrated Planning and Control Integrated schemes have attracted increasing attention ren2025survey,marshall2021survey . It acts as a local predictive planner-controller that uses global guidance and obstacle information liu2023integrated . At each receding-horizon update, it jointly optimizes collision-aware local motion and control inputs, rather than merely tracking a prescribed trajectory without accounting for obstacles reiter2026temporal . As shown in Fig.~ hpc_ipc (b), when wind drives the vehicle away from the reference, the integrated schemes can adjust both the local motion around the obstacle and the corresponding control action. Existing integrated methods couple motion generation and control in different ways. Obstacle-aware NMPC lindqvist2020nmpc imposes a prescribed UAV--obstacle distance as a hard constraint. CBF-based MPC ali2024mpccbf embeds forward-invariant safety conditions into MPC for collision avoidance. MPCC romero2022model jointly optimizes path progress and control for racing but omits obstacle avoidance. IPC liu2023integrated combines A* with SFC-constrained linear MPC, with subsequent extensions to challenging terrain and dynamic environments liu2025slope,wu2025flying . However, its linear triple-integrator model derives angular velocity and thrust through differential flatness, while integral thrust adaptation provides only limited disturbance compensation. IPC liu2023integrated therefore remains partially integrated and offers limited active disturbance-rejection capability. Moreover, its hard SFC constraint may make online optimization infeasible or induce aggressive corrective motion after disturbance-induced deviations wang2021efficient . Overall, these representative methods rely mainly on nominal prediction and do not incorporate reconstructed disturbances into obstacle-aware motion optimization. Robust and Disturbance-aware MPC Robust MPC Robust MPC handles bounded disturbances and uncertainties without explicitly reconstructing them. Robust visual-servo NMPC zhang2021robust maintains target visibility through constraint tightening. Efficient NMPC wang2021efficient converts inequality constraints into cost penalties and imposes a contraction constraint for real-time stable tracking. Disturbance-aware MPC Disturbance observer (DOB)-based quadrotor controllers have been developed for disturbance-rejection tracking and landing Shao2021tmech,zhang2026tie , following the general disturbance-estimation and compensation framework chen2004disturbance,chen2016doboverview . Observer-based MPC further incorporates disturbance estimates into prediction. DA-MPC kim2024disturbance injects an NDO estimate into the prediction model. DR-MPC li2025drmpc combines a generalized extended-state observer with predictive visual servoing for UAV pipeline inspection. Both branches employ MPC for prescribed trajectory or visual-target tracking. Robust MPC does not reconstruct the disturbance, whereas disturbance-aware MPC incorporates its estimate into prediction. However, neither couples disturbance rejection with obstacle-aware local motion generation. Positioning of DR-IPC As summarized in Table~ tab:related_work_comparison , existing obstacle-aware methods generally omit online disturbance reconstruction, whereas disturbance-aware MPC methods, which mainly serve as low-level control strategies, do not include obstacle information in prediction. The proposed DR-IPC bridges this gap by integrating disturbance reconstruction with obstacle-aware predictive control. Building on our previous linear KF+DOB architecture liu2026interconnected , the interconnected observer is extended to nonlinear quaternion dynamics. The resulting EKF+NDO supplies filtered states and reconstructed disturbances to an obstacle-aware NMPC that jointly optimizes local motion, angular velocity and thrust. Without a separate trajectory-optimization stage, the onboard system supports LiDAR-based navigation and suspended-payload transportation in disturbance-rich, cluttered outdoor and factory environments.
