Introduction Geometric understanding from images is a foundation of computer vision. Methods like DUSt3R~ wang2024dust3r , MASt3R~ leroy2024mast3r , and VGGT~ wang2025vggt demonstrate that transformers can produce rich, transferable geometric representations, when trained on large-scale annotated 3D data. This supervision requirement is a fundamental bottleneck since dense 3D ground truth is expensive to collect at scale. Novel View Synthesis (NVS) offers a compelling alternative jin2025lvsm,zhao2026erayzer,jiang2025rayzer,kim2026svsm . These models must reason about 3D scene structure to predict unseen viewpoints, providing a rich geometric supervision signal only from posed images, which are abundantly available across videos, robotics platforms, and structure-from-motion pipelines. However, representations produced from feed-forward NVS methods transfer poorly to downstream geometric tasks. We argue this poor transfer is not a signal failure, but rather an architectural failure, driven by two identifiable and independently addressable choices that dilute signal. First, spatially expressive decoders tend to absorb the representational load of the task. When a decoder has sufficient capacity to reconstruct a target view from any encoder output, the encoder is not pressured to maintain structured, locally discriminative features. While the reconstruction task is solved, the latent representations are not geometrically grounded. Second, pixel-space reconstruction targets require modeling high-frequency aliasing statistics that are weakly related to 3D structure and semantics. Consequently, the reconstruction loss produces gradients that encourage the representation encoder to preserve fine-grained, image-specific statistics that are not directly informative about the underlying 3D structure or semantics. We present , which addresses both failure axes with two targeted interventions. First, a pose-conditioned local decoder built on ~ li2025cameras restricts the decoder's receptive field via an explicit mask applied to queried-view self-attention. This constraint forces the geometric structure to reside within the encoder's scene representation rather than being an effect of the generative capacity of the decoder. Second, operates directly on frozen ViT-B patch features to provide a richer supervision signal than RGB reconstruction. This structured grounding is jointly aware of appearance, geometry, and semantics and produces higher quality representations. Our main contributions are: , a self-supervised multi-view spatial reasoning backbone that builds upon frozen 2D semantic latent spaces with an asymmetric NVS prediction objective, and latent feature targets to learn geometrically transferable representations without dense 3D supervision. Mechanistic analyses isolating the independent impact of decoder expressivity and prediction space on geometric transfer, via receptive field sweeps and prediction space landscape experiments. Empirical evaluation across five tasks matching or exceeding self-supervised baselines and competitive with geometry-supervised methods that require large-scale annotated 3D data. Related Work \ sits at the intersection of self-supervised representation learning, novel view synthesis, and geometric foundation models. Detailed discussions are provided in Appendix~ sec:appendix_related_work . Self-Supervised Representation Learning. Masked Image Modeling (MIM) has evolved from pixel-reconstruction (MAE~ he2022mae , SimMIM~ xie2022simmim ) toward latent-space prediction (I-JEPA~ assran2023ijepa , V-JEPA~ bardes2024vjepa ). In multi-view regimes, CroCo~ weinzaepfel2022croco and Muskie~ li2025muskiemultiviewmaskedimage leverage cross-view completion to learn implicit 3D priors. \ extends this trajectory by utilizing frozen ~ simeoni2025dinov3 features as opposed to pixel space targets used in Muskie~ li2025muskiemultiviewmaskedimage , which act as semantically structured latent distillation targets to provide a cleaner supervision signal for optimization. Novel View Synthesis (NVS). Feed-forward NVS was established by architectures such as SRT~ sajjadi2022srt and RUST~ sajjadi2023rust , recently scaling to large-view models such as LVSM~ jin2025lvsm , RayZer~ jiang2025rayzer , with contemporaneous works LagerNVS~ szymanowicz2026lagernvs and SVSM~ kim2026svsm continuing to extend the paradigm. However, most of these variants utilize expressive decoders that absorb the representational load of the task, leading to ungrounded latents. By constraining the decoder's receptive field via a mask, adopting ~ li2025cameras , and targeting a latent feature space, \ ensures its representations prioritize 3D structural awareness over reconstruction statistics. Geometry-Supervised Models. Recent foundation models, including DUSt3R~ wang2024dust3r , MASt3R~ leroy2024mast3r , VGGT~ wang2025vggt , and D4RT~ zhang2026d4rt , achieve state-of-the-art performance but rely on massive 3D-annotated datasets. Similarly, ~ wang2026pi3 and Depth Anything 3~ lin2026depth provide robust spatial priors via explicit 3D supervision. Conversely, \ approaches the geometric transferability of these models while remaining self-supervised and training on significantly less data and compute. Method \ operates in two stages, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:architecture . First, a pose-free multi-view encoder aggregates frozen \ patch features from reference views into scene tokens via full cross-view self-attention. Notably, no camera parameters are provided at this stage. Second, a pose-conditioned patch decoder then queries using -rotated cross-attention to synthesize the target view's feature map. The target and context camera intrinsics and extrinsics are fed into at this stage. Two design choices jointly force geometric structure into the encoder: a \ mask restricting the decoder's spatial receptive field (Sec.~ sec:prope_decoder ), and a latent reconstruction objective against frozen \ teacher features rather than RGB pixels (Sec.~ sec:objective ). title: RIFAR: Reliability and Forgetting-Aware Replay for Continual Robot Learning
summary: Genuine embodied agency requires robots to turn continuous real-world experience into lasting, transferable skills. This demands continual learning that integrates new capabilities without eroding prior knowledge as tasks and environments evolve. Experience replay mitigates forgetting, but storing complete demonstrations becomes costly as tasks accumulate. World-action models offer a generative alternative, reconstructing past experience through joint predictions of actions and future observations. However, visually coherent rollouts may contain actions that cannot realize the predicted transitions, while new-task adaptation can disrupt previously learned behavior. RIFAR therefore combines reliability screening with drift-aware replay selection. It reconstructs trajectories from compact demonstration prefixes and uses a frozen inverse-dynamics model to assess action-visual consistency. Training first combines current demonstrations with the highest-quality screened trajectories. RIFAR then compares action predictions before and after this adaptation on identical historical inputs, reselecting trajectories with larger normalized drift from the same screened pool for continued training. Across three LIBERO suites and real-world experiments, RIFAR surpasses the previous state of the art in WAM-based generative replay. On LIBERO-Goal, it achieves 90.97 AUC while retaining only 320 historical time steps per task, approximately 4.9% of the steps retained using 50-demonstration replay.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments LIBERO Evaluation Setup We evaluate RIFAR on the LIBERO benchmark libero2023 using Cosmos Policy kim2026 , initialized from Cosmos-Predict2-2B. The policy receives third-person and wrist RGB observations, proprioceptive states, and language instructions, and predicts a 16-step action chunk. Across the Goal, Object, and Spatial suites, we jointly train on Tasks 0--5 and then introduce Tasks 6--9 sequentially. We train all methods for 800 optimization steps per new task and evaluate all seen tasks after each stage. For RIFAR, we select the first 20 demonstrations of each past task in dataset order. We retain only the initial 16 time steps of each demonstration for replay generation. Both training phases combine current-task demonstrations with replay. Phase 1 uses the highest-quality IDM-screened trajectories for 500 steps. We then reselect trajectories from the full reliable pool based on action drift and continue training for another 300 optimization steps in Phase 2. We compare RIFAR with sequential fine-tuning, EWC, PackNet, REGEN, and ER( ), which stores complete demonstrations per historical task for replay. We report AUC, FWT, and NBT for each compared method, with metric definitions and the evaluation protocol in Appendix~ app:evaluation . Main Results and Memory Efficiency As shown in Table~ tab:main , RIFAR achieves higher AUC and lower NBT than REGEN across all three evaluated LIBERO suites, indicating better retention of previously learned skills. On LIBERO-Goal, RIFAR improves AUC from 67.8 to 90.97 and reduces NBT from 46.7 to 7.45 compared with REGEN. The smaller AUC gains on Object and Spatial are 5.39 and 9.93 points, respectively. RIFAR also remains competitive with experience replay using stored demonstrations, while retaining only compact initial-state anchors rather than complete trajectories. We further examine the relationship between retained historical data and performance in a separate study on LIBERO-Goal (Figure~ fig:anchors (b,c)). RIFAR achieves an AUC of 90.97, slightly exceeding ER(10)'s 90.70 while retaining approximately one-quarter as many historical time steps (320 versus 1,300). ER(50) achieves a higher AUC of 91.80 but retains approximately 6,500 time steps per task. These results show that RIFAR remains competitive with experience replay while retaining substantially less historical data. Ablation Studies Effect of the Number of Anchors. We vary the number of anchors per historical task on LIBERO-Goal to assess the trade-off between retained context and continual learning performance (Figure~ fig:anchors (a)). AUC increases from 80.5 at to 86.8 at and 90.97 at , then rises more slowly to 91.2 at and 91.5 at . We therefore use as our default setting for each task, which retains 40 as many anchors as with AUC only 0.53 points lower. IDM Screening and Drift-Based Selection. We compare anchor-only replay with IDM screening, drift-based selection, or both (Table~ tab:ablation ). Either component improves AUC and reduces NBT. On LIBERO-Goal, adding drift-based selection to IDM screening raises AUC from 87.14 to 90.97 and reduces NBT from 10.61 to 7.45. RIFAR achieves the best AUC and NBT across all three suites. Analysis of Replay Selection Criteria. Table~ tab:selection_validation compares high-ranked, randomly sampled, and low-ranked trajectories for replay at stage 6 of each LIBERO suite, evaluating IDM reliability and drift priority separately. High-ranked selection yields the highest success rate for both criteria in all three suites. On Goal, high-drift replay exceeds random replay by 3.1 percentage points; on Object, IDM-based selection improves success by 4.4 points. Reliability Analysis of IDM Screening. In Figure~ fig:idm_case (a), generated observations suggest task completion, yet executing the paired actions in the simulator fails. This case motivates checking action--visual consistency when selecting generated trajectories. IDM screening retains a subset with a 76.9 execution success rate, compared with 44.0 for unfiltered candidates, a difference of 32.9 percentage points (Figure~ fig:idm_case (b)). The higher success rate of the screened subset supports IDM agreement as a reliability signal for generated replay. Action-Drift Analysis. We compare fixed replay and drift-aware reselection on LIBERO-Goal under the same 800-step training budget. Both variants use current demonstrations and the same screened replay set for 500 steps. The control retains this set; the other reselects the ten trajectories per historical task with the highest from the full screened pool. Both then train for 300 steps with current data and their respective replay sets. We evaluate both final policies against a shared reference using identical observations, proprioceptive states, and instructions from ten trajectories per evaluated task, with matched inference settings. Following Eq.~ , each input's drift is the normalized action difference averaged over the 16-step chunk. Mean and Max summarize the average and largest input-level drifts; Tail averages the largest , ranked separately for each variant. For fixed and reselected replay statistics and , we define relative reduction for : Positive values indicate a reduction in action drift and negative values an increase. For task~3, Figure~ fig:drift_reduction (d) shows reductions in all three statistics across M6--M9. Some other tasks show increased maximum drift (Table~ tab:detailed_drift ). These diagnostics measure agreement with reference actions and do not directly measure task-level forgetting. Real-World Continual Learning sec:realworld We evaluate Cosmos Policy on three real-world tasks using a Franka robot (Figure~ fig:budget ). Cube pick-and-place requires grasping and placement; board wiping requires controlled motion while maintaining eraser contact with the board; and table cleaning involves sweeping with a broom. Their differing motion and contact requirements test whether a shared policy can acquire new behaviors while retaining earlier skills. We compare RIFAR with sequential fine-tuning, ER(50), and REGEN. Sequential fine-tuning uses only current-task demonstrations. ER(50) replays 50 complete demonstrations per historical task, whereas REGEN and RIFAR replay generated historical experience. After each stage, we evaluate all compared methods on all tasks seen so far and report FWT, NBT, and AUC. Table~ tab:realworld shows that REGEN reduces forgetting compared with sequential fine-tuning, while RIFAR further improves both task acquisition and retention. Relative to REGEN, RIFAR raises AUC from 50.39 to 57.78 and lowers NBT from 26.77 to 8.84. FWT also rises from 57.67 to 61.00, supporting improved new-task acquisition. Although ER(50) remains stronger overall, RIFAR approaches its AUC (57.78 versus 59.83) while retaining only compact historical contexts rather than complete original demonstrations. These results support reliable, targeted generative replay as an effective way to preserve earlier manipulation skills while retaining only compact historical contexts.

title: ManifoldSplat: Language-Guided Semantic Shape Editing of 3D Gaussian Head Avatars
summary: High-fidelity 3D head avatars have reached near-photorealistic quality. While recent methods enable text-driven manipulation, they struggle to provide fine-grained localized control, often entangling features or lacking geometric consistency. Modifying geometry through natural language currently requires slow per-prompt optimization or compromises identity and rigging. We present ManifoldSplat, the first end-toend framework for language-guided semantic shape editing of animatable 3D Gaussian Splatting avatars reconstructed from monocular videos. By performing edits within the structured FLAME manifold rather than directly optimizing an unstructured Gaussian cloud, we strictly preserve identity and animation. We introduce DeltaRegion, a per-region disentangled Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) delivering feedforward shape deltas, alongside a refining stage to recover view-consistent details. ManifoldSplat reconstructs and edits an avatar in ~90 seconds on a consumer GPU, rendering at ~800 FPS. Extensive evaluations demonstrate our approach sets a new state-of-the-art in localized prompt alignment, geometric coherence, and identity preservation. Project page and code: https://a-canela.github.io/manifoldsplat/

Project page and code: Introduction sec:intro Photorealistic animatable 3D head avatars are a core building block of telepresence, virtual production, and assistive technologies. By combining a parametric face model such as ~ flame17 with 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl3Dgaussians , recent methods~ qian2024gaussianavatars,xiang2024flashavatar,shao2024splattingavatar,HRAvatar,li2025rgbavatar can reconstruct a personal, drivable head from a short monocular video in minutes and render it in real time. Once reconstructed, however, these avatars are frozen identities: there is no built-in way for a user to manipulate specific facial attributes through text and obtain, in seconds, an animatable avatar of the same person with the requested change (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Closing this gap remains challenging. Text-to-3D-face generators~ wu2023describe3d,aneja2023clipface,semantify synthesize meshes from scratch, failing to preserve personal identity. Distillation-based editors~ brooks2022instructpix2pix,liu2025gaussianavatar-editor require lengthy per-prompt optimization, focus strictly on appearance, and often break multi-view consistency. Meanwhile, generic 3D scene editors~ gaussianeditor,wang2024gaussianeditor2 demand multi-view captures. Crucially, no existing method achieves localized geometric editing of a personal monocular avatar while preserving its animation rigging and sub-minute latency. Our key observation is that 's identity subspace is already a structured manifold of plausible head geometry, but it lacks explicit correspondence with individual facial attributes, making isolated edits inherently difficult. Learning a text-conditioned generator inside this manifold - rather than in the Gaussian or NeRF parameter space - yields edits that are by construction physically plausible, identity-preserving, and trivially compatible with downstream animation. The remaining challenges are then to localize an edit to the region the user names without entangling unrelated attributes, and to make the Gaussian avatar robust to the resulting geometric change without a full per-edit optimization. We propose , a two-stage pipeline on a mesh-bound 3D Gaussian Splatting avatar: a text-guided shape-editing stage produces a localized identity delta on the manifold, followed by a targeted rendering stage that adapts the splats so the re-parameterized identity renders cleanly (Sec.~ sec:method ). In our evaluations, outperforms GaussianAvatar-Editor~ liu2025gaussianavatar-editor and InstructPix2Pix~ brooks2022instructpix2pix on prompt alignment, identity preservation and visual cleanliness while being one to two orders of magnitude faster; at the shape level, it significantly outperforms ~ wu2023describe3d and Semantify~ semantify in edit locality. Contributions. : an end-to-end pipeline achieving state-of-the-art language-guided semantic shape editing of animatable 3D Gaussian head avatars reconstructed from monocular video, with targeted rendering enhancements that address the characteristic geometric artifacts. : a text-guided shape editing model that, given a free-form prompt and a source identity, yields a localized shape delta in a single feed-forward pass. A synthetic dataset of per-region vertex-displacement edits defined on the topology. Related Work sec:relatedwork sits at the intersection of multiple lines of research: parametric 3D face models, animatable head avatars with neural and Gaussian representations, and text-driven 3D generation and editing. Parametric Face Models. Linear morphable face models~ lyhm,flame17 and the encoder-based identity predictors built on them~ mica_eccv22 derive their shape spaces via global dimensionality reduction, so their parameters are highly entangled and lack explicit correspondence with localized semantic attributes. While mapping linguistic descriptions to global shape spaces has been explored for parametric body models~ streuber2016bodytalk , achieving localized, disentangled control over specific facial attributes on the manifold remains an open challenge. addresses this gap by operating entirely inside the identity shape space, giving us a strong inductive bias for plausibility while enforcing localized, semantic control, and keeping every edit trivially compatible with downstream -rigged assets. Head-Avatar Reconstruction. Early monocular head avatars relied on neural radiance fields~ mildenhall2020nerf,nerface,zielonka2022insta,Zheng2023pointavatar . Driven by its real-time efficiency and high visual fidelity, 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl3Dgaussians shifted the dominant paradigm toward explicit, animatable Gaussian representations rigged on a parametric mesh~ qian2024gaussianavatars,shao2024splattingavatar,xiang2024flashavatar,HRAvatar,li2025rgbavatar ; a parallel branch tackles cross-identity, feed-forward avatar synthesis from one or a few images~ chu2024gagavatar,he2024head360,avat3r . We build on the Gaussian-blendshape formulation of~ li2025rgbavatar because its identity-shape-driven parameterization makes shape edits both fast and well defined; our rendering-side enhancements (Sec.~ sec:method:enhancements ) are nonetheless orthogonal and could be integrated into other mesh-anchored Gaussian avatars. Text-Driven 3D Face Generation. A growing body of work generates 3D faces or full heads from a text prompt, either via Score Distillation Sampling~ poole2023dreamfusion on top of generic text-to-3D backbones~ lin2023magic3d,tang2024dreamgaussian or with face-specific pipelines~ wu2023describe3d,dreamface,aneja2023clipface,zhou2024headstudio,liao2024tada,liu2024headartist ; CLIP-space stylization methods~ michel2022text2mesh,wang2022clipnerf explore a related formulation. All of these target generation rather than editing of an identity reconstructed from a user-supplied video, so comparing against them would conflate two problem statements. To still isolate the shape-editing aspect of our pipeline, we benchmark against ~ wu2023describe3d and Semantify~ semantify as the closest practical shape-level counterparts, noting that both synthesize from a neutral mesh without conditioning on a source identity. Editing 3D Avatars and Scenes. Text-driven scene editing was popularized by InstructPix2Pix~ brooks2022instructpix2pix and its 3D lifts Instruct-NeRF2NeRF and Instruct-GS2GS~ haque2023instructnerf2nerf,vachha2024instruct-gs2gs , followed by multi-view-consistent editors~ gaussianeditor,wang2024gaussianeditor2,chen2024dge . Head-avatar-specific methods include GaussianAvatar-Editor~ liu2025gaussianavatar-editor (per-prompt InstructPix2Pix iteration on an animatable 3DGS head), FATE~ zhang2025fate (textural edits), AvatarStudio~ mendiratta2023avatarstudio (dynamic-actor editing via 2D diffusion priors), and ShapeFusion~ potamias2024shapefusion (localized shape edits via a 3D diffusion model conditioned on sparse handles). Most multi-view scene editors require COLMAP-style calibration or assume a static scene, both violated by monocular talking-head video. The only published methods that meet our constraints (animatable, monocularly reconstructed Gaussian head, free-form text instruction) are GaussianAvatar-Editor~ liu2025gaussianavatar-editor and an InstructPix2Pix-based editor of the trained avatar, which we use as our two avatar-level baselines. Method sec:method takes a short monocular RGB video of a subject and a free-form prompt (e.g.\ ``shorter nose''), and produces an animatable 3D Gaussian Splatting head avatar with a semantically edited identity. As overviewed in Fig.~ fig:method , our pipeline bridges parametric mesh edits and splat-based rendering in two stages: (i) text-driven shape editing via for a localized geometric edit on the manifold (Sec.~ sec:method:shapemodel ), and (ii) a targeted Gaussian refining stage that adapts splat parameters to the new geometry (Sec.~ sec:method:enhancements ). Background - Preprocessing and Mesh-bound Backbone sec:method:background . We adopt RGBAvatar~ li2025rgbavatar as our reconstruction backbone and inherit its preprocessing stack: MICA~ mica_eccv22 for identity initialization, metrical-tracker~ mica_eccv22 for per-frame pose and expression, and Robust Video Matting~ RobustVideoMatting for foreground extraction at . ~ flame17 parameterizes a head mesh as with identity , expression , and pose in separate linear subspaces, so editing alone changes who the subject is without altering how they move. -bound Gaussian-blendshape avatars represent a personal head as a set of 3D Gaussians whose canonical centers are anchored on the mesh and deformed by a small set of learned linear blendshapes driven by the tracker's expression vector. Each Gaussian stores a rest position expressed in the tangent-bitangent-normal (TBN) frame of its anchor triangle, a set of per-blendshape offsets in the same local frame, plus rotation, scale, opacity and spherical-harmonic coefficients (DC band in our setting). Triangle-local parameterization is key: any deformation of the underlying mesh - including a change of identity - is automatically propagated to the Gaussians through the triangle TBN, bypassing full re-optimization. Synthetic Dataset sec:method:dataset Training requires a large pool of triplets , each pairing a source identity and an edit prompt with the target identity realizing the prompted edit, densely covering both the identity manifold and the space of region-localized semantic edits. No public corpus pairs free-form prompts with identity-preserving shape deltas, and hand-annotating target meshes per subject does not scale. Our key design choice is to specify each edit once as a sparse set of 3D vertex displacements on the canonical mesh, rather than as a precomputed shape-coefficient target. Since all identities share the same topology, the same prototype can be projected onto any source identity by solving for the whose induced vertex motion best matches the prescribed displacements on that subject's deformed mesh, turning a small library of prototypes into a combinatorially large supervised set without per-subject mesh annotation. Scalable Generation.
